THE POTTER. lAN IT/IPITIILISHED POEM BY TILE LATH BENJAMIN GOUGH ) See the potter with the clay Working—working day by day, Labouring on with patient skill, lldoulding—shaping to his will: Vessels unto honour made Moulds he to a rainbow shade, Beautiful, and chastely bleat, For a royal palace meant. Gilded with a golden hue, Sparkling in cerulean blue, Starred with flashing gems of light, Tinted with vermillion bright. Man he wields his humbler art For the cottage or the mart, Furnishes the shining rows Which the frugal housewife shows. Moulding with untiring 'laid, See the industrious potter stand, Ever moulding, day by day, Working still the plastic clay. Workmen! wheresoe'er ye be, So it is with you and me: We are moulding every hour, Moulding with a dreadful power. Moulding character for time, Either wretched or sublime; As we mould, so shall we be • Moulded for eternity! As we shape our hearts and lives, So the future fails or thrives; God has giv'n us a free will, God bestows the moulding skill. Now another new year smiles, Up! and sanctify our toils! Now 'begin and put away All that mars the moulding clay.

Set the wheel in motion now, Sign the pledge, a new year's vow; All this year to moulding give, Work! and thus begin to live! Brother workmen! work and win; Fight against the power of sic; Be ye potters, and produce Vessels for the Master's use!
Tarittieo.

If thou desirest to be borne with, thou must bear also with others. If you are slandered, neve.* mind it; it will all come off when it is dry. No true woman, married or single, can be happy without some sort of domestic life. A curtain lecture is Werth all the sermons in the world for teaching the virtues of patience and long suffering.— W. Irving. You may wish to get a wife without a failing; but what if the lady, if you find her, happens to be in want of a husband of the same character. ‘laster : What made your cabsin stay so late last night ? —Servant : Faith, 8111-• he was afeard to go home, sur.— Master : Why didn't he go home earlier in the evening, then ?—Servant: Share an' it wasn't till it was late that he was afeard. An old Dutch tavern-keeper, who had his third wife, thus expresses his views of matrimony; "Veil, you see, de first time I married for love, dat vos goot; then I married for beauty, at vas goot, too, about as de first; die time I married for money, and this is petter as poth." A vigorous old fellow in Maine, who had lately 'buried his fourth wife, was accosted by an acquaintance, who, un- aware of his bereavement, asked, " How is your wife, Cap'n Plowjogger ?" To which the captain replied, with a per- fectly grave face, "Wall, to tell ye the trewth, I am kinder est of wives just naow." Not long since, a contemporary tells us, a gentleman was watching the process of packing some hundreds of wooden legs for exportation for the future benefit of the gallant soldiers of the Sultan. " Ah," quoth the moraliser, "these pieces of timber are but so many eloquent protests against the horrors of warfare !" "Exactly," said a bystander, " stump speechee !" The more one lives the more one learns to act towards people as if they were inanimate objects—Viz, to do what you can for them and to utterly disregard whether they are grateful or not. 'This is what God does to us. He lets His rain fall on the just and unjust. He never gets grati- tude, and is furthermore totally ignored in the ordinary circumstances of life.—General Gordon. At a school in the country, the sentence," Mary milks the cow," was given out to he parsed. The last word was disposed of as follows: —" Cow is a noun, feminine gender. singular number, third person, and stands for Mary." "Stands for Mary !" said the excited pedagogue; "how do you make that out ?" "Because," answered the intelligent pupil," if the cow didn't stand for Mary, how could Mary milk her 9" Having discovered, as he believes, that the sense of taste is more acute in the tongue than in the roof of the month, a Western economist tells the poor to put very little butter en their bread, and to hold the slice with the buttered sur- face undermost whi!et eating it. That nature intended it to be so held is Thorn by the fact that when a boy drops hie bread and butter it invariably strikes with the buttered side down. A clergyman who owns a farm found his ploughman sit- ting on his plough, resting his horses. Qaoth the clergy- man—" John, wouldn't it be a good plan for you to have a scythe here, and he cutting a few bashes along the fences while the horses are resting a short time 9" "Yes, sir," said John • " and,wadn't it be weel for you tee hoe a tub o' tttties in the poopit, and when the folk were aingin', peel them a while to he ready for the pat 9" RELATIVE VA LOB OF BEER AND BREAD.—Liebig, the famous chemist, stated, years ago, that " more real nourish- ment can be hid out of a five-pound loaf of bread than out of over 3,000 quarts of best beer." If the eighty million bushels of grain—the amount wasted by brewers and others every year in the manufacture of intoxicating liquors— were made into bread loaves, it is calculated that it would provide bread enough to supply every family in the king- dom with four 410. loaves every week all the year round. Another calculation has also been made, by which we ar- rive at the startling fact that two millions of persons could be provided with 21bs. of bread each day for a whole year. MANNERS Bereventa Boys.—There is a good deal of rude- ness between boos in their intercourse and bearing with one another that is not really intended as such; bat is not therefore any the less to be disapproved. It Is often simply the overflow of excessive high spirits. But the very best good humour, unrestrained by proper bounds and limitations, may become the most positive incivility. We often apologise for coarseness of people by saying " He means well." It is well we can make such an apology for them ; for if their radeness is really intentional they are not fit to be received into any worthy person's society. But they who mean well should also do well, and the ways of politeness are never so easily learned as in youth. The boy who is habitually coarse and rude in his bearing to- wards other boys will be such as a man towards men, and all his life will never gain the reputation of being a gentle-

man. THE PICTURESQUENESS OF THE CROW.—No landscape is clmplete without a line of crows. Look around you any- where in the country, be it the flat lowlands, the hilly slopes, or the gray links ; you will find the black line wing- ing the homeward flight when all other birds are silent, or pillaging in a sheep field, or a stubble field, or following the plough in dark do' a. Crows are everywhere, and they bring with them the seriousness northerners love. They are birds of rainy weather, and every wet day you are almost certain, in a country walk, to eee them on the move and hear their wings slowly flopping heavy with rain, and to notice how their dull voices harmonise with the gray sky and the brown fields. In summer they make the air eloquent with their loud din, and the evenings are drowsy with their dark bodies "athwart the concave of the dark blue dome." Our scenery is every- where covered with them. Their sober blackness brings out the colour of the loam, the delicate tints of spring, the mel- low ripeness of autumn, and the dead of winter. They are the commentators on our scenery and our seasons. They make a world of picturesque contrasts, and nowhere do they look out of place. They fit in naturally wherever they alight.—Good Words. SHOP WINDOWS.—Oar wives and our country cousins would have had no shop windows to amuse them had they lived, say, in the days of Queen Bess. A few stuffs dis- played in a gingerly manner at the open door of the fashion- able draper's shop, which might have a frontage as large as a modern huckster's, would be all that could be inspected in an afternoon's ramble. Scarcely any such :establishment such as it was, had a pavement in front of it, and to stop be- fore it was to incur the risk still incurred in such streets in Rome, of being splashed from top to toe with mud, if not !on over. Furthermore, on a rainy day, the spouts on the eaves Cr of the hones poured little cataracts of dirty water the I;iarisera by. To do your shopping in those days you o enter the mercer's den, and thus put yourself more directly in the way of his temptations. Even in the flays of Charles 11. a shop window was a rarity. In Queen Anne's time they were common, but a glance through llogarth's prints will show that they were dingy, ,pokey affairs, such as you might now find it a chandler enop . a Clare Market alley. The modern shop window may be maid to have come in with plate-glass. Plate-glass, from! the dwelling-house architect's point of view has been a worry. To the shopkeeper, however, plate-glass hasbeena revelation. It has given him large mirrors with which to Illuminate and extend the apparent space at his disposal in his windows. It has also opened up this space to the street public, by the actual outside glazing, so that the contents appear to belong almost as much to the thoroughfare as to the proprietor. The result is that the streets are turned into a vast milage of picture galleries, in which any taste may be suited, and any lioterer can dawdle from window to window to amuse himself. div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTICULTURE, &c.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

LAND TEAMSTER IN CANADA.—The people of Ontario aid other parts of C made are taking active steps to secure the adoptioa of a simpler mode of transfer of real estate. A large number of petitions have been presented to the On- tario Provincial Legislature in favour of such a change, and a bill is to be introduced into the Dominion Parliament this session with this object in view. REPAYMENT OF INCOME-TAX TO LANDLORDS.—Accord- I ing to a Parliamentary return just issued of the repayment of income-tax (schedule A) under certain conditions to landlords wsose farms have been thrown on hand, the amount repaid in the year 1881-2 was £2,328 on 99,521 acres. In 1882-3 the acreage was 51,617, and the amount repaid £1,374. The return is confined to England, Scot- land, and Wales. " Tata GOOD OLD Tistas."—Here is a remarkable illae- tration given in a New Year's sermon (1884) describing a country parish some 50 years ago. It was then a community of paupers !--and of a population under 100, more than 60 (inc(uding the children of the able-bodied) were receiving parochial relief. The expenditure, exceeding the total rental of the parish, forced all the land out of cultivation, causing a parochial bankruptcy, and the poor to be main- tained by rates in aid levied on other parishes! But there- after a great change for the better occurred, brought about by the allotment system, and now there is but one pauper (a paralytic) in the Union house. A RECORD OF SERVICH.—A correspondent writes:—" In these days of short service, the following is worthy of re- cord :—A service, in each case reaching over half-a-century, has just been brought to a close through the death of three faithful servants in the employment of Mr. Papillon, of Crowhurst Park, Sussex, and Leaden Manor, Essex. James Head, for 60 years head gardener at Leaden Manor, and five years previously in the same capacity with another member of Mr. Papillon's family, making up a service of 65 years in the same family, died January 12th, aged 85. Samuel Saxby, five years estate carpenter, and 50 years bailiff and woodreeve at Crowhurst Park, died February 3rd, aged 82; and on the same day, aged 77, James Saxby, for 60 years sawyer on the same estate." Tins Pinar HEREFORD.-111 a pamphlet written by Mr. R. Jasper More,in connection with the Shrewsbury meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society, that gentleman states that near the Lydham Heath railway station is to be found a herd of the old smoky-faced Montgomery cattle, "the aborigines of the jclistrict," from which the Herefords are said to have been derived. In reference to this, Mr. More says :—" There is a local "story that the Snit Hereford having sprung as a lusus naturce from the smoky-faced Montgomeryshire cattle alluded to, the farmer having or- dered the white-faced and etherwise red calf to be killed, his daughter begged its life for a pet, and that from tithe ' Hereford descended. Another version is that the calf was preserved by a cowman, who fancied the appearance of the calf." A MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND AGRICULTURE.—At a meeting of the Associated Chambers of Commerce held in London on Wednesday, on the motion of SirJacot:Behrens, seconded by Mr. Sampson Lloyd, it was resolved, after a short discussion, by a large majority :—" That, whilst ac- knowledging the good effects already experienced from the extension of the Board of Trade functions in the direction of improved trade legislation, this Association must once I more place upon record their conviction that no re-arrange- ment of Ministerial duties will be satisfactory which does not give to the Minister of Commerce and Agriculture a position in the Cabinet equal to that of his colleagues, and the power to give effect to the measures which he may pro- pose in the interests of the great industries, for.which he is especially responsible." ENSILAGE IN INDIsa--40 August last a pit, 20 feet wide and 10 feet deep, was used at Kirkee as a silo. It was filled with upwards of 60 tons of green Jowari and Bajri stalks. These were cut when the plants were in flower, and with the produce of 12 acres the bundles were packed as tightly as possible, and were kept in their place by heavy weights, consisting of iron sheets and large stones; a pressure was thus obtained, equal to about 2001bs. per square foot. The silo was opened on January 16th, in the presence of Mr. Oyanne, Director of Agricultute for Bombay, and a large number of gentlemen. The upper lavers for a few inches deep were decayed, but all below was Of a dark green colour, and emitted a strong acid smell, similar to that given off by stored grain in a brewery. Some of the forage was offered to a number of bullocks, who ate it with relish. It is said that the result will be much better if the stalks are cut into small pieces by a chaff-cutter. A LANDLORD'S Tarca.—A tenant farmer writes to the Mark Lane Express :—" Permit me' through your columns, to call the attention of my brother farmers to what appears to be a landlord's trick to evade the operation of the Agri- cultural Holdings Act, 1883, trusting it may prove a warn- ing. A friend of mine lately received a new agreement, which he was requested to sign and return upon very short notice. As it gave compensation for unexhausted improve- ments, he was at first disposed to look upon it with approval, but having a quantity of land which he was anxious to lay down to grass he naturally looked out for the security it provided, when, lo and behold! there was a penalty unless he had two-thirds of it under grass He thereupon wrote to his landlord, stating that he was quite willing to come op to that standard providing he gave his written consent to do so. This has since been refused; thus it has become evident what the landlord's motive was. I have seen this agreement, and I do not hesitate to affirm that under it it would be quite easy for a landlord to recoup himself for any compensation which he would have to pay by imposing fines for liquidated damages to double the amount of compensa- tion. As there is probably another scene in this little drama, I withhold for the present the landlora's name." HOUSING Pros.—Ten Berkshire pigs, five in a warm barn basement and five outside, have recently been the subjects of experiments by Professor Shelton, of the Kansas Agri- cultural College, the results showing that farmers and others who neglect to furnish their swine with suitable artificial protection against cold weather must supply protection of another kind in the shape of fuel for the "internal fires" of the animal. The pigs within the barn consumed 2,877A1b5. of corn, and those without 2,8441b5., the increase respectively being 6041b5. and 4781b5. The coat of lib. of increase in the barn was 4.761b5. of corn against 5 951bs. for the like quan- tity of increase by those outside. During the cold period the pigs outside expended nearly one-half the food they consumed in keeping their bodies warm, and they gave dur- ing every week of the experiments less of total gain and gain per cwt. than those inside the barn. In these as in other experiments, the Professor observed that the quietest pigs and the " best feeders" ate the best, suffered least from cold, and gave the largest return for the food consumed. We have often urged the necessity of warmth in styes, al- though we cannot find that the majority of breeders appre- ciate it; but it ought to be better understood that, failing artificial warmth,'the animal appropriates heat from a por- tion of its food which ought to make meat instead. OATS AS • HAY CROP. —" New Zealander" writes : "On many farms where red clover is uncertain there is a difficulty in providing sufficient hat; for winter use, and I would suggest that a few acres of oats be sown for the pur- pose of making them into hay, as we do in this country. All kinds of stock are very fond of it, and in my opinion it is little if at all inferior to the average of grass or clover hay in quality. We mostly sow Black Tartarian oats, as they do not grow so coarse a straw as some other sorts, and rather more seed is used than if intended for a corn crop. We allow the oats to attain their full growth, but cut them ' before they show signs of ripening. Oaten hay requires to be more thoroughly made than grass or clover. Instead of being better for getting warm in the stack, it loses quality by becoming dusty, and, instead of smelling sweet, the scent will be unpleasant. It will be found that oaten hay does not take the harm from rain that grass or clover does. If cut at the stage of growth I have indicated oats are not sup- posed to exhaust the soil much. Of course clover is a better preparation for after-corn crops, but lam fully convinced that Italian rye-grasY, which is often used to make up the proper proportion of hay, leaves most of the land that I am acquainted with in far worse condition than oats will if cut green. For amount of food per acre the oats are better." APOPLEXY IN SHEBP.—To fat two-teeth sheep and to get 1 them off early they must necessarily have a very liberal allowance of corn and cake, and I have seldom known a flock so fatted without several dying of apoplexy. I have fatted two-teeth sheep myself for many years, and when towards the spring they begin to show signs of apoplexy (which by great attention can sometimes be seen, the most marked symptoms being staggering in their walk, or refus- ing to come to the troughs when the corn or cake is put in), I have found that copious bleeding from the eye will gener- ally save them. But they will sometimes die without any symptoms being seen. As a general rule, it is better to give the whole flock an entire change oe food, but at this time of the year this is not always practicable. Under these cir- cumstances, take off about half their corn or cake for a week or two, and then gradually increase it till they kayo their full quantity again. I have adopted this plan many times with very good effect. When las fatting a flock of sheet) I never like to have more than 100 in each fold, as each one is then more likely to have its fair 'share of corn. When there is a larger number together, the first troughs are gener- ally nearly or quite emptied before ,the shepherd has put the corn in the last one, and soros of the sheep get much more than their fair share, and it is generally these fattest sheep that are attacked with apoplexy.—George Bing, of Potterne,in the "Salisbury Journal." ANarnER CATTLE DISEASES BILL—The following is a copy of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, Amendment Bill, brought in by Mr. James Howard, Mr. Borlase, and Mr. Duckham :—(1) From and after the Rais- ing of this Act the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act,lB7B, shall be read and construed as though the provisions follow- ing were inserted in and formed part of Section 22 of the said Act, that is to say :—(1) A local authority shall in ease of any fresh outbreak of foot and mouth disease in a dia- trict which has been or declared to be free of the disease, cause all animals affected with such disease to be slaughtered within two days after the existence of the disease is known to them. (2) A local authority may, if they think fit, cause any animals being, or having been, in the same shed or herd, or in contact, with animals affectel with foot and month toeisrt of eeasdeb, to be slaughtered. (3) The local authority shall, u ythtehleoircalordraetre, such,pay compensation for animals value egohf im - the animals immediately before they were w.: la vided, nevertheless, that in the case of animsalesu gthheetepid of which shall have b slaughtered; . een recorded in any public herd or flock book, the value of • such animals shall be estimated apart from pedigree so recorded. (4) The local authority may, upon an application by the owner f affected with foot and mouth disease,mje .1 flock or herd writing to the clerk of the local authority, suspend the order for slaughter, and shall in that ease forthwith call upon the police authority' ta establish an efficient cordon round the infected acefo

(5) The local authority shall, before ordering the establish- ment of a cordon, require the owner of the flock or herd to give an. undertaking to pay a moiety of the expense in- carted, and the local authority shall, out of the local rate, pay the other moiety. The following explanation is printed with the bill :—The object of this bill is to provide for more vigorous and uniform action upon the part of local authori- ties in case of future outbreaks of foot and mouth disease. The principle of the Act of 1878, in respect of slaughter and compensation upon outbreaks of pleuro-pneumonia is adopted, with modifications to prevent the necessity for slaughter in the case of pedigree or other exceptionally valuable herds Of flocks. An outbreak of contagious disease it is maintained should be treated like the occurrence of a fire, and the centre rigorously watched until all danger of ' the disease spreading has passed away. It is believed that ' if the provisions of the accompanying bill are properly carried out, the country may enjoy an immunity from the ' disease which has hitherto caused so much loss and incon- venience to the farmers of the United-Kingdom.
THE ASHTON CHARITIES. SENELEY GREEN GRAMMAR SCHOOL NEW
SCHEME.

On Wednesday afternoon a special meeting of the trustees of the Ashton Charities was held at the Local Board Offices, Bryn-street, Ashton, for the purpose of conferring with Mr. Durnford, assistant Charity Commissioner, on the provi- sions of a scheme to be established for the regulation, &C., of Seneley Green Grammar School, in accordance with the 32nd clause of tile scheme of 18th March, 1881. In addi- tion to Mr. Durnferd, there were also present at the confer- ence the Rev. W. J. Melville (in the chair), the Rev. H. Siddall, Dr. Hannah, Messrs. J. Gaskell, T. D. Grimke, Clarke, C. H. Astle, W. Valiant, Lives- ley, Knowles, Crompton, and James Hill (clerk).— The CHAIRMAN (the Rev. W. J. Melville) said that the trustees were prepared with a scheme for the management of the school, which had been suggested and gone through at a meeting of the whole body of trustees, who came to t a unanimous conclusion as regarded the &tails laid before - them. It had been thought that it would facilitate matters if the scheme was placed before Mr. Durnford, who could deal with it as he thought best.—Mr. DURNFORD said the Charity Commissioners were of opinion that the present as a favourable opportunity for considering the establishment of a scheme for the school under the 32nd clause of the Charitable Trusts Act. He believed the present school was some distance from the great bulk of the population, and it would have to be considered whether the buildings should be placed nearer to that class of people whose children would be likely to attend the school. ' Evidence went to show that the present school was incon- venient for the inhabitants, and perhaps the trustees would see their way to erect one in a more suitable place. What the amount likely to be derived from the old school would be was a matter which he should very much like to hear something about. He supposed they were agreed that the school be established within the meaning of the 32nd Clause. With regard to the obligations cast upon them they would have to provide scholarships for boys under the old conditions from the apprentice money. If they took that money they must have due regard to scholarships for toys of that class who would be likely to be entitled to that charity, and he thought there would be no difficulty in establishing such scholarships as would satisfy the Commissioners and the conditions of the original deed.—Mr. HILL, in answer to Mr. Durnford, said there had been no Apprentice Stock Charity for three years —Mr. Caoatrrox remarked that it did not follow that there would be no applications in the future.—The CHAIRMAN said the present system of education obviattd in a great measure the necessity for making apprentices.—Mr. VALIANT : Parents will not have their children boand.—Mr. Durtagroan said

it would appear that the object of the trustees was the ap- plication of the Apprentice Stock Charity to purposes of education.—The CHAtnerew said that was so. It was not as if the money was being used for purposes of no benefit at all. They would be able to get as mach if not a larger bene- fit from the money, only it would be through a different channel.—Mr. DURNFORD said that would depend upon the trustees signing a formal document for the application of the apprentice money for the purposes of education. If they found that the majority of the trustees declined to sign it the Charity Commissioners could not proceed in the matter. —The CRAIRMAN : I think it will be found that a very con- siderable majority of the trustees will sign it —Mr. DURN. I FORD said the trustees would have to make formal applica- cation for including apprentice stock to the purposes of edu- catidn. The CHAIRMAN said the only objec- tion there seemed to be against it was some groundless fear that there might be some future demand for the money which was not made at the present time.—Mr CnomProx : A portion of it—there is a possi- bility of it.—The Rev H SIDDALL : The experience of the past for a considerable number of years has been that the money has net been required.—Mr DURNFORD said he un- derstood so. He would assume that the whole of the ap- prentice stock, £lOO, would be available for the scheme, be- sides which they had £97 15s ad income from the Grammar School, including interest on consols. In round numbers, therefore, the Trustees would have about £2OO at disposal for the purposes of education. —The meeting then proceeded to discuss the proposed new scheme in detail, the CHAIRMAN remarking that the great bulk of the clauses were copied from a scheme supplied by the Charity Commissioners.—At the close a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Durnford for the kind manner in which he had conducted the inquiry.—In responding Mr. BORN- Tour, Raid he was much obliged to them for their expres- sions of thanks. He hoped that good results might follow the application of the new scheme which would benefit the township generally. He should use his best endeavours to get it pushed forward before the Charity Cummiasioners. Although the bands of the Commissioners were full at pre- sent he would endeavour to get their scheme pushed for- ward as rapidly as possible. (Hear, hear.)—The conference then concluded.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnighly meeting of this Board of Guardians was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday,Mr. William Tyrer presiding. There were also present Messrs. W. New- some, R. Leigh, T. Dobell, John Matthews, J. T. Hall, W. Birehall, W. Gore, Ashton, Edward Syder, Henry Hulme, William Gerrard, W. Uilbody, P. Longton. MASTER'S REPORT.

The Worm:rousts MASTER reported that there were 487 inmates in the Workhouse, compared with 477 the previous week, and 590 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 167 boys and girls in Kirkdale schools. Forty- four vagrants had been relieved during the past week, as compared with 50 in the corresponding period of last year. There were 301 inmates sleeping in the Workhouse

div.p: NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.
NIONTHLY MEETING.

A monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Come missioners was held at the Town Hall on Monday afternoon wh,n there were present—Messrs. W. F. Gooch (in the chair), T. J. Gillespie. J. E. Parlcy, B. B. Glover, J. W. Emmett, James Fairclougb, norms Hunt, and T. Forster; J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (cur- -1 Yeyor).

SCHOOL A.TTENDANCE. At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, held on the 18th February, the School Attendance Officer read his report, and the Chairman examined the attendance book as to irregulars. The parents of several children were called before the committee and cautioned for their children's a:-.• sence from school. The following report was read for the quarter ending December;—Number of school children on the books 2,280, last quarter 2,292, loss 22; average attend- ance 1,781, or 781 per cent; last quarter 1,773, or 771, be- ing a gain of Bin the average attendance, and in the per- centage.—The minutes were confirmed.

HIGHWAYS, EVELIO- WORKS, AND SANITARY COMMITTER. A meeting of this committee was held on the 18th ult., , when the medical officer attended to read his annual report for the year 1883. After some discussion the same was adopted, excepting that portion having reference to the , deposit on land between Park-road and the brook. The following tenders were read for the removal of nightsoil : William Ellam £340, Richard Hunt £4OO, and Wm. Gorse £425, per annum. It was ordered that the tender of Wm 111 am at £340 a year be accleted for three years on his giving two approved sureties for the carrying out of the same according to specifications and conditions, and that a proper contract be prepared by the Law Clerk. The Sur- veyor reported the removal of a boy from the Reformatory School to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at Warrington on the 15th February, certified by the medical officer to be suffering from enteric fever. Plans for engineering works for Messrs. J. Slee and Co.; two cottages, War ,rave- road, for John Hateblett; alterations to premises in Market-street, for Williem Hill ; two •vottages in Legh-street, for J. Sharp and D. Forrester; and six cot- tages in Legh-street for Mr. Chadwick were submitted and approved. A plan for alteration to house in Park-road, by Mr. E. T. Evans, was referred back for better accommoda- tion to back prenaiees.—Mr. PARDRY said that with regard to the non-confirmation of a portion of the Medical Officer's report, he thought some explanation should be given. They all knew that the Medical Officer's report had been printed and circulated before the public. In it a statement appeared that there had been a deposit of noxious and offensive matter on the premises of Messrs. Birley. They had not confirmed that portion of the report, however, because instead of being noxious matter it was simply rubbish put in to fill up a large hollow. It was only fair to Messrs. Burley that the explanation should be given and go forth to the public, because every Commissioner present was satis- fied that there was no noxious matter. He was sure the Medical Officer did not make the report from what he had seen, but on the statement of ether persons. —Mr. EMMETT asked if the sureties for the removal of the nightsoil had been found satisfactory.— Mr. BRIERLEY reported that on the previous Saturday two names had been brought to him as sureties, and they were attached to the agreement.—Mr. WORSLEY : They were William Berry, of St. Helens, and George Burrows, of New- ton.—Mr. BRIERLEY thought they were quite satisfactory. —1 he minutes were then confirmed.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTER. A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the 18th ult. The gas works carbonizing account for the past month gave fuel used 301 tons 9 cwt,, and the gas made 3,018,000 feet; averaging 10,009 feet per ton of fu,l used. Mr. Brierley reported the necessity for additional coal storage accommodation at the gasworks, whereon Messrs. Glover, Gooch, T. Hint, and Emmett were appointed a special committee to consider the same. It was ordered that the selling price of gas coke and other materials be left in the hands of Mr. Brierley.-0a the motion of Mr. EMMETT, seconded by Mr. PARDEY, the minutes were passed. FINANCE COMMITTEE: TRIO NEW CEMETERY.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the 18th February, the SURVEYOR reported that he had submitted the "Main roads" accounts under the Highways and Locomotive Act, 1878. to the district auditor at Warrington, on Wed- nesday, the 13th February, and that in the presence of Mr. Johnson, of Preston, the county auditor, he had certified them correct. The Surveyor submitted a statement of the loan for private improvements, with an estimate of the work not yet carried out. The committee recommend that £2,000 be cancelled on the private improvement loan, and a further sum of £3,000 be taken up, making £5,000 for cemetery purposes at 4t per cent interest with the Economic Life Assurance Society, for 30 years, repayable by annual equal payments. Accounts amounting to £306 5s id were examined and passed for payment.—After the minutes had been passed, Mr. GILLESPIE asked: Can we legally take £2,000 from the improlement fund for the purposes of a cemetery ?—Mr. WORSLEY replied that they could not, and that was the reason why they had adopted the new plan as mentioned in the minutes. The application to the Local Government Board for the transfer of balances from one fund to another was not granted, but while he (Mr.Worsley) and Mr. Brierley were in London they thought something might be done by asking the Economic Assurance Company to accept the repayment of £2,000 of the loan on the improvement account, and then lend the same amount with £3,000, or whatever. more was required, on the cemetery account. That was perfectly legal, and it could be done. He had alai to report that he and Mr. Brierley attended Me the Local Government Board for the purpose of endeavouring to get them to change the area aed positicn of the land for the cemetery. After an interview with Mr. Forster, secretary, the Inspector who in- spected the site, and Sir Robert Itawlinson, the sanction was given. The area of the land had been reduced, the site a little altered, and the same amount of money sanctioned as was previously given. After that they went to Messrs. Lee, Houseman, and Boody, solicitors to Mr. Lest), with the draft of the agreement for the land in order to get that matter put in band at once. They had a conversation with Mr. Housemad as to possession. He was not enabled then to answer anything definitely, but the draft was settled, and he (Mr. Houseman) said he would write them as to possession. He (Mr. Worley) had since received a letter stating that they could have immediate possession of the land on paying a' deposit of £l4O, and also five per cent, interest on the balance of the purchase money until it was all paid off according to the agreement. As the agreement had been signed by Mr. Legh'e trustees he (Mr. Worsley) had pre- pared a counter part which only required signing by two members of the Board.—Mr. GLOVER moved that the agree- ment be signed as suggested, and Mr. HUNT seconded the motion, which was passed.—After some further discussion Mr. Gwynn. moved, Mr. HUNT seconded, and it was decided that a cheque for £l4O be drawn up and paid to Mr. Legh's trustees as part of the agreement for taking possession of the land.—With regard to the loan from the Economic Life Assurance Company, the Lew CLERK said that he and Mr. Brierley had waited upon the company with regard to the £5,000 required for cemetery purposes. He had since received a letter saying that subject to certain •arrangernents being carried out to the satisfaction of the society's solicitors they would consent to accept repayment of MPG, and would re-lend that amounf with additional sums amounting to IA 000 when required; to be repaid by annual instal- ments during 30 years at di per cent per annum.—Mr. GLOVER asked what interest they were at present paying for the £2,000 they proposed to repay and reborrow.—Mr. BRIRRLEY said they were paying di per cent ut present, and hey agreed to reborrow it on the same terms—The sub- ject afterwards dropped; and, as there was no other busi- ness, the Eoard rose.
RA
SAD OCCURRENCE AT ASYLUM.

A LUNATIC KILLED-IN.-A-ITT-E.-SIFTING TO ESCAPE An inquest was held on Tuesday at Rainhill Asylum, by Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, on the body of John O'Rourke, 32 years of age who died on Friday evening last from injuries sustained by falling from a window in the asylum. Before proceeding with the evidence the Coroner requested that the jury should be allowed to view the scene of the accident, and Dr. Roberts, the medical superintendent of the asylum, courteously conducted all present who were interested in the inquiry to the place.—On returning, Thos. Weaver, an attendant, was called. He said he was in charge of No. 2 Ward, to which the deceased was admitted .011 the 6th October, 1882. On Friday last, about half-past one o'clock, he was in the gallery, when he heard a noise as at glass falling, and, turning round, he saw deceased halfway through a pane of glass in a window about twenty yards from him. The pane was about fifteen inches by eleven inches. He ran to the place, calling oat to the patients to atop deceased, but when he got there he could only just touch deceased's fact ere he fell through and dropped on his bead on the mould beneath. In answer to the coroner, witness said that under- neath all the gallery windows, with the exception et this one, there was either the glass of the conservatory or the asphalte. Deceased had never before attempted to escape. When the door bad been opened he had tried to push past the doctor and attendant, but nothing more. He was quite a harmless lunatic. All the attendants were in their proper places when deceased got through the window.— Alfred Flack, another attendant, who was in charge of the day-room, gave corroborative evidence. He said he was just in time to see deceased's boots going out of the window, but not in time to save him,—Dr. Rogers said deceased was admitted to the asylum on the 28th September, 1881, from the West Derby Union., 'Nothing was known about him; he seemed to have no friends, and nobody ever came to visit him. Witnesa thought deceased was trying to escape. He never exhibited suicidal tendency. Witness then de- posed to seeing him immediately after he was picked up by the last witness. The only thing he could pos- sibly detect then was a fracture of the breastbone Deceased was exceedingly restless, and would not allow them to cut his coat off. He died about ten o'clock the earns night. A post-mortem examination was made, and it was found that in addition to the injury to the breastbone there was an injury to the spine—the spinal cord was com- pletely severed, and death was inevitable.—The jury re- turned a verdict that deceased met with his death acciden- tally whilst attempting to escape through the window.—Dr. Rogers afterwards stated to the jury that deceased aeern4 to have had a kind of mania that he was to run away; and in some cases men would run away from their own homed just as well as from asylums when they were possessed with such a mania.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

The wet weather we have experienced had become obstructive to most garden operations, and more especially in low or ill-drained positions and where the soil is of clayey nature. It is useless under such circumstances to attempt meddling with the ground. The last day or two has allowed us to plant a few Mona's Pride potatoes on a well-sheltered border facing the west; here they are not forced out of the ground so soon as on a border facing south or south-east, and for that reason are not so liable to be destroyed by the frost. The departing rays of a setting sun play on a westerly aspect, so that the temperature there does not descend to the freezing point for some hours after it has elsewhere. Another advantage derived from an easterly screen is that the first rays of the sun do not strike on the plants, which is most disastrous when they are in a frozen state. In planting this time, our mode of proceeding has been to take out a trench at one end and wheel it to the other, and then we dig a space about 21t. wide, and in front of it stretch the line and make a perpendicular cut fin. deep, which forms a channel for the row of sets placed Bin. distant, with the sprouts upwards, which are covered over with the most friable portion of the soil. Digging is con. tinned another two feet or a few inches more, so as to allow space for the line to rest upon, as well as something to cut to form the cavity for the sets. We make no attempt to , break the soil between the rows, preferring to leave that for nature to do. .

PEAS should be sown as soon as the weather and the 'state of the soil will permit. Our first were sown last year on the 26th February, and very well they did. We attempted to get them in last week, as the weather was mild, but we were so pelted with the rain, and the soil so stack toourghoes, that we had to give it up till we get the surface a little dryer. Though we provide ourselves with a board or two that will reach across the border to stand upon when draw- ing the drills and sowing the seed, it is not a pleasant task under such conditions. The distance between the rows of peas should be regulated by the nature and richness of the soil. On poor sandy soils they seldom exceed the height usually given in nurserymen's seed catalogues. With as, those, whose height is fixed at 3ft. run up quite 6ft. We therefore have to allow nearly that space between each row. Various experiments have been resorted to, to prevent mice burrowing in the earth and devouring the seeds, but we have seen nothing so effectual as red lead, used as follows: Place the peas in a water-tight vessel, and pour a small quantity of water over them. Give them a few shakes; then pour out any water that may be visible in the bottom, and take two or three good pinches of red lead and sprinkle it over them. Give them another shake or two, and it will be found that the whole will be more or less covered with the lead, and it is easy to cover them wholly by adding water and lead as required; and they can be sown as soon as they are done. Our favourite sort for the first crop is William ' the First—a green marrow pea of excellent quality, and a most prolific bearer. Suttons' Ringleader and Sangster's No. I are two good standard kinds that have been in culti- vation for years, and might have a place where more than one variety is sown. CELERY, for an early batch, should be sown in a box, and placed in a slight hotbed with a frame over it. The soil should be light and rich, and made tolerably fine, more espe- cially the upper portion. It is seldom we find any celery fail to germinate ; it is, therefore, needless to sow it too thick. Last year we tried several sorts, and we found Troughton's Prizetakers (red and white) equal to any and far superior to some; whilst his "Ne Plus Ultra" was sound and good three weeks after six others had had become use- less in consequence of their centre decaying. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The surface of the soil in the borders and beds has been beaten nearly smoodeby the rain; it will be therefore advisable to snatch the first opportunity to either run the hoe over them or slightly fork them. This

will improve the appearance of the beds as well as benefit the plants by admitting sun and air into the soil to sweeten it and increase its temperature. If there are any gaps in the rows of such spring-flowering subjects as Wallflowers, Silene, and Forget-me-not, they should be made up at once. We are at a loss how to account for the paucity of the latter in cottage gardens. It requires no skill or care, and if left alone it would cover a moderate-sized front garden in two or three years. The Lily of the Valley is another plant treated with the greatest indifference, and yet most people love and admire its flowers, so much so that we have known ladies to giver from is. to is. 6d. for each spray of the flowers at Christmas-time. As several roots can be bought for a few pence, there is no reason why every cottager pos- sessed of a front garden should not e.ijoy his Lily of the Valley at its natural season of flowering. The roots or crowns of this plant are, as a rule, planted too thick; in fact, as thick as they can be. We plant our strongest crowns 3in. distant, the others a trifle closer; treated in this way, they throw up strong sprays the second year after planting, and in two or three more years they become crowded and require thinning, which we usually do this month and transplant in moderately rich ground. THE WlNlDOW.—Faoheias that have made half an inch or so of growth should be turned out of their pots and the greater portion of the soil shook away and some of the longest roots cut off. The pots for their reception should be thoroughly cleaned—not wiped, but washed, and al'owed to get perfectly dry before they are used. To grow the plants well, they should have good, sweet soil to root into. Three-parts loam, one leaf mould, with one-eighth of the whole of coarse sand, will be a suitable compost, and it may be still improved by adding bone meal at the rate of two or three pinches to every quart of soil. This may appear a modicum, but it must be remembered that bone meal is very powerful and will poison the soil to such an extent as to kill the plant if too freely used. Hyacinths will now have filled their pots with roots, and should be treated to an occasional dose of liquid manure. The best way is to apply it alternately with clear water after the first applica- tion or two. We have on previous occasions referred to the best kind of stimulants in a liquid state, and we need only add that soot-water is excellent if there is a disposition to make too much foliage, otherwise guano-water may be used. Plenty of fresh air will prevent the foliage getting in ad- vance of the flower spike. To keep the latter erect, attend to turning it round, and as it progresses place a stick in the pot and tie the spike loosely to it.

Parsons, the lawyer, was lame—one leg being shorter than the other. Limping up to Curran, he inquired for a brother barrister who was similarly affected. "Curran, did you iee M6Nally going this way ?" "Why," replied Curran, "I never saw him going any other way." A well-known Judge came late to court, although in busy session ; whereat his clerk, in great surprise, inquired of him the reason. "A child was born," his Honour said, "and I'm the happy sire." An infant Judge ?" "Oh, no," said he ; "as yet he's but a crier." "Your daughter? It is impossible. Why, you look more like twin sisters." "No ; I assure you she is my only diughter," replied the pleased mother. And the polite old gentleman spoiled it all by remarking, "Well, she certainly look old enough to be your sister." When the corn is nearly ripe, it bows the head and stoops lower than when it was green. In like manner, when the people of God are near ripe for heaven, they grow more humble and self-denying than in the days of their earlier development. A religious man in the progress of his know- ledge and grace is like a vessel cast into the sea--the more it fills, the deeper it sinks.—RaveL RESPONSIBILITY OF nrs FRA.NCUISE.—The municipal and political franchise is a trust; it is to be used, not for private but for public purposes. If in appointing an am- bassador to Paris, St. Petersburg, or Berlin, the Prime Minister and the Foreign Secretary were influenced by im- proper motives; if they appointed a man, not because they thought that on the whole he was the best man available for the post, but because he was an old friend; or if they recalled one ambassador and sent out another on the ground of personal pique, and to gratify personal resentment; or if a man obtained the appointment by giving splendid enter- tainments to his political patrons or friends; it would be a public scandal. If he obtained it by a bribe—by a bribe given in any form—by a heavy subscription, for instance, to the election fund of the Carlton or the Reform Club—it would be a public crime. But the same moral laws that govern the exercise of political patronage, govern the exer- cise of the franchise. If in a municipal or a political con- test you vote for a man for no other reason than that he is a friend or a neighbour, and it would not be pleasant to dis- oblige him; or because the rival candidate passed you in the street without speaking to you, or omitted to invite you to a dinner party, or forgot to tell his wife that your daugh- ters were to be asked to a dance—this is a clear violation of public duty. If you vote for a man for no other reason than that he has subscribed to a hospital, or a school, or a church, in which you happen to be interested, or because he sustained your application for some public office; if. you refuse to vote for him because he told the manager of the bank of which he happens to be a director to refuse to in- crease your "over-draw," or because he gives you no orders for coals or meat—this is positive corruption.—" Public ds of cases, be,•ause it contains more nutri- Essence In thouean W.propfea.lieo,n :2neG,ooovid Words."orderig Cadbury's Cocoa Duty," T h:by medicalß. div.head: MR. HARRISON'S AccouNrs.
div.p: MR. HARRISON'S AccouNrs.

The CLERK said a meeting of the Finance Committee had been called to take into consideration the accounts of Mr. Harrison, the late relieving officer, bat, as only Mr. New- some and Mr. Lowe attended, no business could be proceeded with. With respect to Mr. Harrison's accounts, he (the Clerk) thought the Guardians ought to require Mr. Harrison to make up his accounts and lay them before the Guardians at a time to be fixed by them a true and complete account of moneys and other matters to his charge on bshalf of the Union in such a form as he would have to produce them before the auditor at the end of the current half-year. He (the clerk) might explain that on this being no committee meeting, on Tuesday last he advised Mr. Harrison that it would be desirable for him to pay the tradesmen to whom orders had been issued in the shape of food tickets out of the money belonging to the Guardians he has in his hands.— Mr. Harrison had in his hands £l4 15s Id, and there were about LW owing to tradesmen which had not been paid by Mr. Harrison within the time allowed by the Guardians. If the tradesmen were paid they would have got their money, while in the event of the auditor disallowing these sums it I would fall upon the officer. In the event of Mr. Harrison not paying these sums the Guardians could pay them and debit them to his account.—Mr. DOBELL moved that Mr. Harrison should be requested to make up his accounts be. fo:e next meeting, and this was agreed to

A MISTAKEN CLAIM. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. Harris, solicitor to the Liverpool Incorporated Trades Protection Society, making a claim of £2 l3s. 7d. on behalf of Messrs. F. Harrington and Sons, Liverpool, as damage done to a vehicle. It seemed from what he (the clerk) could gather that a van belonging to Messrs. Harrington had been passing through Hale town- ship when one of the wheels got into a hole in the road and one of the shafts was broken. It was thought that the Guirdians were liable for this damage, but he had written back to say that the Guardians were not the highway authority for that district, but no notice seemed to have been taken of that letter. It was tlireatened that unless the claim was paid by twelve o'clock last Saturday proceedings would be taken, but these proceedings had not yet been commenced. He (the clerk) asked for instructions to resist any claim which might be urged.—These instructions were given.
WIFE DESERTION IN THE UNION.
In asking for authority to take action against certain defaulters the CLERK mentioned that at the present time they had an enormous number ef deserted wives in the Union.

A letter was read from Mr. Dennett, of Pres-cOt,-On behalf of the Butchers' Association, asking the Board to sign a petition to be sent to the House of Commons against the amendments made by the House of Lords in the "Act to Amend the Contageous Diseases (Animals) Act,lB7B."—The Rev. Father FINEGAN thought the petition ought to be signed as, if the Bill was passed, it would b 3 a serious thing. —The CHAIRIBAN said that personally he was ia favour of the petition.—On the suggestion of Mr. DOBELL the petition was sent round for Guardians to sign if they thought fit.

The CLERK asked that cheques should be signed for £1.600, which, he said, was the amount to be paid for legal expenses and witnesses in connection with the late appeal by the London and North-Western Railway Company against the assessments—The Rev. Father FINEGAN commented upon the largeness of this sum, but after a little discussion the cheques were signed.—This concluded the business.

A VSHY KEMANYABLH WOMAN.—The Bridport (Dorset) Times tells the following astounding story medical gentleman of Eastbourne has received a letter from a woman residing in that town, who is totally armless, she having , been, at the time of her birth, through a freak of nature, minus those useful appendages. Being without arms she is of course without bands, yet, marvellous to relate, she manages to write with her feet, and as a specimen of—we were going to say hand-writing, but suppose we must term it caligraphy or penmanship,—the one before us is remark- ably clear, readable, and good, particularly for ajperson in her humble position in life, and no one would ever imagine tont that it had been written by hand. Stranger and more curious still is the fact that she is married, has a family, performs her domestic duties, nurses her babies, threads her needle, sews, cooks, makes puddings and pastry, and all with the aid ,of her feet alone, and the house is kept in creditable order, and Would shame many a housewife who is blessed with all her limbs, but is without the heart to care for tidi- ness and home comforts.

THE PROPOSED COTTON MILL FOR EARLESTOWN. MEETING AT EARLESPOWN LAST NIGHT. The proposal to establish a company for erecting and carrying on a cotton mill in the neighbourhood of Earles- town has evoked the greatest interest in the town. All classes of the community have discussed the matter, and the suggestion seems to meet with the approval of the inhabi- tants generally. Mr. Thomas Molyneux, of Market-street, lEarlestown, has announced a meeting for next Monday evening in St. John's School-room, at which he will explain a scheme for securing a mill. Last evening (Thursday) a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of the tradesmen and workingmen of Earlestown was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, The gathering was hurriedly called by handbills, which contained the following :—" Contemplated cotton mill for Earlestown. In accordance with the ex- pressed desire of a large number of persons at a meeting held in the Viaduct Institute, on February 23rd, 1884, a preliminary meeting in favour of the above object will take place in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening, when all those desirous of furthering the same are respectfully invited to attend, and give it their presence and suppert." Among those present I were Messrs. Birkhead, B Harrison, Toft, E T Evans, P Hall, W Mills, B Corlett, J Stringer, E Howarth, LI Hough- ton,T Scott, William Davies, Lambert, dia. Mr P Hall was elected to preside, and ha was accompanied on the plat- form by Messrs. B Harrison and John Davies. The CHAIRMAN said he would much rather some one of more influence had occupied the chair at that first meeting for promoting a cotton mill for Earlestown. He did net think he would be able to give it the influence:it deserved, as the matter for consideration was a very important one. But as regarded any feeling in the matter, he did not think any- one in Earlestown had a stronger feeling than he had re- garding the establishment of a cotton mill for Earlestown. The works they had at present in Earlestown and the district, as everybody knew, did not employ that labour which so many females had to dispose of. (Hear, hear.) That was a very important point indeed—to get that labour properly utilised. He did not think anyons present could measure as full as they ought' the advantages that would arise from establishing a cotton works in their midst. He felt satisfied in his own mind that if every head of a family in that meeting could for a moment consider the pecuniary and other advantages which they would have if a cotton mill was at work in Earlestown at the present time, they would very soon shoe a practical interest in the subject. (Hear, bear.) Apart from any pecuniary in- terest, however, he thought it behoved every man with a family to do all he could to get that family employed— (hear, hear,)—because if they were not employed at some particular kind of work, they all knew that they would be employed in some not very profitable way, but one that tended not only to a loss of money, but was not very beneficial in another res- pect. He knew families in Earlestown who were going wrong simply because they had no work to do, (Hear, hear.) On that ground a mill would be a good thing if :hey never had any profits. He would not go into the consequences regarding profits If a mill was established, be- cause he was not then prepared to do so. The meeting had been hurriedly called, and it was for them to say if they were prepared to go in for establishing a cotton mill. He was prepared, like a good many more, to give it all the moral and practical support he possibly could. (Applatse.) He felt satisfied that if they had the support of the various employers of labour in that district at the onset. there would be a possibility that a large cotton factvy would soon be established. He afterwards observed that the meeting was open for anyone to express an opinion, and he hoped they would not be afraid to do so. (Applause.) Mr. B. Hanurson said he thought all present would be satisfied that a cotton mill for Earlestown would be a very excellent thing. The questkin had been spoken about for the last 20 years, and he believed that the late Mr. Thomas Stone frequently spoke about what a grand thing it would be it there was a cotton factory in Earlestown. But a good many had been so grievously disappointed with cotton fac- tories that some people seemed to be getting afraid of them. Of course they knew a burned child dreaded the fire, but at the present time they were doing a very pros- perous business, and they did not need to be afraid. If they took hold of the subject and handled it firmly they would find there WAS nothing to be afraid of, and he would ask them to look at the subject, regarding how it would pay. He had looked at several prospectuses of cotton factories and he found that the prospects of the weaving trade were at tha present time of a most cheering description. Many of the concerns where weaving was carried on were earning good dividends, and from balance sheets of a large number of firms in North East Lancashire he-found the average pro- fits for the last four or five years had equalled 12 per cent. per annum. ,One particular firm had repaid its shareholders from the reserve fund their original capital besides paying an average dividend of 20 per cent. lie carefully looked over the returns of the Rochdale Spinning Company, and taking 19 years, from 1862 to 1880 inclusive, he found that the average dividend was just a fraction under 7 per cent., and he thouaht taking the bad times they had had that it was a very good dividend indeed. (Hear, hear.) The question tor them to consider that night was, if they were to have a factory, what kind of one should it be. Should they go in for a cotton manufactory, Including weaving shed and spinning, or should they just have spinning alone ? They might look at the affair from many standpoints. Spinning, of course, always paid the best dividend, but from the prospectuses he had found that weaving, taking the average of various mills, had paid about 12 per cent. The question might be asked, how was the capital going to be raised provided they decided to start a mill? He thought if they were to make a start they would find no difficulty about the capital. He believed it would be forthcoming, but the question for them to consider first was should they have a factory? On looking over the prospectuses he found that most of the spinning and weaving concerns were worked principally by loan capital instead of share capital. Of course it was a great strain on any small place such as Earlestown to start a factory by share capital alone. He found that Staleybridge mill had share capital amounting to £30,000, but the loan capital was £56,000. He found that Guide Bridge had share capital £35,000 and loan capital £59,000. As money was very cheap at the present time and they could get loan capital at about four per cent, he did not think they would have any great difficulty in getting sufficient capital to float the Concern. He had glanced over a few balance Isheets and prospectuses to see what it would cost to float a concern either for weaving or for spinning. For weaving purposes it would cost from £2O to £5O for every employe they engaged, while, if they took spinning alone it would cost from £250 to £3OO. If they considered the question, it would be for them to decide whether they would have weaving and spinning combined or one of the two by itself.

Mr. B. Conuerr observed that very few of them were experienced in factory matter, and he thought it would be best to select a committee to gather all the information about the matter they possible could, and then present a report on the subject to a future public meeting. They would then be better able te judge hoW to proceed. Mr. GILMOUR endorsed what Mr. Corlett had said, that 1 it would be better for the cause they were advocating if ' they appointed a provisional committee to get all the de- tails they could. He did net think there could be two opinions about the want of a cotton factory for Earlestown. The children and girls there were unemployed and un- likely to find employment at present had driven working men from the neighbourhood. In fact there were men working in the town 10 and 15 miles from their families, and why? Because the females were working in factories, and it would not do to bring them to Earlestown where they would have nothing to do. (Hear, hear.) If females could earn from 125 to £1 per week at Preston, Chorley, Wigan, and other places, why could it not be done in Earles- town ? They had the coal at hand, and they had the market at hand—half•vvay between Manchester and Liverpeel, and they had plenty of willing hands ready to work the concern. In a town where cotton mills were running a working man with a family could better defend his rights, as he would not be so afraid of being discharged, but in Earlestown any man who got discharged had to migrate to some other part of the country at once. If a cotton factory was established it would bring other concerns into the neighbourhood, asd they would have fitting shops, moulding shops, and other works springing up. All the mills in other towns had nut been built in a day, and if they got one cotton factory in Earlestown he did not think it would be long before they had others in the neighbourhood. They had them in Got. borne, and he was sure Golborne had had reason to rejoice that they ever had a cotton factory. The workingmen of Earlestown must sacrifice a little and go into the movement thoroughly, for it would benefit the entire neighbourhood, and It would be one of the greatest blessings they could ex- pect. If the werkingmen did the best they could he felt sue that the gentry of the district would help them. He would recommend that a committee be appointed to draw up full details, but would like an expression of opinion from that meeting as to whether they intended to take the matter up, and what shares they intended taking in the con- cern. (apptause.) Mr. B. HARRISON supported the suggestion that a com- mitted be appointed to make all enquiries with reference to the matter, and elaborate a scheme to be laid before a future public meeting. He would move that a provisional com- mittee be appointed. Mr. JOHN DAVIES, in seconding the motion, said the erec- tion of a cotton mill had been mooted for the last 28 years, but no definite steps in the matter were ever taken. lie was glad to see that large meeting as it showed that the people were taxing an interest in the matter. Mr. BIRKHEAD, after a few amusing introductory refe- rences, said he thought it desirable before they did anything else to get an expression of opinion from the meeting whether or not they should go on with the movement. They might appoint a committee to make a lot of eaquiries and do a lot of work, but unless they were prepared to support them and subscribe to the affair it might end only in smoke. He would support either a factory, foundry, or anything that would give work to unemployed hands, and it would be fa benefit to the neighbourhood. (Hear, bear.) There were lots of girls running about, and women too—(laughter) —who would be a good deal better off at work. If they could do anything to net that unemployed labour at work they would benefit themselves and the neighbourhood. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGH R&TCLIFFE said he did not think anything was more greatly needed in Earlestown than a cotton factory —(hear, hear)—and its establishment would be very benefi- cial to the town. He would suggest that those in the room be asked what amount of shares they were prepared to take up if a cotton mill were started. Mr. BIREHEAD replied that they could scarcely do that for they would not know until the scheme was befve them

what the amount of the shares would be. Be thought if the committee decided upon anything it might be left to the honour of those present to support them. They could not expect a man to sty how many shares he would have, and they could not bind him to any number unless they knew what their price would be, Mr. RATCLIFFE said he understood the shares were to be each. at least that was suggested or mentioned at the Co-operative Stores annual meeting. Mr. Was. DATIES said before the proposition for the ap4 pointment of a committee was put to the meeting he would like to move a resolution as follows That this meeting is of opinion that it is desirable to start a cotton mill in the district of Earlestown." (Applause.) He would heartily support the movement even if they had no return for their money. He thought, however, that their interest lies in another direction, for it was that of finding employment for female labour. That questim had been before the publiC for a long time, and a gentleman in Oldham had promised to render them all assistance in his power in starting a ir!bvejt and had also promised to address a meeting on the su if desired. (Applause.) Mr. PAUL CRITCHLEY, in seconding Mr. William Davies' motion, swill a gentleman who had a very large interest in a cotton mill at Blackburn had told him that he would take up a few shares in the proposed cotton mill for Fades - town, and he would also give what information he could regarding the working of it. _

The motion was then carrried unanimously; after vrhich the resolution that a provisional committee should be ap- pointed was put to the meeting and p4ssed. After a little further conversation, Mr. RATCLIFFE moved that the shares be £1 each, but the motion was not pressed, after Mr. HARRISON had pointed out that it would be beet to wait until they had received a report from the committee they had decided to appoint. A SPEAKER said he knew weaving sheds whi,la had been conducted on co-operative principles' and which had been started at meetings like that, and the shares were £1 each. Mr WILLIAM DAVIES said he found that during the last 10 years 325 mills had been started on a plan similar to the one they were now proposing for Earltstown. The general rule for the shares was £5 a share, which were very easili taken up by working men. The money was not paid down at once, but was called in by easy instalments. Mr GEORGE HILTON: I should like to know if it is to be conducted on co-operative principles, and then we shall know what we are doing. Mr WILLIAM DAVIES replied that it was not exactly On co-operative principles—it was on the joint stock principle. There was an idea got abroad that the agitation had sprung from the Co.operative Society, but it was not correct- Many members of the Co-operative Society took a great in• terest in it, but there was not the slightest connection be- tween the two.

Mr. B. HARRISON confirmed this statement, adding that if they started a mill on co-operative principles they would be debarred from receiving any loan capital. Considerable discussion ensued as to the number of per' sons who should be appointed to serva on the committee. 10, 14, and 20 each beim: moved. It was decided that 14 should be the number, but the following 10 were afterwards! elected as committee :—Mesers B Harrison, P Hall, Geol. Ratcliffe, William Davies, E T Evans, John Davies, Ben Corlett, Birkhead, Gilmour, William Mills, T Molyuealr. T Ellison, W Rmberell, T Haselden, H Houghton, and r Critchlay. Mr B Harrison was unanimously elected secre- tary pro. tem. A resolution was also pawed that any expense incurred by the committee in eliciting information should be de- frayed at the next meeting; and after a hearty vote of. thanks had been accorded to Mr. Hall for presiding, and Mr. Harrison for his information, the proceedings VA" eluded.

EARLIER OPENING OF THE SEASON AT BLACKPOOL. Arrangements are being made at Blackpool by reason of which the summer season will this year be opened a month or six weeks earlier than usual. The matter is in the handl of a Season Extension Committee, formed of members 0 the Town Council and the leading tradesmen of the town, and who have so far proved successful in that, in respOige to their appeal, the L. d`. Y. and the L. & N. railway CO pause have intimated their intention of putting on their summer service of trains on June Ist instead of July let, aS in former years, and of running them without intermissfo.r; until after the close of the season. These cempanies 10" also run their cheap excursions from all the stations 01 their lines to Blackpool from Whitsuntide instead of from July, as previously. In connection Witri this movement, great efforts are being made by the Corpora' lion and the managers of the places of amusement, to pro' vide an unusually attractive programme for- the earlier weeks of summer, and the month of June more especiallY* For that mouth a promenade band will be engaged, whiO, will be selected, one for each week, from the crack bands 0` Lancashire and Yorkshire, and which will be maintained at the expense of the Corporation. At the piers, the theatre!, and the other places of amusement, some of the most eoor nent vocalists and instrumentalists before the public haVO been engaged, in addition to the leading London and travel', ling operatic and dramatic companies. A special novelty 101' be provided at the Wint,r Gardens in the form of a Marl- chester Ship Canal Exhibition, which will be .00 a realistic scale of considerable magnitude, showing all the features of the canal from Manchester to the sea by means of moving scenery, with mechanical bridges, 100115' Jic., and in connection with which, trips will be taken down the canal on a steamer capable of accommodating 600 Pas' sengers. The great employers of labour, who are favourabl! to the scheme, are taking an interest in this unique exhibr thou, and have promised it their support, one Lancashire firm having undertaken tosend 10,000 workmen to witnel, it. It is expected that the Ship Canal Exhibition be opened with some ceremony, on Monday, May 26th, an'. that Mr. Adamson, the chairman of the Ship Canal Coal: mittee, and many of the provincial Mayors, together Yitf` ll,nsuls, and other gentlemen of influence, will be presea' on this occasion.

div.head: 1111, FXAMINER. SATURDAY. MARCH B, 1884. IMPFAIAL PARLIAMENT. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: 1111, FXAMINER. SATURDAY. MARCH B, 1884. IMPFAIAL PARLIAMENT. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

MISCELLANEUS. The death is announced of Dr. Isaac Todhunter, the well- known mathematician, of the University of Cambridge. ' The election at Brighton on Saturday resulted in the re- tarn of Mr. Marriott by a majority of 1,457 over Mr. .Itomer. Sarah Mallinson and Samuel Smart, who were sentenced to death for the murder of Louisa Brierley, at Broughton, Manchester, have been respited. The Princess of Wales on Monday presented medals at Marlborough House to two coxewains of the Royal Na- tional Lifeboat Institution for gallant services in saving life. Two of a party of four men who had visited Pie! Island on Sunday afternoon from Barrow were drowned through the upsetting of the boat on the return j mrney at night. By the fall of a scaffeld at the gable of a new house in 'Dumbarton six men were, on Wednesday, thrown into the street, one of the number being killed deed the others badly injured. A parliamentary writ issued shows that the total amount of the National Debt in 1863 was £758,180,936, and the net balance £719,463,828. These were the lowest amounts for several years. FALL or A TUNNEL NEAR BANGOR.—By the fall of a tunnel on the Bangor and Bethesda Railway, on Wednesday, two navvies were killed and three others seriously injured. Heavy rain is believed to have caused the subsidence. The Mayor of Northampton presided at a public meeting on Wednesday nie,ht, a which a protest was urged against , the decision by which, without constitutional or statutory I warrant, a majority of the House of Commons continues to ; deprive the burgesses of Northampton of the full enjoyment of their electoral rights. It having been brought to the notice of the Prime Minister that Mrs and Miss Roebuck have been left in very straitened circumstances' a grant of £5OO has been pro- mised by Mr. Gladstone from the Boval Bounty Fund, con- , ditionally upon a further sum of £2,000 being raised for the ' benefit of these ladies. The Earl of Sandwich, who has been ill for some week., died on Monday. He was born in 1811, and has been Master of the Buckhounds when a Conservative Government was ' CU power. His death ceases a vacancy in the representa- tion of the borough of Huntingdon by the succession of 1 his son, Lord Hinchingbrook, to the title and estates. The explosion on b ,ard the Australian passenger steam- , ship Aberdeen will probably result in the lose of three or four lives. The calamity was caused by the explesien of a quantity of powder which had been received from the float-I lug magazine and placed under the bridge, on which the , captain and his officers and the pilot were standing. Mr. Bradleugh in a letter to Sir S. Northcote informs the I right hon. gentleman that Ids turn is coming, that he is about to make his appeal to the constituencies, and the answer will be heard when he from his place in the House moves that all the resolutions passed hindering him from Obeying the law be expunged from the journals of the House. Mr. G. J. Holyoeke has offered to contest Leicester with S view to solving the oa he difficulty. In the event of Mr. ' Taylor's immediate retirement, Mr. liolyoeke expresses hie confidence that if returned for Leicester he would bring about a condition of things which mast finally , Settle the oaths difficulty befOre the close of the present I tWasion. On Saturday William Hertner, late master of a Hull ! Smack, was committed for trial, charged with having, con- I vary to the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, gone 00 shore with two other hands at Grirrieby, leaving only two boys in charge of the vessel. They stayed two nights, on the second of which a gale came on, drove the vessel down the river, where it stranded and capsized, both boys being drowned. On Saturday morning, during thick weather' the driver of a Forfar train for London, dashed into a Perth train standing at Kirriemuir junction, on the north-eastern eec- lion of the Caledonian Railway, with the result that both lines were torn up fora considerable dis•ance. IMPUDENT FRAUD.—A very impudent fraud has been ex- posed at the Surrey Sessions. A man named James Schnei- der obtained various sums of money on pretence of having an interest in the well-known "Bade claims' against the French Government. One of his victims was a girl who had saved £25 out of her wages. She was induced to ac- cept as security a bond" wliictr pretended to be issued by the "Baron de Bode Trust Fund," and it should be needless to say that she lost the whole of her money. Schneider was convicted, and received the exemplary sen- tence Of 18 mouths' imprisonment with hard labour. The case is worth noticing as another proof of the boundless credulity which persons who are apparently sane in other in utters display when they are invited to throw their money away. THE EwarAsie LAND Commisslotenns.—The report of the 'Lend Commissioners for England for the year 1883, which was published on Thursday as a Parliamentary paper, states that the number of applications for provisional orders under the Commons Alt, 1876, recorded in the last report, was 85; 23 for regulation, and 62 for inclosare, embracing 102,922 acres. The applications since received relate to 9,015 acres, making a total of 112 837 acres for regulation and inclosure since 1876. The inclesure of 22,430 acres and the regulation of 22,205 acres have been sanctioned by Parliament. Under the Metropolitan Commons Acts, 1866 and 1869, the Commissioners had only one case to consider —that of Streatham Common, Surrey, which is to be secured in perpetuity as an open space under proper manage- ment and control. It appears that altogether 14 commons in the counties of Middlesex, Kent, and Surrey, comprising about 1672 acres, have been the subject of schemes under the Acts, which have been approved and certified by the Commissioners, and confirmed by Parliament.
