THE NATIONAL REFORM UNION.—At a meeting of the Executive Committee held on Tuesday evening the follow- ing resolution were unanimously passed on the subject of the Representation of the People Bill :—" That the Execu- tive Committee of the National Reform Union, while be- lieving that the establishment of one uniform franchise for the whole kingdom would be consistent with justice and expediency, is of opinion that the bill introduced by Mr. Gladstone is a large and honest effort to remove the injus- tice and inequalities of the present electoral system, and as such deserves the hearty and united support of the Liberal party." With regard to the Merchant Shipping Bill it was resolved—" That the Executive Committee of the National Reform Union deems it of urgent necessity that every effort should be made to protect the lives of our merchant sailors, whose avocation precludes them from helping themselves by agitation; and that this Committee heartily approves of the Government measure to this end, and calls upon all Liberal members of Parliament to sup- port Mr. Chamberlain's motion to refer this bill to the Grand Committee on Trade, in order that the passing of the measure during the present session may be secured. —On the subject of the representation of Northarapton, it was resolved—" That the Executive of the National Reform Union desires to record its emphatic protest against the persistently illegal and and unconstitutional action of the ' majority of the House of Commons in depriving the con- stituency of Northampton of the services of the representa- tive whom it has' four times elected in strict accordance .with its unchallenged rights; and thanks 'the electors of .that borough for the courageous and determined assertion of their electoral privileges shown by the recent re-election of their representative by so triumphant a majority;, and this committee calls upon the Liberal party throughout the 'country to unite in an earnest and vigorous protest against the continued invasion of the rights of constituencies, and to insist on the rescinding by the House of Commons of the resolution proposed by the leader of the Tory party, whereby the duly elected member for Northampton is ex- cluded from the House and prevented from discharging his duty to his constituents." Tha encounte7oerween General Graham's force and the insurgent Arabs took place on Friday last week, at A.l Teb, and was most decisive in its character and results. The ex- pedition, which had passed Thursday night at Baker's Fort, marched out to meet the enemy early on Friday. After a few miles had been traversed, the Arabs began to show in force. Sir Gerald Graham had formed his brigades in an "oblong square," with machine guns at the front corners, and cavalry covering. Tue enemy, who retired slowly before the advance of our men, maintained a heavy rifle fire, and they also used with considerable effect the Krupp canon taken from Baker Pasha. The square moved steadily on under a ceaseless fire until an intrenched position was discovered. Sir G. Graham thereupon changed the formation of the troops, and attacked the position in the rear. A desperate struggle ensued. No body of troops could have fought better than the Soudanese. In the "open " they repeatedly charged up to tvithin a few yards of the face of our square, and when charged in turn by our cavalry they refused to retreat, but stood up and gave back blow for blow. In their entrench- ments they fought with the same desperate courage, and lost many hundreds of their number before they abandoned the struggle. In the course of the fight our loss WAS rather severe. The cavalry Buffered most. Baker Pasha was severely wounded by the fragment of a shell. Colonel Burnaby, who was present out of a sheer love of fighting, wis also wounded, and at least half a dozen officers, naval and military, were slain. The killed and wounded were little short of 200. Sir W. Hewett was pre- sent with the naval detachment, and left them to the attack. The Arabs appear to have acknowledged the completeness of their defeat. They made no further opposition to Sir G. Graham's march on Tokar, which Was resumed on Satur- day. In Tokar—which surrendered without resistance— the British found the Egyptian garrison. The men surren- clued on the 16th February, and although their lives were spared they, together with the townspeople, were plundered and oppressed by the Arabs. The report that Sir G. Gra- ham had sent a flag of truce to the Arabs on Thursday ap- pears to be confirmed by his own brief account. The full details of the battle show that the struggle was the most trying in which our troops have been engaged since the defeat of Ayoub Khan by General Roberts. Their bravery and steadiness are thrown into the fullest relief by the ample justice which all observers render to the Arabs. The wounded are reported to be doing fairly well. General Gordon's position is said to be rather critical. The Madhi's lieutenants on the White Nile have refused to receive an embassy which the General sent out. General Graham remains with his forces at Tokhar. It was reported from Cairo that he had been instructed to re- turn at once to Trinkitat, but the statement appears to have been unfounded. The most important news—if it be true —comes from Khartoum. The second armed reconnaissance sent out by Gordan appears to be of a most satisfactory character. Some of the Sheikhs who were hostile to the first expeditioe have "come in," and they state that the Mandi has commanded his lieutenants not to engage in hos- tilities or to advance against Khartoum. Egyptian soldiers who have come into Khartoum report that a reign of terror exists at El Obeid. They add that the Mandi received Gordon's decree appointing him Sultan of Kordofan "with ectacy," and gave the messenger a robe of honour. - The Foreign Office has issued copies of a correspondence which passed between Lord Granville and the Turkish Go- vernment with reference to Egyptian affairs. The Sultan was anxious in January to send an expedition to the Soudan, but in replying to Lord Uranville's inquiry as to "where the money was to come from," the Turkish Ambas- sador in London frankly admitted that his truster could not Pay. and suggested that Egypt should raise a loan for the purpose. Thereupon Lord Granville at once closed the dis- cussion, but added that he had no wish "to diminish the rights of the Sultan." The Bluebook also contains an ac.- count of a conversation between Sir A. Paget and Count Kalnoky, in which the Austrian Minister admitted that England had no alternative but to remain in Egypt until peace and order were restored there. Later reports state that General Graham has returned to Trinkitat, and the British force has evacuated the "miser- able mud village" called Tekhar. Such of the inhabitants as desired to leave were escorted to the coast. Osman Digna remains, according to a telegram, in his camp, about a day's march from that port. He is still represented as bitterly hostile to the British. The defeat of his men and their allies at Teb he accounts for on the round that they abandoned their usual weapon, the spear, and relied on rifles and cannon. The Arabs may possibly accept this ex- planation although it does not accord with the facts. The number of Arabs killed at Teb was much larger than at first reported. The Black Watch are said to have buried more than 2,000 up to Tuesday morning. Few prisoners were taken, the Arabs preferrlng,even when they were surrounded, to sacrifice their lives in attempts—which were sometimes successful—to kill our men rather than surrender. General Graham has issued an order of the day, in which he an- nounces that the objects of the expedition have been accom- plished, and the foe so effectually humbled that the force may now safely retire from Tokbar. The General praises the men under his command for their gallantry, many no- table instances of which are given. We learn from Suakim that General Graham has issued a proclamation to the tribes calling upon them to chase the Arab leader from the country.

Snomma MURDERS IN SPAIN.--.A Reuter's telegram from Madrid states that four women were murdered in Tarragona on Saturday last by a shoemaker named Jose Perez, 19 years of age. The victims were Florentine Matheu, 80 years of age, Josefa Mallol, her daughter, the step-daughter of the latter, aged 17, and a servant. Josefa Mallol kept a tobacco shop, her mother and st,p daughter residing with her. Early on Saturday morning Perez en- tered the shop armed with a dagger, and attacked and stabbed the four women one after the other. Florentine Matheu and the girl was killed on the spot, and the other two are not expected to survive. The murderer succeeded in escaping, but was subsequently arrested and brought be- fore the authorities, when he denied the crime. It is sup- posed that Perez was aware that, Josefa Mallol intended to lay in a stock of tobacco on Saturday, and that his object was to obtain possession of the money collected in the shop for that purpose. THE CONGO AND TELE ZAMBE9l.—Parliamentary papers were issued on Monday evening containing correspondence relating to the negotiations between the Governments of Great Britain and Portugal for the conclusion of the Congo treaty, together with a copy of the treaty and a corrected translation of the Mozambique tariff of 1877. The corres- pondence extends from November Bth, 1882, to February 25th, 1884, the day before the treaty was finally signed. By the first article England agrees to the sovereignty of the King of Portugal over that part of the West Coast of Africa situate between 8 legs. and sdegs. 12 minutes of south lati- tude, and inland to Nokki, on the river Congo, the inland eastern frontier to coincide With the boundaries of the pre- sent possessions of the coast and riparian tribes. • This ter- ritory shall be open to all nations conforming themselves to the laws of the country for purposes of trade or pro- prietorship of land. The rivers Congo and Zatubesi shall be free to the commerce and navigation of all nations, and the claims of Portugal on Shire River shall not extend be- yond the confluence of the River Rao with that river. The treaty provides for a mixed commission of delegates of Great Britain ant Portugal to frame regulations for the navigation and supervision of the Congo, and that the cus- toms tariff shall not exceed the Mozambique tariff of 1877 for a term of ten years from signing the treaty; the high contracting parties to which bind themselves to use all pos- sible means for the purpose of finally extinguishing slavery and the slave trade on the eastern and western coasts of Africa. _Jaw

The Government considered that the instructions given to General Graham were thoroughly judicioue, and they were efficiently and admirably carried out.— Sir W. Lamm; moved the adjournment of the House, and proceeded to discuss the affairs of Egypt and to denounce the "horrible slaughter of Friday," than which, he said, "a more dastardly and cowardly deed had never been done." He asked the Prime Minister to check the country in its wild career of crime, and declared for his part be would rather be in the position ot those poor savage.' whom our soldiers mowed down last Friday than in the place of those who dealt death and destruction amopg them.—Mr. GLAD- E/Dm; in replying, said the hon. member for Carlisle was at liberty to make the most illogical and unaromentative argument he might please; he was perfectly secure on ac- count of the sacredness of the object he had in view and the consistent profession of what might, perhaps, be an ultra-pacific policy; but he wished to know if concurrence in these motives had prompted hon. members opposite. His hon. friend Sir W. Lawson acquiesced in the operations for the relief of Tokhar, and be, Mr. Gladstone, did not be- lieve that oPeratioas could possibly have been effected without the fighting of the action which had just taken place. He was therefore at a loss to understmd why he should fall upon the Government with such vehemence. The Government deemed that the interests of peace and of humanity required that the port of Suakim should be secured. He challenged his hon. friend to move a resolu- tion if he thought fit declaring that the Government was in error in declining the immediate abandonment of the Soudan.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE contended that if the position of England had been what it ought to have been' none of the slaughter would have occurred. It was difficult to understand why we were fighting She Mandi's Lieutenant while we were proclaiming the Mandi Sultan.—Lord R. Cetuncamr, hoped that till the Government had a definite policy to announce the House would refuse to vote the supplies for carrying on the operations in Egypt. Lord Hartington denied that What had taken place on Friday was an unprovoked slaughter.—Sir W. LAWSON expressed his willingness to withdraw his motion for adjournment, but a division was Insisted upon, and the motion was rejected by 150 to 103. Tau REFORM BILL—Mr. BLENNERHASSETT then resumed the debate on the introduction of the Reform Bill, and he I was followed by Mr. Edward Clarke.—Mr. W. H, SMITE( dwelt upon the unequal distribution of favours to Ireland in the matter of redistribution of seats, a theme taken up with much force by Mr. Goscaux, who followed him. Mr. Goschen argued that the effect of the proposed extension of the franchise would be to place the destinies of this country in the hands of a class under that of the £l.O householder. He spoke strongly in favour of representation of minorities. —Mr. Pm:mu, cordially supported the Bill.—Mr. Tan- morale also supported the Bill, and was followed by Sir John Lubbock, with whom rose Mr. Forster, Mr. Chaplin, and Sir S. Northcote —The opposition was not insisted upon to the point of a division, and leave was given to bring in , the Bill.

TEE SOUDAN EXPED/TION : TrIE VOTE OP CREDIT.— In Committee of Supply Lord HARTINGTON moved a Tote of £370500 to defray the expenses of the expedition to the Soudan. Toe noble Marquis stated that on his return from Tokhar General Crrahain, in conjunction with Admiral Hewitt, had issued a proclamation to Osman Dignsa's force calling on it to disperse, and warning it that if not dis- persed voluntarily it would be by force. The General and Admiral proposed to land troops at Suakim for the purpose of enforcing the proclamation, and they recommended that

if necessary the force under General Graham's command should advtnce to the position occupied by Osman Digma's force and disperse it If neces- sary. Their opinion was that the operation would not be seriously resisted. We had no intention of taking any operation to punish or take revenge on Osman Digma, and no intention to exterminate him or make war on his adherents.—Colonel STANLEY said in view of the proclama- tion referred to the Opposition thought it their duty to ask the Government to indicate in broad outline what was the policy they had approved and to which they intended to adhere. The country expected the Government to say what they meant and do what they said.—The right bon. gentleman sat down without moving the reduction of which he had given notice.—Mr. GLADNIONN asserted that the proclamation issued was to make known to the people with whom we had been in action last week the purpose for which we were there, and to assure them that if they would dis- perse and Cease to threaten Suakim they were per- fectly safe, and to show that our purpose was not to avenge our arms, but to convince them that British influence and responsibility were engaged in the Soudan to relieve the people from the grievances under which they had been suffering. Toe Government felt precluded from any pro:, fi.able discussion upon their general policy in Egypt, and as regarded the Soudan they remained precisely where they were. They were there for certain purposes, aad having made provision for those purposes they would endeavour as soon as possible to withdraw their military force. Mr. Laboachere moved a reduction of the vote by a sum of £206,150, on the ground that the cost of the expedition ought to be borne by the bondholders, who were at the teettom of all the trouble in Egypt—The debate was con- tinued in an almost empty House by Mr Tomlinson, Mr Rylands, Mr Macfarlane, Sir George Campbell, and Mt Kennard, who more or less agreeably filled up an awkward interval by reading extracts from the correspondence uf Lord Granville. At half-past ten Mr Finch Hatton found a favourable opportunity for delivering his maiden speech, an effort listened to with generous attention by the committee, though kindly intent was overceala by uproarous laughter, when the hon. gentleman pictured Mr Gladstone asleep dreaming of his victims, and a little later called him "Achilles," and sternly sumtnoned him from his tent. , Sir W Lawson declared that "our gallant troop had been sent into the Soudara as bum-bailiffs of the Egyptian bond- holder.' Lord Eastace Cecil was scarcely audible among I the buzz of conversation on the benches near him as he dis- cussed the critical situation. In similar circumstances Mr O'Donnell and Mr Wartou continued the debate. On the motion of Lord George Hamilton, progress was, at half-past 12, reported, after a protest from Lord Hartington.

BLUE RIBBON ARMY—Theßltie Ribbon Gospel Temper- ance Army have established a branch at Frodsham. A service is conducted every evening in Mr. Harrop's Auction Mart by Captain Kerr, and attracts large congregations. GOLBORNE.

ACCIDENT TO A Commtn.—A serious accident betel a collier named Henry Burchall, residing at Golborne, on Tuesday. He was working in the Golborne mine of Messrs Richard Evans and Co., and while engaged in propping up the roof a portion of the roof fell and alighted upon Burch- all, who had both of his thighs broken. He was conveyed home, where he remains in a serious condition. LEcrunst AT GOLBORNE.—On Tuesday evening last the Rev. James Wayman, of Blackpool, delivered a lecture, en- titled "Very familiar bodies," in the Congregational School, Golborne. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr Thomas Twist, Mr H Yates being also pre- sent. The lecture was divided under four heads—" Any- body, nobody, somebody, and everybody "—and was of a very interesting character. HAYDOCK.

" BOOZED " ON THE WAY TO HATDOCE.— At the War- ringten County Petty Sessions. on Wednesday, before Messrs. H. Bleckly (in the chair), and T. Comber, William Lee, a labouring man, pleaded guilty to a charge of being drunk and disorderly on the 29th of last month. At twelve o'clock at night, on the date mentioned, he was found by a constable in Winwick-road, Orford, where he was creating a disturbance. He informed the constable that he was going to Haydock, but as he was not in a fit state to do so he was accoramodated with lodgings. Defendant was tined ss. and costs.

div.head: HOUGH GREEN.
div.p: HOUGH GREEN.

BURGLARY AT HOUGH GREEN STATION.—At an early hour on Sunday morning a burglary was committed at the Cheshire Lines Station, Hough Green. The booking office was entered through the house of the stationmaster, to which entrance had been gained by a back window, the burglars having first scaled a high wall which encloses the private yard of Mr. Hawbrooke. A drawer was forced open in the office, and a leather bag, in which had been placed upwards of £3, was cut open and the money abstracted. From the house of Mr. Hawbrooke a quantity of provisions were taken, besides an overcoat and several other articles. The police are investigating the robbery. HUTTON.

HIJYTON TEXPERINCE 9.9SOCIATION. - At the usual weekly meeting of the above on Tuesday evehing, held in the Huyton Park Schools, addresses were given by Messrs. W. Tharme and F. H. Ropes, of Liverpool. The Rev. J. W. Walker, 8.A., presided. There was a good attendance.

TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.-At the .Prescot Police Court on Tuesday, Thomas Bellis, a young man was North- Western with having travelled en the London and man, Railway without a ticket, on the 14th November last.—Mr. Preston, jun., prosecuted.—On the night of the 14th November last the defendant got out of the 10-45 p.tn. train at Huyton station He tried to evade the ticket col- lector, but not being successful, he denied that he had come by train. The next night, however he came back, and wanted to pay the fare, which, however, was not taken. A summens was taken out, but prisoner's whereabouts had not been ascertained till lately.—A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed, or in default one month's imprisonment.

ENTERTAINMENT AT lineTow.—The well-known enter- tainers, Walter Roselle and Harry Collins gave their "Flashes of Fun" and "Merry-making" diversions in the Huron Park Schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. The ,proceeds were devoted to the Horn's Smithy Mission. Mr. Alexander Eccles presided, and briefly alluded to the work being done in that neighbcurhood ; it was gratifying to see such a number present that evening. The entertainment was then proceeded with, and the varied programme of vocal, and the performance on the amusingly-contrived musical instruments, ventriloquism, conjuring, dm., by the continuous laughter and applause elicited, afforded an evening's delight to the crowded audiences, and proved very successful in every respect. CONCERT AT HIITTON.-0a Monday evening, in the Huyten and Roby Schools, a concert was given under the auspices of the Church of England Temperance Society (Huyton Branch), by ladies and gentlemen of the neigh- bourhood and was of a very successful character. The Rev. Canon Fenrhyn presided. Mr. Clark Aspinal, of Liverpool, during the interval was present, and gave a lengthy and amusing address on the temperance question, dealing with it from every aspect, illustrated with his own experience as magistrate and coroner, dwelling on the responsibility of the upper classes in their want of sympathy with the trials, sufferings, and snail condition of the working class of our large centres of population. He was hopeful of the efforts of the Church of England Temperance Society, and acknow- ledged the pioneer wink of the nonconformist societies. , His address was frequently applauded, and his characteris- tic and pungent hits created roars of laughter. The following was the programme :—Pianoforte duet " Schiller march," by Meyerbeer, Messrs J Hodgson and H Howell; song "The Storm Fiend," Mr E Jackson; song, "Two's Com- pany," Miss Farrington; song, "The anchor's weighed,'! Mr JJ Dawson; duet, Mrs Moss and Mr E 13 Moysey ; ad- dress by Clarke Aspinall, Eeq., J.P. ; pianoforte solo, "La Sonambala," Miss Leigh; duet, "Trust her net," The Misses Parrington ; song, "My lady's dower," Mr E B Moy- say ; song, " Sun,..hine and rain," Mrs Moss; song, "Out in the deep," Mr G Bernard; pianoforte duet (Weber), "Jubilee overture," Messrs J Hodgson and J H Howell. The accompaniments were played by Mr Hodgson and Mre Moysey ; the several pieces were well received. Miss Par- rington received an encore, and gave "Punchinello" in res- ponse. Miss Leigh was enthusiastically recalled for her clever performance, as was also Mr Bernard, who gave "Mother be proud of your boy in blue." A cordial vote of thanks to Mr Aspinall and the tidies and gentlemen was given, on the motion of the Rev Canon Penrhyn.

SANDBACH.

FEVER EPIDEMIC,—ATitTe—MOnetI7I;7 meeting of the Sand- bach Local Board, on Monday night, the Rev. J. R. Armit- stead presiding, Mr. Stringer said that fever was assuming a very serious aspect in the town. The absentees from, school on account of fever were more numerous than ever.—The Chairman said that there was mote scarlet fever now than there was when the recent Government inquiry was held. There had been two deaths, and in several families there were three or four children down.—The Surveyor said he disinfected the houses where deaths had taken place from fever; but the Chairman thought that houses should be die. infected at once without waiting for dealb.—The Surveyor said it was a very difficult matter to know when he could enter houses to disinfect them. Medical men said that nothing but burning sulphur in the room was effectual. The surveyor was urged to do all be could in the way of disin- fecting the houses, and to report to a special meeting of the Board.—Daring the past two months scarlet fever has also been epidemics in Astbury, Smollwood, and Betchton. In Astbury, Dr. Fox reports, it seemed probable that an undue desire on the part of the management to secure school atten- dance has had something to do with the spread of the disease.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY,
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY,

TEE SOUDA-N.—Lord l. FlTimm:melt said that no ex- pedition was at present contemplated for the relief of the beleaguered Egyptian garrison at Katenila. The Govern ment had reason to believe that the garrison would be with- drawn without difficulty. As to Khartoum, the Govern- ment had no unfavourable report of the state of affairs.— The Marquis of HARTINGTON repeated his statement of the previous day that Admiral Hewett had received instructions to negotiate with the leaders of the rebel troops surrounding Tokhar and in the neighbourhood of Suakim, and in reply to a further question said General Graham had not received orders to leave Tokhar and return to Trinkitat No Intel- ligence had been received from General Graham since Mon- day. The Government, added the noble Marquis, had no information whatever of an intended attack on the camp of Osman Digrna, and no orders had been sent subsequent to the instructions which he read to the House •on Monday.—The PRIME MINISTER told Mr. Ashmead Bartlett that the Government were not aware of any neces- sity for taking any steps at all with regard to the communi- cations between Khartoum and the Egyptian territory, and en that subject the intentions and views of the Government remained unchanged. General Gordon went to the Soudan to conduct the important operation of withdrawing the Egyptian military forces, and as those forces were the symbol of Egyptian power their withdrawal meant the abandonment of any Egyptian supremacy over the Soudan. , THE HOUSING OF THE POOR.—Mr. A. BALFOUR moved resolution in favour of making advances to public trusts and corporations to enable them to improve working clans dwellings. He contended that sanitary regulations alone would fail to meet the necessities of the case, and desired that charitable associations should be allowed to draw upon the Public Works Loan Commissioners for fends. He was followed bY Sir Lyon Playfair, who gave interesting etatistics showing the improvement that had been effected In the past forty years, dwelt upon the necessity for dealing with the question of land tenure in relation to working class dwellings, and pointed to the working of the Educa- tion Act as proving that the abolition of overcrowding would greatly benefit the public health.—Sir Camar.ss DILHE moved the previous question, chiefly on the ground that the Royal Commission on the whole subject had already been appointed; and after some further debate the motion was withdrawn, and the House was counted out a little before nine o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNEsnay. THE LAND LAW (IRELAND) ACT (18811.—Mr. BARRY moved the second reading of a bill to amend the Irish Land Act with respect to the commencement of the judicial rent, the inclusion of leaseholdere, the purchase clauses, and the expedition of hearing appeals.—Mr. BRODRICK moved the rejection of the bill.—Mr. TREVELYAN declared that while the Government were prepared to bring in a bill to make small amendments in the Land Act which its working had proved almost necessary, they had "given the act a character of permanence and immutability." He added that the Government had not said their last word about the question of peasant proprietary, but he declined at present to give the slightest indication of what they would ulti- mately propose. After Easter either the Chancellor of the Exchequer or himself would state to the House the line the Government would take on this sabject.—Mr. SEXTON re- minded the right hon. gentleman that finality had once before been written across the Government Land Bill, and he predicted that the principle of every clause in the bill which had been introduced by the hon. member for Wex- ford would be accepted by the Government.—The motion was negatived by 235 against 72. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. TRH MEDICAL Acr AMENDMENT BILL.—The Medical Act Amendment Bill was read a second time, on the motion of Lord 0.4\111,1MM/ORD, who explained that its main object was to place upon a more satisfactory footing the system of licensing for the practice of medicine and surgery, so as to give security to the public that every licensed practitioner was re tsonably qualified. The bill proposed to create a Medical Board in each of the three kingdoms, which Boards, acting under the superintendence of a Central Medical Conseil, should alone have the right of cmferring the licence to practice. Eovp rum AFFAIRS.—EarI GnaNviLLE. replying to Lord Bury's imerrogations aoout our position in Egypt and the policy of Her Majesty's Government, said that, as he had often declared, an obligation had been thrown upon thin country, in consequence of which we were occupying Egypt; but the Government did not intend to annex Egypt, nor did it intend a permanent military occultation. His lordship announced that a telegram received that afternoon stated that a thousand men sent from El Obeid to Khartoum had been totally defeated by the tribes friendly to General Gor- don.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said the policy of the Government was dark and mysterious and marked with b.ood, and there was every reason to believe that under our fostering care Egypt was bleeding to death. He called upon the Foreign Secretary for a declaration of policy.—Lord KIMBERLEY reproved the Opposition for making Egyptian affairs the occasion week after week of a violent party attack, and after a 'bort discussion the subject dropped.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

DROWNING ACCIDENT—On Wednesday a little boy, the son of Mr. Robert Duncan, of Weaver-street, went out of the Navigation School at play time and ran down to the river's brink. He was warned away, but it seems returned again as soon as his monitor's back was turned. Ere long he fell into the Weaver' which had a freshlet from the rains of the two previous days. The sluices were open also, hence the current was strong, and the boy soon went under. The river was dragged in vain for the victim up to the time we went to press.

TEMPERANCE MEETING.—There was a temperance meet- ing at the Free Methodist Schoolroom, High-street, on Mon- day. The room was crowded, and the interest well sus- tained by a host of performers, who went through "The teetotal chairman in a fix." The speeches of some of the young men were remarkably good, and abounded with in- struction and humour. The choir rendered a number of pieces of a like character ; Miss Buckley presiding at the harmsnium. The collection at the close realised £3, and will be devoted to the purchase of a banner for the Band of Hope. , OVERHEAD TELEGRAPH WIRES. Mr. Foulkes, Mid- Cheshire County Court Judge, has given his decision as arbitrator in the dispute between the Post-office authorities and the Winsferd Local Board regarding a proposed line of overhead telegraph wires through the Board's district. The Post-office are enlarging their lines from London north- wards, in view of greater demands by sixpenny telegrams, and consent was obtained for an extra " line " of 15 wires from London to Liverpool, the only objecting local authority being that of Winsferd. They suggested an underground line, which was impracticable by reason of cost, and, in the alternative, a change of route, but as this latter proposal would have necessitated the payment of some acknowledg- ment the postal authorities referred the matter to arbitra- tion. Mr. Foulkes decides on all points against the Local Board, who are condemned in costs. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

The Conservative candidates for West Cheshire addressed a meeting of the electors of the Tarvin polling district on Wednesday night. Resolutions thanking the Duke of Rich- mond and Mr. Henry Chaplin for their exertions in promo- ting the bill dealing with the importation of cattle from foreign countries where there was disease, and condemning the home and foreign policy of the Government, were unani- mously passed. There are now 13,000 voters in West Cheshire, and it was stated that the new franchise bill would add about 10,000 more to the electorate. Large masses of the workingmen would be enfranchised in Crewe, Birken- head, Wallasey, and Runcorn. Examen's cm A SEWAGE FAME.— Another interesting experiment with ensilage was demonstrated on Monday, on the Corporation sewage farm at Crewe. The difference between this experiment and others was that the silo was filled with rye grass not cut. No silt or bran was used. The size of the silo is 14 feet by 12 feet and ten feet deep. Wet grass was mixed with a little closer. There were about 20 tons. In five weeks, under a pressure of 70lbs to the square foot it bad sunk about 5 feet. The silo was then re- filled, and a pressure equal to 1201bs to the square foot was placed upon it. It was found that with grass uncut there was considerably more waste than when grass was cut before being placed in the eilo. The ensilage, however, turned out well, though scarcely so good as lhat cat. The farm mana- ger states that cut grass is much more preferable, because if cattle do not re:ish it well a little corn may be mixed with it to tempt their appetite. The results of the experiments have been so satisfactory that another silo is to be con- structed on the farm. Silos promise to be very useful on sewage farms, where oftentimes there are crops of gross in the autumn, and if this can be utilised it will become very valuable as fodder. It may be stated that the Crewe sewage farm is successful, and for the last two years has returned a substantial profit.

div.head: FAREWELL SERMON OF THE REV.
div.p: FAREWELL SERMON OF THE REV.
A. P. REYNOLDS, OF FRODSHAM. SENSATIONAL RELIGION.

On Sunday evening, the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, senior curate at Frodsham, preached a valedictory sermon in the Parish Church from 15 Romans, 13 verse: "Now the Ged of Hope till you with all joy and peace in believing that ye may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Ghost." After speaking of (1) the little which is here given to God—the God of hope, (2) the gifts which He bestows—joy and peace, and (3) the manner in which they are bestowed—power of the Holy Ghost, the rev. gentleman said: I am going to venture on this, the last time that I *hall address you, my friends, as one of the curates of the wish, to sty a word or two in reference to sensational ireligion. I don't wish to speak against any body or any system; God forbid. I always feel that the safe ground for us to occupy is that taken by Gamiel when speaking of the .Apostles' work, "If the work be of:men it will come to nought, but if it be of God ye cannot overthrow it, lest haply ye be found to fight against God." Notwithstanding that some good may be done, this will not binder me from a word of friendly warning to any who may perhaps be too ready to mistake mere ecstaticism for real faith. I speak, my friends, with the less hesitation for two reasons, first, It is known that I am not prejudiced in the matter, and have attended several services and helped in them; secondly, because leaving as I am it cannot be said that I am jealous of the numbers who gather night after night. I say, therefore, that the fruits of faith will not be forthcoming where outwardly faith is fostered by exciting sensational services; neither will any mere profession of faith bring forth the fruits of joy and peace in the heart which, from the time of conversion, is left all untutored in the things of God. I feel there is a real danger, and I want you to feel that danger too; there is danger in the fact of young children being allowed to stay out until a late hour in the streets night after night when they should be at home, and I would impress upon you who are parents and guardians of children that there is also a great danger in allowing children scarcely beyond the years of infancy to epeak in meetings where grown-lap persons are present. My friends, if I may dare to say so, we are not concerned to know that 40 were converted last night, and the same number the night before; but we, who are called to minister in spiritual things among you, are much concerned to know that fruit corresponding to such announcements should be seen in an increased appreciation of the House of God, of privileos offered there' and the means of grace freely outbeld to all as well as that by use made of these means of grace. There may be a large increase in the number of those who know that joy which no man taketb away from them and are secure in that peace which the world can neither give nor take away. My friends, I feel in parting from you that there are no words that could better express my desire for you one and all than the words of my text. You can hardly perhaps know the feeling that I have in parting with you, and of how much more I might and ought to have done on yoar behalf One always feels lost opportunities when they are lost for ever, but for all left undone or done amiss I have to ask pardon from above. I only ask of you that you will sometimes grant me a place in your prayers that I may myself be blessed and be made a blessing to those to whom I go. lam glad of this opportunity to thank all whom I may only be ab'e to thus thank publicly for the many kind- nesses to me, the only return I can make is a continual re- membrance of you in my prayers that the God of Hope may fill you with all joy and peace in believing that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Ghost.

DARBtSEURE informed the Board that the lad Was going on as bad, if not worse, than before. The youngster continued his depredations and thefts, and was always running away, having lately left three nights in succession. It seemed that from the com- munications made with the authorities of the traiuini ship, ! that Warrington was under age, and he could not be taken aboard, so before long.he was afraid they wou:d bs obliged to take him before the magistrates to he dealt with. The lad was a bad example to the other boys at Padette. He find spoken to the Chief Constable on the matter, who suggested that the youngster should be brought Mete the magistrates to be dealt with in some shape or form. as be erole cheese and all the provisions he ccu:d lay Lis hands on. Mr. Bhaciturnsv thought t.otne action should be taken at once, as the lad was an incorrigi- ble, and a bad example to others—the Chntrx considered the Schools Committee shou.d take what action they thought advisable, and if necessary to a:low them to hand the lad over to the police, and he would hen Come nefore the magistrates.—The subject then dropped.

The Clerk having react over a long het of articles re- quired for the purposee of the schools at Padgate, Mr. HAR- RISON facetiously put the question to the Clerk as to whether the latter could tell them when those requirements would cease, but a general chorus of v.;ica replied " Never."

div.head: MAINTENANCE OF FAUPEZ LUNATICS.
div.p: THE MAINTENANCE OF FAUPEZ LUNATICS.

The CLERK said that some time ago a conversation took place at that Board with regard to the maintenance of pauper lunatics, and he had since then prepared a statement which had been laid before the auditor, and which gave the full particulars of each case, viz., the name of the patient. the period of maintenance, the total cost, the amount if Government grant, &c. Their Government claims amounted te £BOO 85.—Major CARTWaIGHT Wadt is the Cost ?—Ttle Czang replied that it was not totalled, although the sum they had received showed about a half of the en- • tire expenditure.—Major CARTWRIGHT : That's only a six months' statement is it 7—The CLERK: It is for 12 months. —Dr. MACKIE asked whether the Clerk could inform them as to the rate which lunacy had been growing since tke Government became so good as to ply a portion ef the ex- penses P—The CLERK said that undoubtealy it was greatly on the increase. Some time ago he and one or two others visited the Rainhill Asylum, when Dr. Rogers very coar- teouslv conducted them into the new building, which he be- lieved would cost something like a quarter of a million of money. It Was really a wonderful place to inspect. The doctor told them in course of conversation at that time that he had received a letter from the Local Government Board asking him to look over the whole of his patients and report who in his judgment were the pr .per people to be kept at the Workhouse by the Guardians and not sent to asyleins, and the result was that be knocked off a considerable num- ber, including some sent from the Warrington Union. tie (the Clerk) said that they had no accommodation for such people at their Workhouse, and that they could not do with lunatics there, and the doctor, therefore, agreed to allow them to remain. At Bolton the Union had a special building set apart for pauper lunatics.—Major CART- WRIGHT: For dangerous lunatics as well ?—Tbe CLERK said it was for the whole of them. A place like Bolton had reason to complain of the coat of keeping the lunatics, be- cause they had to provide an establishment of officers neces- sary whilst they received nothing from Government towards the cost, whereas other Unions having their lunatics away at asylums received 43 per week for each case.—The Cwstamitir observed that the Salford Guardians kept lunatics on their own premises with the exception of the very dangerous portion, a separate building being I provided for the purpose. When he went there a short ; time ago he saw a large number of thorouLti lunatics and f imbeciles. The very dangerous lanatics were sent to the asylum.lllajor CARTWRIGHT thought the expense must be heavy, as he should think lunatics would cost 2s per week more than the ordinary inmates of the house.—Dr. - MACKIE : The Government is getting frightened about the rapid increase in their payments for lunatic paupers.—The CHAIRMAN said that all the lunatics which they paid for in asylums were really pauper lunatics. People who werein a position to pay for themselves were not chargeable to the rates. If they refused to pay for the poor imbeciles which they had in their asylums they would have to provide a place for them at the workhouse, so they could see the ex- pense would come on the rates one way or another.—Tbe discussion on the matter then dropped.

div.head: RATING OF RAILWAY PROPERTY.
div.p: THE RATING OF RAILWAY PROPERTY.

Dr. Macietie intimated his wish to offer a few remarks with reference to a discussion which took place in that room a fortnight ago on the question of rating and with the view that the Clerk might be reqiested to furnish them, if necessary, with some returns as to assessment of neigh- bouring townships over which the railway passed. He had been furnished with a statement which showed that in 1864 the valuation of Sankey was £150; last year, when be supposed it was re-valued, it was raised to £625; Grap- peahen was £B5, and it had been increased £584. Mr. DARBYsHIBE : That refers to railways 7—Dr. MACKIE replied in the affirmative. Continuing, he said that in 1864 the valuation of Thel- wall was £282, which had been raised to £926; Latch- ford was £248 and it was now £1,487; Penketh £282, raised to £1,124; Buttonwood £3,035, raised to £5,236; War- rington £5,406, raised to £9,763; Winwick £2,794, in- creased to £5,878; Newton and Etrlestown £8,377 had increased to £14,737. Ihe total amount of valuation in 1864 was £20,819, and in 1883, £41,488, or an increase of 99 26 per cent. That statement, he thought, showed the importance of their being exceedingly careful as to any future steps they might take and any future statements they might make with regard to the railway rating. fie was told that every additional goods shed pat up or any passenger station enlarged had been immediately rated—in fact it was rated before the plastering was dry.—Mr. BLACK- /IT/EST observed that with regard to previous remarks which be and Mr. Cooper had made as to the railway asses- ment, they were not prepared with figures at the time, but it was the general belief of the Assessment Committee and other people that the property was not rated sufficiently high. If not, how was it net there had been so much con- troversy about the matter, and that the Northwich aci Prescot Unions had taken the action they had? Dr Mackie in the figures which he gave did not deal with the number of additional miles of railway that had been put down —Dr. MACKIE said alit in 1864, the company owned 1,000 miles, but last year that number had risen to 1,700. There was no mystery or secret about that, and he hoped Mr. Blackhurst would net consider he had been "cooking' the figures, as they were given to him.—Mr. BLe.cultuosT observed that he and. others had only been actueted with a deeire to put the rail- way company on the same footing as other bodies. Nant- wich and other neighbouring Unions had very largely increased the assessment, and it was only fair to suppose that Warrington was in a similar position with regard to railway property. However it might be he did not thisk the present was the time for the discussion of the question which was in abeyance and heing considered by the Assess- ment Committee. If he had made any tins-statement hewas sorry for it.—Major CARTWRIGHT slid he was rather disap- pointed that Dr. Mackie did not move a resolution that the 'London and North-Westera Railway and other railways in the Union should be ce-valued. (A laugh) The assess- ment Committee had the matter in hand at present, end perhaps that day fortnight the Board would hear of some oi the movements of that committee.—Mr. COOPER !bought that was an unwise time for discussion on the question. The Assessment Committee had met since the last Board day, and had resolved to send Mr. Sutton and Mr. Owen, valuer, to London to go through the whole accounts of the com- pany, so that a complete statement might be presented. He referred to the enormous increases which. the company had made in their property, and said that weest farmers in the agricultural districts could hirdly keep the wheel going owing to low prices and bad seasons, it was only natural that they should look roand and see that those who had not a fair share of rates should have it. (Hear, hear.):—In reply to the Clerk, Dr. ftisci.3 said the figures he ban given referred exclusively to the London and North-Western Railway—both their lines.— The CLzus said Dr. Mackie bad stated that the total valua- tion in 1864 was £20,819, against £41,488 last year. show- ing a difference of £20,669. The total rateable value of that Union from the time he had been connected with the ATesinent Committee came to £305,747 against what he believed was about one-half when he first became associated with the Committee, so it would be seen that the growth of the Railway Company had only been proportionate with the growth of the property of tho Union. He should, no doubt, be in a position to tell the Board shortly what the rateable value of the London and North-Western Railway Company was 20 years ago and what it was at the present time.—The discussion then ended. There was no other business of interest.

Fresh Butter and Fresh Biggs (for twelve msntlis); Flour, Oatmeal, Gro- ceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the' price to include about 301bs. per week of the best hatcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; Beet Brand ists American or English Bacon; Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery tube named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death. to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of coat to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other con be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and furl her particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the C}erk's office, Frodsham, on or before Monday, the 17th day of March. 1884, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held In the Board Boom, Dutton, on the 18th March, 1884 at Two pm. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter Into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. A fair amount of business has been going forward during the past week at slightly varying prices, influences having acted rather irregularly. During the early portion of the week values received little or no impetus, and consequently the ten- dency was towards ease, but on the publication of yesterday's traffic returns the tone went somewhat better. The above re- marks refer of course to home railway investments, The balance of alterations for foreign funds is favourable. SATURDAY, MARCR 8, 1884.

the House of Commons, on Wednesday, one of Mr. PARNELL'S followers, Mr. BARRY. hloVed the second reading of a bill to amend the Irish Land Act of 188 r. The provisions of Mr. BARRY'S measure are of a four-fold character. By one it is proposed to fix the Judicial rent from the gale day following the application to the Court, and to give the Land Commission power to suspend eviction While a case is pending ; a second provision reserves to the tenant the absolute right to his own improvement; a third brings lease- holders within the scope of the measure of 1881 ; and by a fourth provision it is proposed to extend the purchase clauses of the Act. The various points raised by this bill have been discussed in both Houses of Parliament before, Parliament has decided upon them in One form or another, and it is not surprising, therefore, that Mr. BARRY'S measure should have been thrown out by a majority of 163. It by no means follows, however, that there is not in the hon. gentleman's proposals much With which the Government and Parliament qinpathises. For instance, the provision 'Which reserves to the tenant the absolute right to his own intprovement—and which is Perhaps the most important clause in the bill --is the same, practically, which the Govern- ment introduced into their own measure when Passing through the House of Commons; 'but the Peers, in their superior wisdom—and alive, of course, to their own landed interests --threw it out. Again, it will not be denied that the purchase clauses of the Act of xBBl 'have not in their operation given that satis- faction which it was expected they would do. These clauses must be amended sooner or l„ater, and to the importance of this the ‘3overnrnent are as much alive as any Irish representative. But the present is scarcely the time for disturbing the peaceful relationship which now exists between land- !Ord and tenant in Ireland. Imperfect though I,t May be in some respects, the Act of 1881 has done more for the emerald isle than was ever anticipated by its most sanguine promo- ters; and it is, consequently, the more neces- sary that its beneficial operations should not •De interfered with. If the Act is allowed to develope itself, and to work its own excellent results unhampered, as it now will be, by any alteration, even the purchase clauses may Prove more attractive,than they have hitherto done; this is not 'likely to be the case While the minds of both buyers and sellers are •alike upset by proposals for amending the Act, and which proposals they naturally wait .to see the upshot of, in the hope, no doubt, that an advantage may be gained by delay. It :,eems opportune to call attention here to the work of the Land Commissioners, whose , report of their work for the year ending August 22nd, 1883, has just been issued. From this interesting document it appears that the total number of fair-rent cases dis- Posed of by the Sub-Commissioners during the twelve months was 4,6,14.2, and by the Civil Bill Courts 4,34.5. This shows a marked improvement in the despatch of business on 'the Previous twelve months, when the num- bers respectively were 15,676 and r,807. What may be considered a necessary conse- luence of thzis is, that there ig a correspond- ing increase in the number of appeals -a:waiting trial. The number so awaiting in ;Tlgust, 1882, was 2,61 z ; whilst the number ill August, ,g ,g 3 was 7,215. The Court, "'ever, has not been still, for during the twelveof, months 2.655 appeals were disposed against 1,024 in the previous year—a rate of progress which is very satisfactory. It :as hitherto been a source of complaint ingainst the Court that there has been delay th. disposing of appeals; and in regard to may be -well to point out that the rounissioners state that what delay there s been "is absolutely inevitable under the p, b:ev,sions of the Act as it stands." The num- r 'r of joint applications under the Arrears Act 2 "L the time of its passing until last Oct. 417ith was, we are informed, 95452, whilst t`i e separate applications numbered 40.54-5 ; :2 two classes combined 135,997 Of these 617 were in Connaught, 44,056 in Ulster, ao 2 j4V in Munster, and 13,978 in Le.inster.

DEFAULTING RATEPAYERS AT SUNCORN.—Mr. William Sutton, the assistant overseer for Runcorn,. summoned 77 persons before the magistrates for non-payment of poor rates. Fifty-six cases were settled out of court, and the Bench made the usual orders in 21 cases. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The closing meeting of the session 1883-4 was held on Monday even- ing. The night's entertainment consisted of readings and songs by members of the class, assisted by the choir of the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel. Speeches were made by Messrs. John and Thomas Miller, and R. Hugh-s, and Rev. S. Mees presided. BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES —Six months ago the Rev. R. Yeatrnan was appointed pastor of the Baptist Chapel, Widnes, for a certain period. Mr. Yeatmen has worked amongst the congregation with great success, and has en- tirely fulfilled the highest expectations which were formed of him. His popularity has been so universal that he has rc- ceived an unanimous invitation to become the permanent pastor of the Baptist cause in Widnee. Mr. Yeatman ac- cepted the invitation, and on Sunday preached two sermons to large congregations. SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON THE CANAL AT RUNOOIII.7.- On Wednesday morning a singular accident occurred on the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn to a boatman named Thos. Burgess. The injured man was a captain of a pair of nar- row boats belonging to Mr. T. Williamson, which were being hauled one behind the other from Runcorn towards Preston Brook. On arriving near Delf Bridge the horn was stopped while a tug of the Bridgewater Navigation Company passed with some fiats. The secon 1 boat was thus brought close behind the first, and the captain who was acting as steeper placed the tow rope in a coil beneath his feet. When the horse was again started the first boat was drawn forward and the second fell behind, and gradu- ally the tow rope was tightened. One of the coils was drawn tightly round one of Burgess's legs, and the pressare increasing every moment as the boat advanced,the limb was twisted, and cut in a shocking manner above the ankle. The services of a doctor could not be obtained, and the injured man wastaken to the Liverpool Infirmary. ST. MARV'S SCHOOL, WIDNES.—There is still a debt of £7OO ou St. Maryls Catholic Semi, Widnee, and earnest efforts are being made to clear off the whole sum during the present year. Several successful entertainments towards this end have been held, and another of the series took place on Monday night in the large school-reona, which was largely attended. In the absence of the Rev. Father Clarke, the chair was taken by the Rev. Father Ryan. Mr. S. Quinn gave in a mirth-provoking style "I'm an awful little snub," for which he received =encore. Messrs. Newton and Ryan gave in an amusing manner the humorous duet "Bye and bye," in which the local hits were happily chosen and mach appreciated. The comic operetta "The two imposters" was also placed upon the stage te the delight of the audience, ale characters being sustained by Mr. S. Quinn and Mr. John Williams. Mr. Lawton successfully rendered the "Naughty girls," and the Misses Dugan in the duet "Let music be our pastime to-night" sang very tastefully. In the burlesque " Whats to be done," the parts were efficiently borne by Mr. Newton, Mr. Lawton, Mr. Lee, and Mr. Ryan. Miss Cullen ably acted as accompanist. During the even- ing the brass band of St. Mary's Total Abstinence League, conducted by Mr. Farrel, played several pieces of music. A RUNCORN BOATMAN'S INDIGNATION. Daniel Gre- gory, a boatman, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessioes, en Monday, on a charge at having on the 23rd February used obscene and profane language in High-street; and also with assaulting Henry Tvrigg and Joseph Carter, young men. From the evidence of P.C. Basin and th. prosecutors it appeared that on the evening of the day named Twigg and Carter were in Walker's Vaults, Regent-street, when the defendant entered. Ile called them " knebsticks" for the Navigation Company, and struck them On the face and body. Afterwards he made a disturbance in the street Defendant said he had a "drop of drink" at the time. The prosecutors were nothing but lazy scrawls, and would only work when a strike was taking place,---.Captain Hazlehurst: That is no provocation for you to strike the man when he doesn't say anything to von in any way.—The defendant: R is a pity they are not banished from the face of the earth. They are a ruination to the country.--Inspector Hollingsworth: Stand back and be quiet.—For using ob- scene language the 'defendant was fined lOs and costs 9s 6d, and 5s and costs 9s 64 for each assault, total £2 83 ad, or, In default, 14 days' hard labour. LECTURE ON THE DEVIL AT WIDNES —ln aid of the Wesleyan Methodist Society, Whines, the Rev. Peter Mac- kenzie, the popular Wesleyan lecturer, preached and lec- tured in Widnes on Thursday. In the afternoon a large congregation assembled in Victoria-reed Chapel to hear his sermon,and the collection realised upwards of £ll. Sub- sequently s tea meeting took place in the schoolroom, and there was a good attendance. In the evening Mr. Mac- kenzie lectured on the "Personality, character, and power of the devil," and there was a crowded congregation. Mr. W. Clarke, of Datton, preeided.—The lecturer, in the course of his remarks, which were delivered in his usual humorous and witty style, said the devil was the brightest being ever made by God, and he was the first to rebel against his maker—the first fool who thought he could do better by himself. He avowed his belief in the personality of - a devil, and said to think of him as a mere figure or an alle- gory was to doubt the inspiration of the Sariptures. He bad not the slighteet.doubt that the devil was as much like. the angel Gabriel as he (the leeturer) was like Adam. He had regal power, and was insatiably voracious, going about seeking whom be might deyour..—On the motion of Mr. Joseph Robinson, seconded by Mr. Swale, a vote of thanks was enthusiastically accorded to the lecturer, who, in replying, proposed that a eimilar compliment be paid to the I.chairman.—The Rev. J. Hathersall seconded the motion, and remarked that their church friends had bawd them very much on the present occasion, and the Weslayans were grateful, and would help there when their turn ettee. (Ap- plause.)—The motion was passed, and the congegati‘m separated. The proceeds for the day amounted to nearly £6O.
