vile had with him one companion, also an officer of an English regiment. " Where is he now ?" I asked the colonel. "Probably is a Russian prison," he answered. "He went off to sketch on the Russian frontier, a pursuit of artistic desire with which the Russian military officers deal very promptly." Colonel Colvils has written an account of his journey, which will shortly be pul)lished in book form. He is at present in Egypt, whither he hurried off at brief notice on receiving a staff appointment.
Somebody, it is to be hoped not Lord John, has been play-

lug off a joke on Lady John Manners. In a very interesting article written by her in the National Magazine—or is it Revicw—she descants on the extravagance of modern life, and gravely cites as an illustration the fact that some men smoke cigars to the extent of .£5 a day. She was probably thinking of the Prince of Wales, who, by-the-by, I saw the other day seated in a closed carriage with the Princess and another lady, the Prince smoking a cigar, which I suppose may henceforward be regarded as good maqaers. Or per- haps she had Mr. Chamberlain in her mind; or Sir Charles Dilke, who has in his house in Sloane-street the completest selection of cigars I ever saw out of a shop. But it would be hard work for any of these seasoned smokers, to whom, moreover, .25 is not a serious sum, to smoke it away, even ' through a long summer's day. The dearest cigars I know are the "Rothschild" of Partagos. or the "Imperiales "of , Cabanas. The former can be bought at a box, and ths Latter at 108. Thus, if Lady John Manners' wicked young gentleman got up very early in the morning and steadily set himself to the task of smoking a hundred cigars before he went to bed he would still be within the £5 limit.

Ladies, it must with all respect be admitted, are a little wild on matters of fact, more particularly those limited by figures. I was talking to a lady—or, to be more precise, she was talking to me—on the question of woman's suffrage. Discussing its prospects in the present House of Commons, she informed me that a motion to tack woman's suffrage on the Reform Bill would almost certainly be carried. In proof, she declared that the opinions of five hundred mem- bers of the present House had been definitely ascertained, with the result that 240 had declared themselves is favour of woman's suffrage. This was a remarkable fact stated with precision by an eminent advocate of the cause, It was a new light to me, through which dimly struggled the thought that it was very remarkable, with so strong a leaven of conviction, the female suffrage question was so little heard of in active politics. I took an early oppor- tunity of repeating the conversation to a member of the House, himself a leader of the female suffrage patty. "I am very glad to hear it," he said, with a sad smile, " but Ido so for the first time." I am quite quite sure the lady would shrink from anything even having the appearance of wilfully stating what was not true, but when the delicate fabric of the female mind comes to deal with rude facts, it has a tendency, often unconsciously exercised, to make them "fit."

Mr. Thomas Faed, ILA., whose thoughts are still in the Highlands, will contribute three pictures to the Academy exhibition. His principal subject, to be entitled "Seeing them off," tells one of those pathetic stories that the artist knows so well how to paint. An old Highlander, feeble I , with the burthen of many years, and with care and trouble reflected in his face, stands on the shore of one of his native lakes, with his granddaughter, a maiden of sixteen surnmeks, by his side. He is looking out of the picture, and one feels that he is gazing at the distant sea on which a boat full of emigrants are going from their old home to meet the ship that is to take them to a far-off land. The girl presses close to his side and her eyes are blurred witj'i tears. The dog which accompanies the old man completes the picturesque group. The second work is Called The , Keeper's Daughter." She is surrounded by dogs and dead , birds, and the background is a forest glade where the sun I shines through and tips the foliage. The third picture is entitled "What can she be thinking about," and represents , a bairn about twelve years of age, looking pensively into the fire she has jusl "made up " to boil the kettle for her grandmother's tea. She is lost in thought, and has for- gotten all about it and her old sick charge, whose hand is just visible on the coverlit. Perhaps she is thinking of brighter things that have come into her already careworn little life. Each picture is between four and five foot in length.
_ A ROW IN A WIDNES PUBLIC-
HOUSE,

At WidneS Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and .1 Brock, William Burns and John Burns, brothers, were charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of Arthur James Perkins, Ann• street, Widnes. Mrs. Perkins said the prismers entered the house about half-past ten on Saturday night/ and asked for beer. As they were drunk, she refused to sg-Eve them. Her husband then came in, and gave one of the men a pash to send him out. A row commenced, and the aid of the police had to be obtained. Each defendant was fined 103 and costs 63 6d. In default of payment, they went to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: HALF-DAY HOLIDAY MOVEMENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: HALF-DAY HOLIDAY MOVEMENT AT RUNCORN.

In response to a circular issued conjointly by Mr. F. Fairhurst and Mr. G. Bellamy, a meeting of the tradesmen of Runcorn was held in the Bethesda School yesterday afternoon for the purpose of deciding upon forming a Half- day Holiday Association, or commencing at-. early closing movement. Mr. F. Fairhurst was voted to the chair, and there were about 25 shopkeepers present, including Messrs. G. Bellamy, J. Humphreys, Marshall, Rogerson, Tuna, Woodland,Oldbury, Imison, Marsh, Bowyer, Booth, Critch- ley, Coventry, Blythe.—k motion was made by Mr. Tunna, and seconded by the Chairman, that the tradesmen of the town close their respective establishments at four o'clock. An amendment was made and seconded that the hour for closing should be died at 1 o'clock, and this proposal was carried by 19 votes to 2. Opinions as to the day which should be selected were somewhat more varied, but Thurs- day as ultimately accepted by IS votes to nine. It had previously been ascertained that the minorities would accept the ruling of the majority, and there is no reason to doubt that the tradesmen present will fall to carry out the arrangement. Mr Bellanny was appointed secretary, and Mr. Fairhurst treasurer, and several committees wore formed to carry out a systematic canvass of the town. We may state that Mr. Jackson, grocer. and Mr. Rindle, draper, al- though not present, are in favour of the movement.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the meeting of this Board, on Tuesday last, Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs. J. Lock- wood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, Stokes, Highfield, Campkin, Smith, Darbyshire, Hamilton, Whitlow, Weir, Andrews, Mclntyre, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Lir:taker (deputy clerk).

div.head: lISTIMATES AND THE BATE.
div.p: THE lISTIMATES AND THE BATE.

Mr. NANDLEY said that day was the time for fixing the basis of the Union call for the ensuing half-year. He found from a carefully prepared return that the cipital for the current half-year had been £7,311. Of this amount there was contributed from the various townships £5,701, the rest being a balance that was in hand. The probable expen- diture to March 25th was £5,444, leaving a balance in hand of £1,867. This balance was rather lower than usual. It was scarcely safe for their accounts to have a smaller balance than £2,000, for he believed the Board had that day received notice of a county call ef £l,BOO, which would bring the balance very low indeed. The expenditure during the forthcoming half-year was for school fees of non-pauper children £l2, for that unquestionable luxury of a contested election at Runcorn £39, county rate £2,529, instalment and interest on loans £llO, common fund charges £4.342, less £395 for estimated common fund receipts, and £2028 for balance and contingency fund; total, £8,605. Now this sum had to be raised from the various townships in the shape of a Union call. The rateable value of the Union , was £211,794, being an increase during the 12 months of £5,351. There had been an increase on the rateable value during the past 10 years of £45,248, so that the Union was progressing satisfactorily. A rate of 7P. in the £ would produce the sum of £6,839, being a stool-ease of i t. in the 1£ as compared with the corresponding period last year ; but he thought it would be found that the rate wonld have to be 82. in the £ instead of 7d, so that the basis of this estimate would have to be amended. An account for £165, which would have to be added to the common fund charges, had just come in, while there was an additional £4O for the ambu- lance. He, therefore, did not see how the rate could be less than Bd. He moved that the estimates be amended and passed, and that a rate of Bd. in the £ be passed.—Mr. Nortawe seconded the motion, which was passed.

AN AMBULANCE FOR THE WORKHOUSE. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said the Committee appointed with , reference to providing an ambulance at the workhouse had met and conferred with Dr. Robinson, the medical officer of the house. They had had under consideration a letter from a Arm of carriage builders in London, who offered a one horse ambulance for 65 guineas, and an ambulance to be drawn by a man for 45 guineas. Mr. Darbyshire had, how- ever, been in communication with Mr. Joseph Garner, of Latchford, near Warrington, who would supply a one horse ambulance similar to that in use at Warrington Hospital for £4O. Ihe committee recommended the purchase of the latter, and be moved that it be accepted, subject to the approval of the medical officrr.—Mr. NOIiMAN seconded the motion which was carried.—There was no other businesq nf public Interest.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

REFUSING FACILITIES FOR DISCUSSION "-THE PLAIN FACTS OF TEIE CASE-TORY POLICY- WORK MUST BE DONE-A WINTER SESSION- LORD RANDOLPH'S "DOUBLE" IN THE GALLERY -"IN THE SPEAKER'S CHAIR "-A TRIP ACROSS THE DESERT-COLOSSAL CIGAR SMOKING- WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE - LADIES WRESTLING WITH FACTS-PEEPS AT ACADEMY PICTURES.
LONDON, Thursday.

A great deal of virtuous indignation is agitating Con- servative circles on account of Mr. Gladstone's fresh iniquity in "refusing facilities" for the discussion of Egyptian policy. This is sheer nonsense, though it will doubtless serve its purpose. The simple fact is that the Conservatives have in existing circumstances as full, and indeed, fuller, opportunities for debating the subject as they would have had under the arrangement originally projected. They blundered in the first instance in a way not creditable to old and experienced Parliament men. It was at first sight incredible that ten or a dozen gentlemen, some of whom have been in the House for 30 years, and all of whom as- sisted at making the new rules, should have overlooked the one that barred their intended action. According to this rule (a most useful one) when the House has once got into Committee of Supply, whether relating to army, navy, or civil service estimates, the Speaker leaves the chair without putting the question. That is to say, the House gets to work at once instead of the whole evening being given up to discussing some Collateral qneetien and money being Toted in the last hours of a wearisome sitting. The House has already been in Committee on the estimates to which these are supplementary; therefore Colonel Stanley cannot move an amendment with the Speaker in the chair. But the whole subject can be thrashed out in Committee exactly the same and at greater length, because whilst a member may speak only once when the Speaker is in the chair, he may, and often does, make half a dozen speeches in Committee. Apart from this particular grievance the insistence upon another set debate on the Egyptian question is a little too much. It is juet Over a fortnight since a debate that had extended through five sittings closed with an overwhelming defeat of the combined forces of Sir Stafford Northcote and Mr. Parnell. In addition there have been seven informal debates raised, and every night the House meets the Govern- ment are cross-examined on their policy in Egypt. The real meaning of this fuss is not hidden behind a cloud of words. The design of the Conservatives is two-fold. First to em- barrass the Government in their difficult task in Egypt; secondly, to occupy time so that the Reform Bill shall be I put off till a period of the Session when it may, with some ehow of decency, be rejected by the Lords. Apart from the , Beformßill it is clear that the less work the present Govern- ment are permitted to accomplish so much the better for Toryism and so much the worse for the Government. The people make a hard task-master. They do not look at pro- II fessions or consider efforts. What they want is results, and if at the end of the Session the Government have little or nothing to show they are straightway condemned. Up to the'present, it must be admitted these tactics have been highly successful. It was a month yesterday since Parliament met, and except that the Reform Bill has been introdnced--;a work for the accomplishment of which a single sitting should have sufficed—nothing practical has I been done. This triumph of obstruction has been skilfully planned, and artistically carried out. So far from laying themselves open to the interposition of the Speaker, the ' Conservatives have managed it under the guise of patriotic effort. They have been so profoundly concerned over Egypt, that they have not permitted the ordinary work of Parliament to go forward. This is all very well; but the Government will presently have their turn. They mean business, and will do it either in March and April, or in August and September. Moreover, If after nightly struggles the Reform Bill is got through the Commons, sent to the Lords, and there thrown out, we shall have a winter session. The week in Parliament has been enlivened by the visit of a gentleman delicately described as " of maniacal ten- dencies." He got into the Home on Monday and when he saw Sir W. Lawson rise from the Lib3ral side and make an opening for the Conservatives to 'waste two hours of the sitting and worry the Government he probably came to the conclusion that he was net the only madman on the premises. However it be he broke out whilst Lord Randolph Churchill was addressing the House. Lord Randolph was in one of those oratorical , moods which, as a rule, he happily reserves for the public platform. He shouted at the ten of his voice. Hs smote the open palm of his left hand with his right fist clenched. lie threw his arms up over his head in final despairing disgust with this worst of all Governments, and to the in- tense delight of the Radicals immediately opposite he in- troduced a new oratorical gesture, buttoning and unbutton. ing his coat as if, like Mr. Parnell in view of the Land Bill, he was half inclined to take it off. Tne gentleman of maniacal tendencies having had what was left of his mind unusually exercised by contemplation of Sir W. Law- son's vagaries became dangerously excited as he watched Lord Randolph. As the noble lord threw up his arms, as a signalman warns an approaching train of danger ahead, the lunatic, to the profound astonishment of persons near him, began to do the same. At last, when Lord Randolph had managed to draw Mr. Gladstone into personal altercation, the " gentleman of maniacal tenders- siert" could stand it no longer. Leaping up and throwing one his arms, always in ludicrous imitation of Lord Ran- dolph, he shouted out, and was immediately put out. This is the first interruption of the kind we have had since an Irish patriot, excited by another noisy orator, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, playfully called in Home of Commons confidence "Tin Pot O'Conner," celled out from the gallery, "That's right, T. P.; let 'em have it hot."

I hear of a very pretty picture now on the easel of a well known artist. On the night of the election of the new Speaker the member for a northern borough was in the House with his wife and little girl, a pretty childoictures- quely dressed. Seeing vacant the great big chair which Sir Henry Brand did not take away, the little lady Mimed into it and sat there, a perfect picture framed in the pro- found recess of the chair. It does not require any great effort of imagination to realise what a pretty picture this will make, treated as it undoubtedly will be by the artist who had the good fortune to be present at the moment.

The restless spirit, born of the indolence of the House- hold regiments, which landed Colonel Burnaby first over the walla of Tokar, took another officer of the Guards on a journey, not quite so perilous, but not less in- teresting. It was Colonel Colville of the Grenadier Guards who went to Arabia to survey the site of the proposed Jor- dan Valley Canal. Colville went right across the desert from Egypt riding on camels, and following the old pilgrim track. It was a long lonely journey, though full of interesting episodes. At one time he came upon a vast camp of Arabs on their way to Mecca. The way of getting about in these parts is to pay black mail to the chiefs, who hold sway over successive tracks of country. For this money they provide camels and a safe conduct. The geographical limit of their territory, though it does not appear on any maps, is dearly marked. At a particular spot one chief's territory finishe., another begins, and there arises necessity •for more black mail and a change of camels. Colonel Col-
A MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT RUNCORN. A WOMAN DROWNED.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Burial Board Offices, Cemetery, Runcorn, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of Eleanor Hart, a woman of bad char- acter, whose body was found in an arm of the Francis Dock on Sunday morning. Mr. W. Broadhurst was the foreman of the jury. The following evidence fully explains the cir- cumstances : Elizabeth Ann Hart, who said she lived with Sarah Ellen Jackson, 26, Bick Cooper-street, deposed that the body seen by the jury was that of her mother. Her mother had no settled residence, and was 37 years of age. About a week ago her mother told her that some man had thrown her into the Fenton Dock. Witness asked who the man was, but she would not say, and remarked that she did not know the man. She was not aware that her mother was afraid of anybody doing her harm. When in drink her mother was subject to fits. She saw her mother at the Three Crowns on Saturday night, and she seemed all right. She had a black eye, which she had seen a week before. By Inspector Hollingworth : Her mother some time ago fell into a dell at Weston.

Sarah Ann Cuckow, Zion-place, Mill-brow, said she had known the deceased for some time. Witness was near the Derby Arms in High-street on Saturday night at about a quarter to nine, and saw the deceased, who asked her for three-halfpence. Witness went into the Derby Arms with her and paid for a bottle of chiles. The landlady refused to fill for deceised, as she thought she was not sober, but wit- ness thought she was. As soon as deceased came outside a boatman whom witness knew by the name of "Ned" (and whose name she had since heard was Edward Hodgkinson) put his arm round her neck. She did not hear Hodgkinson speak, but the latter pushed his arms away, two or three times and said, " Take your arms away." Witness told the man to go about his business. Hodgkinson was not sober, and witness left the two standing against the Derby Arms. She did not see deceased alive again. She had never heard the &ceased say she was afraid of anyone. Deceased was in the habit of going with men, and she had seen her with Hodgkinson several times previously. If deceased was in the least put out of the way she was liable to fits. The deceased told her last Thursday that just a week before she had been down the locks with Ned, and that she had got into the water, but she could not say how. She said a boatman and his wife pulled her out and gave her some tea. She did not know whether Hodgkinson used logo and see her.—lly the Coroner : The fits of the deceased lasted about five minutes, and she fought heavily. It was hard work for her to breathe, and she went black.—By the foreman: Her own idea as to how the deceased got into the Francis Dock was that she had a fit near the edge of the water. Edward Hodgkinson, after being duly cautioned by the Coroner, was sworn, and said he had no settled residence. On Saturday night he saw the deceased at the Derby Arms, and she paid for a glass of beer for him. She then asked him where he was going to stay, and he said on John Twigg's boats. She said she would see Lim safe on board. She went with him and saw him safe on board, and she stayed some time, but he could not say how long, as he had had a drop of beer. She said "Good night, love," in answer to him, and that was the last he saw of her. John Twigg said he was captain of the narrow boats En- terprise and Speedwell, owned by Mr. H. Evans. On Satur- day night the boats were lying in the Slate basin, Bottom Locks. He engaged Hodgkinson on Saturday night, and told him to go on board his boats and sleep. Witness did not sleep there that night. About half-past eight on Sun- day morning, when be went to the boats he saw a body in the water with the upper part of the head out of the water. He called to a man named Potter, and the body was taken out with the assistance of two other men. The right hand of the deceased was clenched, and in pulling the body out the deceased's face was grazed against the wall in two places. He noticed that the deceased's clothes were torn about the armholes. Witness sent for a policeman, and then went on board his boat. Hodgkinson was not there. His wife, who was on board, told him that she thought the bed had not been slept in. He looked to see whether there were any marks of a struggle, but he could not see anything. He did not see Hodgkinson until about half-past one in the afternoon, when he was near the Waterloo Hotel at Top Locke. Witness said "I think the police are looking for you." Hodgkinson answered "I think I'll go aburd, and If they want me they'll soon Sod me." He did not say anything more to him, and did not see him till Monday afternoon.—The Foreman: Do you think Hodgkinson slept on the boat ?—Witness: I really believe he did.—By Inspec or Hollingsworth : Before witness went to the boats on Sunday morning he saw Hodgkinson near the Derby Arms, and he said that be had been nearly starved.— John Siddall, of Barnton, near Northwich, said he was the master of the fiat Piggot, which on Saturday night was lying near the Slate basin. Aboat half-past eleven at night he was in the cabin, and heard someone speaking near Twigg's boat. The voice he heard was a woman s, and he caught the words 'your old game." He thought it was Twigg and his wife. Before he heard the voice he heard a noise in the direction of Twigg's boats, as though the scuttle was being opened. Dr. McDougall Said that on Monday he made an inspec- tion of the body of the deceased, and that day bad made a post-mortem examination. The body was scantily dressed. The racket sleeves were torn and the arms were bare above . the elbow. About two inches above the right elbow to the inner side was a punctured wound about half an inch in Isngth. cutting the skin through and the fatty tissue un- derneath. The wound had the appearance of having been produced before or immediately after death. The wound of itself would not cause death. It must have been made by some sharp cutting instrument. The hands were clenched and very rigid. He examined the face, and there were several abrasions of the skin, all of wh:ch were on the right side of the nose, face, and cheek. There was a small piece of skin about the size of a threepenny piece peeled off the ring finger, and in his opinion had been peeled off during life. The lower lid of the left eye was discoloured, and appeared to be the remaius of a black eye. There were no, boner broken and no other marks of violence on the body. The hair on the crows of the head was quite dry, and did not appear to have been in water at all. From an internal examination of the body, he was of opinion that the immediate cause of death was drowning, and that the deceased must have either dropped or been dropped directly into the water, which with excessive fatness of the body partially accounted for the body floating an described by the witness Twigg—By Inspector Hollingworth : There was no appearance consistent with the supposition that the de- ceased had had a fit.

' Elizabeth Twigg said she was the wife of the witness John Twigg. She knew the deceased well, and on Saturday I , night, when she (witness) was in her sister-in-law's boat at Top Locks, about half-past ten, she heard a woman whom she thought was the deceased cursing on the other side of the canal. She saw Hodgkinson several times on Saturday night, the last time being at the Waterloo Hotel, at ten o'clock. He was then drunk. She slept with her hush Ind that night on board her sister-in-law's boats. On Sunday morning she went with her husband to their own boats, and noticed that the bed in the Enterprise did not seem as though it ba,d been slept in. There were no signs of a struggle having taken place.—By the foreman: On Monday after- noon Hodgkinson told her that be left the boats between seven and eight o'clock on Sunday morning.—By the Coroner: She said to Hodgkinson that it was strange be did not see the deceased when he came ashore, and he replied that he did not see her. He told her that he had been in the boats all night. She had not heard any report about the deceased and Hodgkinson been seen together down the locks. She did not doubt that Hodgkinson slept on board the boats.—By Mr. Oliver: She expected Hodgkinson at the boats en Sunday, and thought it was strange that he did not come—By Inspector Hollingwortb : Hodgkinson had been with them before, and they had no complaint against him.

Inspector Hollingworth said although Hodgkinson had been engaged by Twigg to go on his boats as hand he had gone to work for another boatman, and he should like to hare the point cleared up. The Coroner thereupon re-called Twigg, who explained that he did not make a definite arrangement with Hodgkin- son. In getting off the boats on Sunday morning Hodgkin. eon's back would be to the body, and therefore he might not see it.

The Coroner suggested that an adjournment should be made in order to see whether any further evidence was foithcorniug. Inspector Hollingworth said the police bad made every possible enquiry for evidence that would throw light on the death of the decease, and he did not think they could get any other information that would help the jury. Twigg stated he had not heard any reports that would throw light on the death of the woman.

P.C. iSroden, in reply to the Coroner, raid he bad seen the watchmen and dockgatemen of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company who were on duty on Saturday night, and they told him they had seen nothing of Hodgkinsou or deceased.

The Coroner said the police did not ask for an adjourn- ment, and it was a question whether, for the satisfaction of the minds of the jury, one should tale place. There was really no evidence to show bow the unfortunate woman got into the dock, and the only evidence before them was that the doctor who proved that the cause of death was drown- ing, and that of the captain of the boat, who told them where the body was found. If the jury thought that any further evidence could be got, it would be the vrisest course to have the inquiry adjourned. If not, then be thought their course would be to simply return an open verdict, so that if any further light was thrown upon the affair at any future time the police would be in a position to take up the matter. He was bsand to say that the only person who could throw any light upon it was the man Hodgkineon, but placed in the position he was, he thought it only advisable to allow him to make a statement, but not to allow a,,y questions to be asked by him. Whether he had told them the truth and the whole truth be only knew. It he had not there was a certain amount of responsibility resting upon his shoulders, and be (the Coroner) certainly hoped be would feel it. One of the things in the case that looked suspicions was that the woman seemed to have been down the locks according to her own statement, some ten days ago with Hodgkinson, and tben appeared to have got into the tanal. From the statement made by the officer in charge of the case he did not think an adjournment would help them, and as the case at present stood an open verdict would meet all the requirements of the law. The jury, after a brief deliOeration, returned an open ver- dict, the enquirY having lasted upwards of four hours.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COM- MISSIONERS.

I The monthly meeting was hpld at the Town Hall,Water- loo-road, on Wednesday, Mr. J. Meadowcroft presiding. There were present: Dr. Steele, Messrs. Speakman, J. Pritchard, F. A. Lake, P. Briscoe, F. Fairhurst, W. Whittaker, Williams, Timmins, Shaw, Norman, and W. Brookes (secretary.)

• TILE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. In his annual report Dr. Mariam said it was satisfactory Ito notice that the death rate was considerably lower than during the previous year, although at the beginning of the year scarlatina was very prevalent. The number of deaths registered from natural causes amounted to 311, besides 30 inquests, as compared with 393 deaths from natural causes and 20 inquests during the year 1882, being a decrease of 82 in the number of deaths from natural camas. During the first quarter the number of deaths was 105, representing a death rate of 24 per 1,000 of the population per annum, of which 17 were due to zymotic diseases. During the second coarter the number of deaths was 70, representing a death rate of 19, per 1 000 per annum, two being due to zymotic diseases. During the third quarter the number was 62, representing et death rate of 16i per 1,000 per annum, three being due tO zymotic diseases. During the fourth quarter the number of deaths was 74, representing a death rate of 191 per 1,000 per annum, two being due to zymotic diseases. The total represented an average death rate of 20 per 1,000 per annum of the population, and as compared with the rate of mor- tality in 1852, showed a decrease of 6 per 1,000. During the past year the number of deaths among children one year and under WAS 102, being about one-third of the total deaths. Since his last annual report the nuisance from pig-keeping had diminished, the scavenging wag better done, and owing to the chlorine passed into the main sewer drains, also in consequence of the •inhataitants having a copious supply of delicious water, the health of the district might be con- sidered satisfactory. During the year not a single case of bad meat or unwholesome fish Vf 39 brought ander my notice. Permit me to again draw your attention to the want of public lactrine accommodation, The Medical Officer's monthly report stated that the number of deaths registered is Runcorn during the past month amounted to 20. Of the above deaths five were due to compulsory diseases; four to diseases of nervous system; three to heart disease; two to abdominal affection; maras- mus, typhoid fever, scarlatina, cancer, hermorthage, and atrophy accounted for one each. Nine deaths occurred among children five years and under, representing a death rats of 16 per thousand. Five inquests were held. The total deaths were 25.—The CEIAIRmAN obscured that the annual report was very satisfactory indeed, and the decrease in the deaths from natural causes indicated that the sanitary condition of the town was in a satisfactory state. He sug- gested that it should be referred to the Highway and Sanit- ary Committee, and this course was adopted. 'TUE MAKING OF STREETS: IMPROVEMENT OF WATERLOO

BRIDGE. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee contained a resolution that the law clerk having expressed an opinion that the ratepayers were liable for the repair of Cross-street, Princess-street, Nelson-street, and Mason-street, the Surveyor be instructed to submit an estimate of the probable cost of putting the said streets in repair. It was recommended that Mr. Henry Linaker be informed that the Commissioners have decided to have a junction with the Liverpool water main fixed at Norton, and to request him to negotiate with the representatives of the Liverpool Corpora- tion to get the work done under his superintendenee. It was further recommended that in the application for the proposed provisional order powers be sought to borrow a sum of £l,OOO to defray the cost of re-constructing and completing Princess-street, Nelson street, Mason-street, and Cross street, and any other streets it may be found neces- sary to construct at the cost of the ratepayers at large. The following report of the Waterloo Bridge Improvement, Committee was recommended for adoption :—" The Com- mittee recommend that they have powe. 's instruct Messrs. F. and G. Holmes, of Liverpool, to peepare plans and speci- fications for the improvement of Waterloo Bridge, and that the Committee after considering such plane and specifica- tions. and conferring with Mr. Holmes thereon, report to the Highway and Sanitary Committee."—Mr. Fisher was ap- pointed a member of the Waterloo Bridge Improvement Committee.—Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. BRIS'JOE se- conded the motion.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN asked what was tho difference between the property in the streets mentioned in the minutes and those in Dukesfield, as the owners of the latter had to pay their share towards the expense of forming the streets. He sheuld like to have the opinion of the Law Clerk read on the mat- ter so that the residents in Dukesfield and the ratepayers generally might know why the destruction was made.—Mr. LAKE replied that the streets were in existence before the passing of the Improvement Act, and paved sufficiently for the purpose required at that time.—Mr. Swam thought the answer given by Mr. Lake sufficient, but he suggested that Mr. Liniker's opinion should be recorded for future refer- ence.—Mr. SPEAKMAN moved and Dr. STEELE seconded a motion that the minute referring to the formation of certain streets be referred back ; but eventually this amendment was withdrawn on the understanding that Mr. Linaker's opinion would be recorded on the minutes.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: COMMITTEES.
div.p: THE COMMITTEES.

_ Ur. P.. Briscoe was appointed chairman of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee. It was resolved on the re- commendation of the General Purposes Committee that Mr. Dobson, Mr. Briscoe, and the Surveyor consider the advis- ability of re-arranging the lamps in the neighbourhood of the branch Post Office at Top Locks, and report thereon. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for Feb. were : Market rents and tolls £23 12s 7d, slaughter-house rents £1 13s 11d, canal boat fees 10s. general district rate £386 Cis id; total, £412 25 7d. Accounts amounting to £295 Is 81 were recommended for payment, and £5O was transferred to the Free Library's fund. The Finance Committee had bad an interview with Mr. J. N. Lello as to proceedings taken against him for non-payment of his rates, and a resolution was passed acquitting the collector from blame in the matter. The Parliamentary and Legal Committee instructed the Law Clerk to take proceedings against Mr. Beckett for the recovery of the cost of repairing the lamps in Green. way-road. PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL.

Dr. STEELE said about twelve months ago he r.ltarted project for establishing an Accident Hospital fox Runcorn, but very little interest was manifested in the movement, which was allowed to die away. He thought 'at was a shame and a disgrace that in a town like Itunco*Al there should not be a place where a man who had the. misfortune to be injured could be taken to. Only that morning he beard of a man having his foot nearly cut off with a rope near Mr. Timmins's works. There was no place to which the man. could be conveyed, and the services of a doctor could not be obtained, so the injured man was compelled to lie on ti narrow boat for some time. At last it was decided to take him to the Liverpool Infirmary. He thought something ought to be done. When be moved in the matter Mote ho received a little support. One gentleman promiecl £2O and several ferns each promised a similar amount, but there ;he matter ended. He intended to again take the project in hand, and he wished, with the permission of the Chairman, to give it publicity.— Mr. Sassy suggested that the present Infectious Diseases: Hospital should be uqed for the purpose as long as it was unoccupied.—Tbe CHAIRMAN said the promoters of the pro- ject received very little sympathy from the public of Run- corn on the last occasion. But there arose several difficulties in regard to it being a ratepayers' question, lie believed the Board had not power to establish a hospital and n.),ln. tam n it by paying the feeq of the doctors who attetthd and so on, and it was thought that the expense would be such that it could not be maintained by voluntary subscriptions. No doubt if the town would give the Board the power to establish and maintain a hospital the cost would not be so great as to make it a burden to the ratepayers.—Dr.STEELM moved that a committee, consisting of Mr. Speakman, Mr. Lightburn, and Dr. Steele, be formed for the purpose of cos- sidering the ways and means of establishing an accident hospital, and report to the Board.—The motion was seconded by Mr. SHAW, and carried unanimously.—There was no other business.
PORT OF RUNCORN. Vessels arrived at and departed from the Brg, water Navigation Company's Docks, for week ending March 4th, 1884.

DISEBTABLIBHMENT. Sir,—From "(i's" opening lines I Pad great hopes of him. But, alas! these hopes, like other unwarrantable - earthly expectations, were doomed to disappointment. There Was such a grand 'tone of lofty superiority when he said he Would not stoop to use language such as I used in describ- ing his queries as frivolous, quibbling, and impertinent. But this unusual elevation, with him, was unsustainable; he soon found his proper level in the use of a disguised Billings- gate. By implication, he says lam a conceited fool. Now It is not for me to deny this; men are like paintings; Vley are incapable of self-judgement, and in both it needs a little interval as well of time as of distance ere a correct Judgment can be formed. Then, again, I am ungrammatical. VVell,l try to make myself clearly understood. That I sac- Seeded with "CE" his rage is the best evidence.' This gentleman says he still holds the brief, ttc., cfre. "No case, abase plaintiff's attorney." But let "CE" throw aside his yell of pusilanimous anonimity and boldly step into the open arena ef respectable and responsible ' Criticism, and ceasing to sling anonymous abuse, grapple with the following facts. With the Church of England as such I have nothing to do. Ills the Estab- lishment I am dealing with, and this was established by Act of Parliament in the reign of Henry VIII, when that mon- arch was constituted its bead. Prior to this we had only a branch of the Church of Rome. Now, I think that although the specific mention of the word Establishment may not occur in any Act of Parliament, the very fact of this body undertaking to make a King, head of the Church, is in itself sufficient evidence of Establishment in fact, if not in name. Parliament, also, I believe, passed certain Acts of conformity to compel the consciences of the people to ac- cept the church dogmas ; to abolish Dissent, and establish the Church of England. Parliament also enacted the forced payment of tithes to the church which, I regard as estab- lishment with a vengeance. So that I think we may con- clude with some show of reason that it was by Acts of Parliament the Church was established. If not, how, "t?" It is held now that taxation without representation is an injustice. Is not this principle applicable to to tithes? The layman, after paying the impost, has no tiontrol over its disbursement .This latter and more pleasant duty being monopolised by his clerical taskmasters. Thus, in effect, the husbandman is compelled to work a certain number of days in the year for the benefit of dogmas and dogmatists with which and with whom he is utterly unsym- pathetic. Were it not that we know " Britons never, never, will be slaves," I should be inclined to regard this as a species of white slavery. Again, tithes are, to Dissenters, a tax on conscience. Suppose a case. A farmer pays say £lO year off his farm as tithes. If he happens to be a Church- man, it may be supposed to be his contribution to the church of his choice; but if a Dissenter, he: is compelled by law to pay tithes, and by conscience to contribute toward the support of his own creed. In this way the Dissenter is handicapped in comparison with the Churchman. In reply to "A Churchman," I would say that, in my opinion, dis- establishment, if not accompanied by disendownment,would be quickly followed by it. Would he kindly show the analogy between the voluntarily raised trust funds of Dissent and the compulsory levies of the State Church ?—I am, sir, yours, dm., • JOHN PEERS. Penketh, March 4,1834.

POT-HOUSE .ARNANGEMENTS. Sir,—Mr. Whitbam evidently declines the challenge I ' gave him in my last letter, to prove that as good work results from bar parlours as from lodge-rooms. His remark about "full-grown water melons" I like immensely, as the comparison is so very delicious, and in striking contrast to a barrel of beer. "11. W." doesn't seem to have approved of my plan of fighting, and, objects, apparently,•to have his own guns turned upon him. But 'All's fair is love and war." Our pledge is a proof of our narrowness. Then so are all pledges in connection with the various societies that exist, and "H. W." can be found to be narrow also. I have no doubt trades unionism to wit. But I have yet to learn that Sir Wilfrid Lawson is considered intemperate, see- leg that he wins the golden opinion of even his opponents. We are "abusive," so are all who condemn evil in any form. No, sir, " El. W." doesn't like us calling a spade a spade. Oae thing is very apparent, he tries his best to out- Herod us. His remark about my "isms "is irrelevant. „I only attacked hint on his tirade against teetotallers. " H. W." infers that because we do not frequent public- houses, therefore we cannot know what goes on there. My reply is, that when I pass a house and see smoke issuing from the chimney, Ido not require to enter to ascertain whether a fire exists in the grate. In lik3 manner when I see a drunken man sallying forth from a beerhonse I come to the conclusion that drinking alcohol has been going on inside. One word about "despots." "11. W." is here very inconsistent, inasmuch as he prohibits his children from partaking of intoxicants. Ido not blame him for thus actin, only I like sensible men to be consistent, an -I not call others nurom-mind,,d despots for only doing the same thing they themselves are doing. We, as teetotallers, feel that there are big children as well as little that require taking care of, and so we would prevent them from harming themselves by enacting the Permissive Bill. Taking the last letter of "IL W." as a whole, it reminds me of the retreat of the Arabs before the English. They.fought well, but with old fashioned weapons; and "H. W.'s " letter is a reiteration of old hackneyed phrases used generations since, and the last sixteen lines are mere rodomontale.— Yours, W. H. CHAPMAN. Warrington, March 6th, 1884.

DISESTA BUIS HMENT. Sir,—l have read with some interest the letters which have appeared in your -columns on the question "Is the Church of England by law Established?" Then what is the argument between it and the early British Church ? The introduction of Christianity into Britain is somewhat involved in obscurity. There is a high degree of probe. bility that it was introduced by St. Paul. This is evident from the testimony of Clemens, Romanas, Theodoret, and Jerome. From all we can learn on the subject, a Christian Church was founded in Britain in the days of the Apos- tles. What was the mode of worship of the Primitive Church? There was first the reading of the scriptures, then they sung psalms or hymns, then a sermon was preached, followed by a closing prayer. Sir, "For a king's constitution of the Primitive Church," what agreement is there between the elaborate ritual of the Church of England and that of the early British Church? There can be no doubt that the Church of Ancient Britain conformed to apstalic mode of worship. To this succeeded the mission of Augustine with its corruption of doctrine and worship, leading to the " estab- lishment of Roman uniforsaity,". to which the corruption' and decline of the Anglo-Saxon Church paved the way. The question is asked, "By what Act or Acts of Parliament was the Church of England established? " By law? It cannot perhaps be traced to any direct Act of Parliament. It gradually grew up in connection with toe State, and be- came recognised as a department of the State. Hence the successive Acts of Parliament in the reigns of Henry VIII., Edward VI., Elizabeth, Mary, James 1., and Charles 11. regulating its ritual, liturgy, doctrines, and worship. Hal- lam, in his "Constitutional History," speaks of the Church of England as an "Established Church." In the 9th section of the Act of Uniformity it is stated that "J. A. B. will conform to the liturgy of the Church of 2glan d as it is now by law established." (James Smart's History of England, page 439) "The United Church of England and Ireland so designated as the result et Act of Parliament passed in 1801." Do not the clergy on their ordination mike the subscription assert-. log, among other things, the supremacy cf the sovereign in th Church? Are not the archbishops and bishops chosen and nominated by the Crown—sovereign—in accordance with the representaticn of the Prime 51inietei ? And no diocese can refuse that nomination without incurring the displeasure of the law. As to the qm.stion of tithes, "The Tithe Commutation act changed the payment in kind to an annual rent charge." And what the Parliament ban done it can undo. It can dieendow and disestablish with comp.m- ration where necessary. To say that the Church of En.At.nd only, holds the same relation to the State that other churches of the land held is not quite correct. If Dr. j. Clarke NV.II now alive he would hardly re-affirm that it is " the purest national church in the world," honeycombed as it is with Romaniem, which the ?nblic Worship Act was intended to eliminate. Witness the itISIIO of the late le:4M strug,&le in relation to Miles Platting.—Faithfall 7 yoPtiZ.YrESTANT. March 6th, 1884.

THE FOREIGN NEAT SUPPLY. Sir,—l think a few remarks upon the above question will not be considered void of interest. It is a point that has direct interest forth. large portion of our consumers In town and country, and consequently any attempt that may be made in the direction of restricting the supplY of foreign cattle should. 1 tblial7Me'rit-tur strong disapproval, no matter what the plea. may be which a few, like Mr Chaplin and his Tory friends, for the sake of class interest, god expedient to adopt. For it is seldom a cause, however un- just it may be, that a. pretext cannot be found with its sup- porters which is sufteient to render the Sarre instifiable in their eyes_ So with regard to are present question. In consequence of a few of our cattle being in certain districts

!infected with foot-and-mouth disease, Parliament is called I upon to pass a measure which prohibits the importation of ' cattle from certain countries; and although the present amendment professedly is only intended to refer to infected countries, yet I think it not unlikely that on the least ex- cuse this will be applied to all. Now, one would with good reason think that the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act was a sufficiently stringent measure to obviate the call for I any further legislation on this point. There is no special ' urgent demand for the present Bill, for is it not plainly shown by the official returns that the number of animals that are infected is gradually diminishing. But whether this decreate is to be attributed as the result of the Act of 1878 or not I think is open to question, for there are plenty of instances of animals becoming infected in districts where the plea of foreign contagion cannot ba justly borne out. Nobody will dispute that we have not suffered in time past by the impartation of infected animals; but it has, I believe, become acclimatised to our country, and no amount of foreign restrictions will succeed in thoroughly stamping it out. But to come more near to my subject, viz, the meat supply. In which way will the measure that Mr. Chaplin has brought forward affect tho meat markets. ? Well, there is only one way in which it can affect it, and that will be in the undesirable way of increasing the already exorbitant price of beef and mutton, which a great number of our in- dustrial class finds (in spite of the large importations from , abroad) an expensive article to furnish their tables with; and lam inclined to think that if we had restrictions placed on the supply of foreign meat such an article would become • a luxury with a large portion of the poorer class of consumers. And yet this is what would seem to he desired by those "ever watchful servants of the country," (?) the Conserva- tives, who advocate Fair Trade. This they are at the , present time trying hard to convert the agriculturists to, and no doubt they think that in bringing forward the present measure they are bidding fair for the support of that class.. Now in respect to the present high price of beef and mutton, it is, generally speaking, not the farmer that pockets the profits, but such finds its way to what is termed middle- men and the butchers, who are living on the profits of the producers (in this I refer chiefly to the former), and of course any attempt to restrict foreign supply means gain to them, but the reverse te the country. Thanking you for the space you have allowed me, I beg to remain, Sm. - March 4th. POPULI.

MERSEY-STREET.

Sir,—Allow ma, through the medium of your paper, most sincerely to thank the fire brigade men and a few willing hands who so kindly assisted on Tuesday morning to subdue the fire on my premises,io as to confine it to my place only. The manner the steam fire engine did its work was most admirable and the orderly and quiet way the men went about their labour was very creditable and satis- factory.—l am, Mr. Editor, yours most sincerely, JOSEPH MOUNFIELD. Warrington, March ath, 1884.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

The condition of IreTanci-as—ThiWii. by the calendars of the spring assizes opened on Monday is eminently encouraging. At Trim, Chief Justice Morris had only to ask the attention of the Meath gran l jury to six cases, none of which called for any special remark; at Drogheda, Baron Dowse said there was nothing to ha done, and the assizes were only a matter *of form; and at Carrick-on-Shannon, Mr. Justice Johnson said the criminal business was very light and the state of the county of Leitrim satisfactory. Mr. Justice Lawson opened the Clare Assizes on Tuesday, and in his charge he said the returns showed a satisfactory diminution of crime. In reference to the announcement that the Government intend to propose a measure extending the scope of the par chase clauses of the Irish Land Act, a Dublin paper says that this decision was conveyed to Captain O'Shea, Ml' ,by the Premier in a letter which stated that the bill of the Go- vernment would be introduced soon after Easter. Mr. Gladstone expresses "profound gratification at the fact that Irish members of all parties should appear to be in accord with reference to this supremely important branch of the I Irish agrarian question." Be also ventures to hope that "the measure which the Government have in preparation I will be supported with the same unanimity, so that its pass- , I age into law may net be hindered." " MOONLIGHTING " NEAR CAVAN: A MAN SHOT. —On Sunday intelligence reached the police at Cavan that a man had been shot that morning or the previous night in the , neighbourhood of Ballyhighland bridge, midway between Cavan and Killeshandra. Sub-inspector Tilly, accompanied '1 by a number of the police proceeded to the place, where they found a farmer named James Brady suffering from gunshot wounds of such a serious nature as to call for the attendance of a magistrate to take his depositions. Subse- quently a blacksmith named James Robinson was arrested, charged with causing the wounds inflicted on Brady. Robin- son alleges that at a late hour on Saturday night a number of men came to his house and used threats towards him, that ho opened the door and asked what they wanted, when he received a blow of a stone from one of a group of seven or eight men standing in , front of the house, and that in order to in- timidate them he took his gun and fired at them. Brady , was removed to the county infirmary, little hopes being entertained of his recovery. One band is completely shat- tered, and there are go grains of shot lodged in his abdomen. : The accused man Robin3on had also to be taken to the in- firmary owing ta a serious wound in his head. The police are engaged in ascertabaing who the other men present were, as it is considered there are others wounded.

wow A plumber was sent for to the house of a wealthy stock- broker to execute some repairs. He was taken by the bat- ler into the dining-room, and was beginning his work, whoa the lady of the house entered. "John, said she, with a suspicious glance towards the plumber, "remove the silver from the sideboard, and lock it up at once." But the maa of lead was in nowise disconcerted. "Tom," said he to his apprentice who accompanied him. "take my watch and my chain, and these coppers, home to my missus at once. There seem to be dishonest people about this house." THB BOY WHO KISSBD HIS MOTHER.—Tho purest, sweetest kiss Is that given by a boy to his mother. When you see a boy, no matter if he is forty years or one year old, proud of his mother and not ashamed to kiss her, aud not afraid he will be considered a sentimental fool by others for doing it, you have found a man who has a spark of true manhood in him, no matter what or how bad his general record may be. The boy who, when he comes horse, will invariably kiss his mother is generally the buy to be de- pended upon, for there is no boy or man with a guilty con- science who can come up and look his mother in the eye and kiss her. No, the boy who kisses his mother is every inch a man. It is a proud record for any man to have, to have it said he always kisses his mother. KISSES BY POST.—The young postmaster of a village in the district of Znaim WU busy at work in his office when a gentle knock Came to the door and in steppe° a buxom young country lass. Walking up to the desk she handed the official, with a bashful smile, a post-office order, which he closely examined, and paid the young woman the sum inscribed. At the same time he asked her why she had not detached the cotioon from the order, as the sender had written on it a further communication for her. "Indeed?" said the girl; "well, you see, I can't read: perhaps you'll Glancing yrotpuida follows:—" I ybe so bind as to read it for me." The postmaster read as d herewithat thther young ufluogr person, and he thousandadadded, g with his accustomed official gravity: "You have now got the money, and I am ready to give you the kisses at once." The young peasant-woman accepted the balance of her order. On reaching home he said to her folk: Eh, but it's a grand concern—this poet-office: you can now get kisses sent along with your money-orders." geine, Journal.

div.head: EXAMINER SATEJRDAY, MARCH 8, 184.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATEJRDAY, MARCH 8, 184.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Town Council was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday even- ing. Present:—The Mayor (Alderman Harrison in the chair); Aldermen lean, Davies, Burgess, Holmes, and Webster; Councillors W. Pierpoint, Dr. Mackie, Platt, Ashton, Greening, Brown, Barker, Dixon, Monks, Broadbent, Dakin, Wright, Sutton, Bolton, W. J. Burgess, and Whittle; Mr. W. H. Brook (town clerk), Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. C. Chortey (borough treasurer), and Mr. T. Paterson (gas engineer).
ELECTION 01 AI7DITORS. The TOWN CLERIC reported the return of Messrs. John Harrison and J. L. Mostalt as elective auditors for the borough ;.and that the Mayor had nominated Mr. J. Woolf all

as his auditor. WATCH COMMITTEE: RECKLESS DRIVING IN WARRINGTON STREETS.—THE NEW CORONER CRITICISED. When the Watch Committee's minutes came up for Con- sideration, Councillor Dr. MACKIE said he wished to impress upon the members of the committee the importance of having more stringent rules than he presumed at present existed with reference to the quick traffic in the streets of Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) It was racing in some cases and over- driving in others, by young fellows who wished to "show off " their ability by driving, in some instances, wretched animals, and in trying to prove what was utterly incorrect, that the road was made for horse traffic instead of being for foot traffic purposes. The question had been tried again and again in their courts, and the Town Clerk would bear him out when he said that foot passengers could claim the ordinary time in crossing or re-crossing a street or walking from one part to another which was usually allowed for walking, and the owner or driver of a vehicle was bound to pull up to give them time as pedestrians to move along. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the recent sad accident which betel Mrs. Hall in Sankey-street, Dr. Mackie drew attention to the want of a licensing system amongst drivers, and said that the committee should limit the speed of vehicular traffic to such an extent so that there might be comparative safety in their streets. (Hear, hear.) Now that he was upon his feet he would take that oppor- tunity of also calling the attention of the committee to the fact that the gentleman who had lately been appointed coroner of Warrington had taken a position as coroner which he trusted they would never for a moment allow to be yielded to him except under the strictest ruling of the superior courts. He believed it was his friend Alderman Holmes and himself who some 30 years ago had a right good light with a gentleman who was coroner for so many years. The coroner at that time had what they considered the impertinence of ruling that no member of the Society of Friends should be foreman. He (Dr. Mackie) was then a young man and a new man in the town, but he remembered having taken up the matter and fought it to such an extent that at last they made the coroner quail—(laughter)—and he ultimately recognised and conceded to their opinion, that a member of the Society of Friends should not only enjoy equal rights and privileges, but that he was in many respects a man to be preferred for such an office as the one in question. (Hear, hear). The pres- ent coroner was "drawing it on" with them, and he should I like to refer it to the Town Clerk or any Committet, as to the right of what bad been laid down by Mr. Brighouse, as a stranger, and against a practise that had existed there from time immemorial, and against what he believed was a prac- tice in the three kingdoms, viz, that the nearest friend of the sufferer or deceased person could not appear in the coroner's court and ask those questions which he would naturally wish to ask without being obliged to engage a solicitor, who might in the first place be difficult to get, or who might have little sympathy with the person who had suffered, and perhaps be in a great haste to bring it to an end. He trusted that they would let the Coroner know that the people of Warrington, who fought for the rights of the Society of Friends thirty years ago and won them, were not those who were ready now to sit down and allow their rights and what he might call their liberties to be taken away in such an important affair as being represented in a Coroner's court. Alderman BURGESS very cordially concurred in the observations of Dr. Mackie as to the danger there was at present in moving about the streets of their town owing to furious driving. (Hear, hear.) Many of those who were guilty of furious and careless driving were a lawless sort of persons, who did not care anything about what might happen to the less fortunate people who had not the oppor- tunity of driving. He, however, did not think that the at- tention of the Watch Committee needed to be called to it, for his impression was that the police without instructions from the committee had a duty to perform to the inhabi- tants of the town, and if furious driving did obtain, as he maintained it did ebtaio, it was the duty of the police to in- tervene and take measures preventing it. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was the duty of the Chief Crnstable to so in- struct the force that they would not have a repltition of the furious driving. With reference to the latter part of Dr. Mackie's question as to what the Coroner was doing he was in ignorance, and could not therefore say anything about it, but he hoped what had fallen from Dr. Mackie would not be lost upon Mr. Hunt and his force. Alderman Waosran explained that the matter had been under the consideration of the Watch Committee, as the Mayor yould perhaps recollect, and instructions were given to Mr. Hunt to summon all persons who might be driving furiously or carelessly in the streets. lslo doubt the instruc- tions were being attended to, or, at any rate, he hoped so, for the rate at which carts were driven down Bridge-street and other crowded thoroughfares was something fearful to contemplate. Councillor Purr said he quite agreed with Dr. Marine in the view he took as to furious driving, that all persons driving in the.streets should be licensed in some way by the Watch Committee. He did not know whether it would be practicable or not, but there was a need for something of the kind at the present time, because they frequently saw vehicles driven in the streets by youths who had no right to be in charge of them. Young people and boys of tender age were in charge , of horses and vehicles which they would not have power to control if it became necessary to put the animal under restraint, and he thought such a thing ought to be stop- ped. Boys of tender age ought not to be allowed in their crowded streets to have charge of vehicles, for they could not have proper control over them. (Hear, hear.) They were just the persons who were guilty of furious driving—they did not possess the necessary judgment and conszquently drove at a rate which was not safe in their streets. With regard to the latter portion of Dr. Mackie's speech, be thought the thanks of the Council were due to him for bringing the matter forward. He did not know whether or not the Coroner was right in excluding everyone who was not represented by a solicitor. If that was the case he (Councillor Platt) was afraid there would be a great mis- carriage of justice in mmy cases, and he quite agreed with ' the remarks of Dr. Mackie. The MAYOR said he would only trouble them with a very few observations. With reference to furious driving that was a matter of great consequence indeed, and the Chief Constable's attention had been drawn to it, as had been stated. He very vigilantly watched people who were driving vehicles up and down the streets, and he (the Mayor) knew that police officers themselves were constantly on the alert, as was evidenced by the fact that they frequently brought people before the magistrates for being guilty of furious driving. But the officers could not always be at the heels of the offenders or in close proximity to them, and they took advantage of furious driving when no policeman was about. It - was a serious matter, and a very sad accident had occurred within the last few days—an elderly lady having died at the Infirmary from the effects of being run over. With reference to the observations of Dr. Mackie, several gentlemen 'present would remember the somewhat ludicrous termination of that conflict, which un- doubtedly was a triumph for the inhabitants of Warrington over the tyranny, he might call it, of the then existing coroner. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was only proper that that matter should be mentioned there, although it was not on the minutes, and strictly speaking it was not in order. Still the importance of the subject was of such a magnitude that he thought in that case the end justified the means, and he was not sorry Dr. Mackie had introduced it. It ap- peared simply absurd to him that in order to elicit the truth no interrogations should be put except through the mediura of a professional gentleman. He might be wrong, but he did not think any harm would be dens in drawing the attention of the coroner to the matter. The minutes were then passed. THE PROPOSED WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET: WHAT WILL TIER COST BE ?

Alderman HoLtaxe moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion. Alderman DAVIS'S then drew attention to the proposed widening of Bridge-street. He did not want it to get abroad that he was against that improvement—he was only going to ask each member to do what he would ask any business man to do, and that was, that before going into any large question like that, involving the expenditure of large slims of money, they should sit down and calculate the cost before they did it. He pointed out that when the resolution Was passed in August last the then Mayor, Councillor Crosfield, ventured to tell Alderman Burgess that the cost would not exceed £5,000. The Mayor added, that if they got back the price of the land 'they anticipated it might not cost £l,OOO, and at the outside not more than £5 000—it was quite possible it would clear itself. They had since been anxioas about what the cost would be. and in October Councillor Platt said that the committee had taken possession of several plots of land in view of the im- provement. He (Alderman Davies) was not aware that up to then the Council had either inferentially, certainly not directly, ordered the purchase of any of the land in Bridge- street. Hs believed it had never, been given to the Council what the ultimate cost would be, and speaking for himself he never did until he saw it in a newspaper that the ultimate cost after selling the land would be close upon £12,000. That Was, when they passed the resolution in August last to apply for a provisional order it was on the basis that it would cost from £l,OOO to £5,000, and now they saw for the first time that., the £e.s 000 lead gone up to £l2OOO, or rather £11,972. He did not want anyone to think that he was standing in the way of the improvement or that he opposed it, but he wanted them to look at it in the light of business men and see how far they were compro- mi@ing themselves pecuniarily in the improvement. Re proceeded to criticise certain statements made at the Local Government Inquiry, observing that he did not believe the work would be serried out for £ll,972—(hear, hear)—he believed that double that figure would be much nearer the

think that the gross cost estimated would be exceeded at all, and the Street Improvement Committee were of opinion that they would be able to keep it a little under the estimate. All the facts before the committee pointed to the conclusion that in making their gross esti- mate they kept well above the mark, and in inaLziug the nett estimate—in estimating what they should get for the surplus land and so on—they had kept under the mark. It had been said that shop property was not plying at the present time. That might be so, hut if it was, that was the very reason why they should take the matter into their hands at once. If it were to cost them £12,000 and they w,re to take the proporty down to-morrow and sell the land —if they were compelled to pay the amount back during the next 30 years—it would c.iat at the outset Id. in the They would pay a portion of it off every veer, every year they would have less to pay, and at the end of the time it would not amount to above J. in the £. Ile did not think that it wee a prospect that the Council should be afraid of, even if the worst possible estimate was put upon it, and the Street Improvement Committee were expecting that it would turn out more profitable than the figures they had already down indicated.

If it did cost twice the sum named (as he really be- lieved it would) it would be as large a sum of money as they would have to pay for the Town Hall park and grounds and all about, if they had to pay for the whole thing. He , admitted that there was a great desirability that Bridee- street should be widened as a matter of convenience and as a matter of sanitary progress, but they must net shut their eyes to the circumstances of the rates in the town. He did not want to stand •in the way of progress if they could afford it, but the question was—could they afford it? He went on to say that shopkeepers were not doing as much trade as they formerly were, and stated that if the shops they proposed to re-erect in Bridge-street were to pay they must not have shops of less valets than £lOO a year. But they wanted to know whether it was possible to do that in Warrington— whether there was anyone who would build a class of shops at £lOO a year rental on the proposed site they were speakiog of. He thought the Town Clerk said at the hear- ing that the carrying out of the work could be deferred for any length of time. If that was so—it was the material argument for him—he could sit down more s ttiefied. He only asked them as a Council to consider the matter care- fully for a little time, and wanted them as business men to sit down and talk over it a little. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Monies said that the estimate of the cost had not been forthcoming by the Council, and he felt strongly inclined to appear before the Commissioners on the previous Friday and oppose the action of the committee—but he was not quite sure whose action it was. He therefore thought that those who were in the secret of the matter should clearly understand on what ground they were treading. He did not know who were the owners of the property, and he did not know where the money was coming from. He believed there had been no money granted by the Council for the purchase of the property so far, and altogether he felt it was a position he himself would not like to occupy. At that stage he would like to impress on those who had the matter in hand that there might be a danger in delaying a thing too long before the information was forthcoming. Ha did not say anything about the widening of Bridge-street--he had his own opiaion about that. But he believed Warrington was not so rich that it could afford to indulge in luxuries which were costing the lowa about £12,000. No gentleman could tell what the ultimata cost would be. Re hoped the information he bad pressed for, and which he had been assured was forthceming, would come before long. He did net wish to hamper the Council in any way, and it would be very unpatriotic of him to do so. Still he did not care to drift into a policy of which his judgment did not approve. Councillor Dr. MACKIE congratulated Alderman Davies on baying, he should say, the boldness of again coming for- ward, and While they were on what he considered the edge of a precipice, warning them of their danger. He had ap- parently taken a leaf from the great men of the present age in that he had come forward a day too late. (Laughter.) With regard to the question of the shopkeepers he said he felt very proud of that body. He had long been connected with their associations, and instead of representing them as holding up their hands in, should he say, mute despair' at the proposition of building new shops on the ground in question, he would rather say that the shopkeepers would have a regular jollification, when they found that there was to be a proper entry made from Cheshire into Warrington. At the present moment there was no such entry, to say the least, as was suitable for the carriage gentry of Cheshire. There was a very narrow street, a footbridge they might say—a bottle with a very narrow neck—and there was no opportunity for the Cheshire squires to drive into Warring- ton and show off their grand carriages. What was even worse, there were no shops fit, or very few that were fit, for a shopkeeper to take with a view of carrying on an extensive and profitable trade. There were a few good, old-fashioned places, but if they ran their eyes up and down the chief streets they would be painfully struck with the fact that those tradesmen who were supposed to be on the solvent side of matters were those who had large shops where they were able to turn over a good deal of money, and who were able to do so by being able to tempt customers to go to their shops by having a large display and a very codsiderable space for their customers to walk about in. He felt sure that the tradesmen of Warrington would value an improvement in the shops, and he hoped that he should live to see the day when an improvement should be effected at Market Gate, and when it should be made, as it was capable of being made, a magnificent circle, or semi-circle, of shops. An enormous expense bad been incurred in fitting up shops suitable for a class of customers who paid no rates or taxes, and, probably, did not pay them from whence they came, as the chances were they they had no fixed residence. They were told there was something like, he thought £1,200, carried out of War- rington every Wednesday by people who practically paid nothing. These were the men, and the committee had taken them under their protection, whom the shopkeepers feared. In reply to Alderman Davies, he would just state that that gentlemen had overlooked one or two important financial considerations. Mr. Davies said that the money they purposed to spend there would not have any return. His scheme was that the shops, which were to be built at no less than £lOO a year, would be assessed by the overseers at some- thing like £BO. The fact that they would be getting property that would pay and would have to pay its taxes first and STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING. foremost, was a matter that they should seriously consider. Councillor BOLTON thought the whole Council should be formed into a committee to get full information on the mat- ter and not have everything put before them in such a cut and dried shape. If the question was referred to a committee of the whole Council information would be had which they could not otherwise obtain. For his own part be should like to know more about Bridge-street as he was in the dark at present. . _ _ _ _

Alderman DAVIES said he wished to take that opportunity of telling Councillor Platt that the resolution of the Council authorising them to apply fur a provisional order was oased on the statement of the Mayor at that time that the expanse would not be more than £O,OOO. The Council on that in- formation passed the resolution. The MAYOR: Yes, I believe .that was to. . . .

Alderman BURGESS said that that repetition as to the condition of Warrington grated on his memory to a degree which he could not accurately describe. He could not un- derstand why that Council chamber should be made the vehicle for conveying to the world that Warrington was going down, and more than that, he did not believe it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It night be that there was se- vere competition, that there were co-operative stores in Manchester, civil service stores in London, and Lewis's in Liverpool, which, he took it, were no new things to them, as th3y had had them for years; but it was not until the last few weeks that they had heard of Warrington being under a cloud. He did not think that the shopping interest was at 'a lower ebb than it was seven years ago, and then, he asked, how had it happened that they had no external evidence of the want of success in Warrington ? Were there more failures going on? The Mayor, as a member of the Board of Guar- dians, knew as to whether there was a larger number of pcople requiring aid at their hands, and whether there was a larger amount of expend.ture for the relief of their necessities. They were told that a rate of 1(1. in the pound would cover the outlay on the preseat scheme, including the in- terest and Waking fund. At the present moment the rates were 31. in the pound less than they were that day twenty years since. If it was true that there was such a great amount of distress, how did it come about that the rates , were lower? Whether the Council intended going in for the expenditure of widening Bridge-street or into any other expenditure as regarded the future improvement of Warring- ton, he saw nothing that caused him the slightest fear for the future. He believed Warrington was just as good and a great deal better than many centres of industry, and he therefore hoped they would not begin by fouling their own nest in the most abominable way that they could. (Laugh- ter.) Let them have the condition of things fairly repre- sented. Ho knew of no branch of trade which was suffer- ing with the exception of the wire trade, nor of any large number of people out of employment. Their staple indus- tries were not in such a condition that Waariugroa could say there was a large amount of depression existing, and that they must not expend money. If they meant to carry out improvements which were required in a discreet and rational manner Warrington was prepared to meet tha same, and whatever was the position of the shop-keeping interest they would jump through after all. . (Hear, [liar, and laughter.) Tha MAYOR remarked that they had had a very interest- ing discussion, and one which would impart a good deal of information to the inhabitants generally, but he could not help thinking that it had been rather irrelevant. Alderman Davies had given them inform ion about which he hoped every member of the Council would think seriously before giving their votes defloitely on the question. Alderman HOLMES, in replying, said that the statement made by the ex-Mayor regarding the cost of the improve- ment did not come out entirely on his own responsibility but it emanated from the General Parposes Committee in the first instance. They had those discussions several times in that Committee. As had been stated he had no doubt but that the question would have to be argued and re- argued by the Council in the course of the next two or three years. The minutes were then agreed to without further dis- cussion.
