Although they did not take any dlrect action, he thought an expression of opinion on the part of the Council would have he effect in due time if changes were desirable.

The minutes were then confirmed. MOTION' FOR ADJOI7RNMENT. Councillor Dr. Macitta proposed that seeing there were a number of, matters undisposed of that the Council be ad- journed until Tuesday evening nest.—This was seconded by Councillor WarninT.—Alderinan HOLMES moved an amendment that the remainder of the business be proceeded with, which was seconded by Alderman KEAN.—Councillor SUTTON reaurkA that if geatlemen would abstain from making long and unnecessary speeches he would be in favour of proceeding with the business that evening. He was 012 the wrong side of his dinner. (Laughter.) The motion for an adjou-nment was declared carried and the Council separated.

div.head: RUNCORN RlTii-AL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RlTii-AL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Mr. John Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were present—the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Stokes, Ilighfield, I.Vlclntyre, Darbyshire, W.. Whitlow, J. Weir, Andrews, IL Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. FARRINGTON, the nuisance inspector, submitted kis ! triennial report, which contained a number of tabulated I statements of the work he had performed during the past 12 months. The number of sampl,s of water submitted for analysis was 82. Six were returned as first class water, 11 second class, 24 very good, 7 good, and 3 fair, while 31 were more or less bad and unfit for drinking purposes. I Certificates of occupation were granted to fifty- i , five new houses. Nineteen persons were con- victed before the magistrates for infringements ot the Canal Boats Act. Toe graveyards and burial grounds within the district welts in a satisfactory condition, although in many instances the graves should have been made much deeper. The burial ground to Frodsham Parish Church had been recently enlarged and put in a thorough good sanitary state. The Inspector was glad to sty that he consi- dered that the sanitary condition of the entire district would compare very favourably with others of a similar nature. During the past three years many sanitary improvements had been effected upon some of the larger estates within the district, 'amongst which might be mentioned the Alvan- ley, Appleton, Arley. Aston, Choltnondeley, and Walton estates, many of which had been executed without notice h.ing given. The question of water supply was a grave and important one, and had during the past two years received epecial attention. The result so far had been satisfactory, but he regretted to state that the supply in some parts of the district was far from being what it ought to be. Much credit was due to the landowners, the agents (with one or two exceptions), and the general public who had had uotices served upon them, for the kind and courteous man- ner in which they had received the same and the willing- ness they had displayed in endeavouring to comply with them.—The report was ordered to be printed. THE ESTIMATE.

The anus submitted an estimate of the expenditure for the half year ending Michaelmas 1884, which stated that the probable balance at Lady Day was £134, and the estimated expenditure to Michaelmas £2lB, to which was added £lO9 for contingency fund. Deducting the...balance of £134, left the sum of £193 required, and a rate of three eights of a penny would upon a rateable value of £1.01,023 would produce £251 us. 9d. _ _ APPLETON AND Tote SHIP CANAL.

The DEPUTY CLERK said the Ship Canal Scheme would have serious effect upon the sewerage of Appleton. The canal would cut off the sewers from the outlets, and no pro- vision was made in the bill for the disposal of the sewage. The Authority had spent £2,000 of the ratepayers' money on the sewerage works, and he suggested that a committee consisting of the Chairman and the Guardians of the town- ship of Appleton should confer with the Clerk as to the best means of protecting the interests of the Authority so far as Appleton was concerned. If they , could not get terms the Authority ought to appear by deputation before the Committee of the House of Lords. —The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD moved a resolution embodying this suggestion, and authorising the committee to press for the payment by the promoters of the canal of the expenses to which the Authority had been put in defending their in- terests.—Mr. STOKES seconded the m ,ti 00, olaserving that it would never do to have the sewage works destroyed.—The motion was passed unanimously.

div.head: TDB HEALTH OF TUE DISTRICT.
div.p: TDB HEALTH OF TUE DISTRICT.

Dr. Anaras, the Deputy Medical Officer of Health, pre- sented a special report, in which he stated that at a house situated off Church-street, Frodsham, William Forster, the occupier, aged 26 years, and Lilian, his daughter, aged 1 year and seven months, had bsen attacked by diptheria, resulting on the 26th February in the death of the child. Forster was now convalescent. At another house in the same row, occupied by Thomas Forster, Harry Forster, his son, aged seven years, had been attacked with scarlet fever. He had ordered the sale of milk from these premises to be discontinued. At a house at Froelsham Bridge, occupied by Henry Glaaspool, Jessie Ann Glasspool. aged 10 years, had been attacked by scarlet fever. The source of infection in the scarlet fever cases was not easy to trace, bat he was ot ophatou that the disease had been imported from Run- corn. The usual preventative and disinfectant measures had been carried out. He could discover no such sanitary I defects as might give rise to the outbreak of diptheria at Frodsham. Scarlet fever had also been imported into 1 Seven Oaks from Winsford, the two daughters of John Bee- nett having been attacked. A private school in the township I had been closed for the present. At a Ileum in Main-street, Weston, occupied by George Howard. an outbreak of scarlet fever had occurred. John Arthur Howard, his son, aged three years, had died of the disease, while Fred Howard, aged 15 months, was at present suffering from the disease. At another house occupied by Robert Britland, in the same street, his son James, aged three years, was suffering from :markt fever. It was difficult to trace the source of iufec-

tion in this outbreak, but the drainage of the houses was defective, and constituted a nuisance dangerous and in- jurious to health. The cesspools were untrapped, and the odour of the sower gas was distinctly perceptible. lie had examined the sewage arrangements of Mr. Oakell's cottages, Weston, and at the Overbill eettages, Weston, and he con- sidered that they were faulty and insufficient, and that they constituted a nuisance dangerous to health. A death from typhoid fever occurred at Frodsham on the 24th February. —This was all the business.
DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD AND
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

On Saturday, a special meeting of the Darethury High- way Board was held in the Board-room at Daresbury, to receive a report of the committee appointed at the last meeting of the Board with reference to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill now before Parliament, and to give such instructions thereon as the Board might deem necessary. Mr. Edward Greenall presided. and there were also present Sir Richard Brooke, Mr. William Long, and Mr. James Handley (ex-officio:members); Messrs. Joseph Cliffs, James Clarke, P. Percival, James Knowles, Henry tiough,Rigby, Bennett, William Wilkinson, W. Turner, T. S. Burgess, J. Cooper, J. Baguley, Massey, W. Bradford, J. Parr, James Barber, C. T. Whitley-, Mr. Linaker (clerk), and Mr. J. Darbyshire (surveyor).—The Clerk explained that since the last meeting the committee, consisting of the Chair- man, Vice-chairman and Mr. Long bad met and gone over the plan of the particulars of the requirements of the Manchester Ship Canal, and afterwards had an interview at Manchester with the promoters and solicitor.—Mr. Linaker then read a report showing by references to plans laid before the Board the alterations which would be made in various reads in tho district of the Board by the construction of the canal and the clauses for which they had stipulated for the convenience and pro- tection of the inhabitants of Moore, Walton, Appleton, LatchfOrd, and Thal wall.—Lbe Chairman said the interview with the promoters ended with the understanding that the solicitors to the company should send a letter to the Board accepting the terms proposed, while he, on behalf of the Board, should send a letter agreeing to their propositions. The 22ad of February was the last day for petitioning, and as they had net received a letter on bzhalf of the company by the time fixed he wrote to Mr. Linaker. They would have a mile and a half of new roads thrown upon their hands, which would be a serious matter for the Board. There was no time to call anyone together, and therefore he ordered a petition to be presented. Now he wanted the Board to confirm his action.—The Clerk said the pro- mised letter reached hint on the night of the day when the petition was sent off. He gave them to clearly understand that if he received from the company an accept- ance of their terms on the 20th the Board would not petition against the Bill. He did not receive that petition, and accordingfy sent off a petition.— Mr. Long remarked that the promoters appeared very anxious to meet their requirements, and it was rather a pity that the petition had been sent—After some conversa- tion the action of the sub-committee was approved, and the members were re-appointed with the addition of Mr. Knowles to watch over the progress of the Bill and with full powers to act on behalf of the Board.—Mr. Knowles suggested that a clause should he inserted in the Bill to guard against the bridges being open longer than ne- cessary, and this was approved and. resolved to ba acted upon.—There was no other business of interest.

div.head: ......m.01..r..*
div.p: THB QUABBIL AND TRH PARSON'S TITHBS.—A. Quaker, who was a barber, being sued for tithes, went to the parse* and demanded the reason why he troubled one who had never any dealing with him. "Why," says the Parson, "it Is for tithea." "For tithes," says the Quaker. "I prithee, friend, upon what account ?" "Why," says the Parana, "for preaching in the church." "Alas, then," replies the Quaker, "I have nothing to pay thee, for I come not there." "Oh, but you might," says the Parson, "for the doors are always open at convenient times ;" and thereupon said he would be paid, seeing it was his due. Yea and Nay here- upon shook his head, and making several wry faces, de- parted, and immediately entered his action against the par- son for forty shillings. The parson, upon notice of this, came to him, and very hotly demanded why he put such disgrace upon him, and for what he owed him the money. "Truly, friend," replied the Quaker, " for trimming !" "For trimming?" said the Parson; "why, I was never trimme.t by you in my life." "Oh ! but thou mighest have come; and been trimmed, if thou hadst pleased, for my deers are always open at convenient times, as well as thine.' div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held in the Commissioners' Board-room, Town Hall, on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were present Dr Steele, Messrs F A Lake, T Riley, P Briscoe, J Simpson, W Handley, and J D Jones (librarian).—The LIBRARIAN reported during the month of February there were borrowed from the lending library 1,263 volumes, a decrease of 206 compared with the corresponding period last year; from the reference department there were borrowed 104 volumes; total 1,367, classified as follows :—Theology 34, philosophy 12; history, travels, and biography, 145, science and art 47, poetry 11, fiction 1,039, miscellaneous 79. There had been presented during the month by Mr Simpson 64 vols.. including Henry's History of Great Britain (12 vols.), Sir W Jones' Works (13 vols.), and 21 pamphlets; Mr E Imison, Beamont's Halton Castle; Mrs Evans, Australia Illustrated (8 vole.); Dr Bagnall, English Illustrated Magazine three parts to complete the series; Mr R Moore, service of songs "Pilgrim Street."—On the proposition of Mr BRISCOM ac- counts amounting to £3l 19s were ordered, to be paid.—A thousand new catalogues having been obtained, it was de. cided that they should be sold at the price of 8d each.—Mr JONES asked the committee to fix his remuneration for drawing up the new catalogue.—Mr HANDLEY remarked that Mr Jones' salary was under consideration prior to the re,noval of the Library to Waterloo House, but it was deemed advis- able to postpone a decision on the matter until the Library was settled in the new premises. He thought Mr Jones' re- muneration should be increased, the payment for his services in connection with the cata. logue being Included in the salary. He moved that Mr. Jones be appointed secretary in place of Mr. Brookes, resigned, the question of salary to be submitted to a committee.—Dr. STEELE thought £5O per annum would not be out of the way for the two offices of librarian and secretary, considering the work he had had and would have. —Mr. SIMPSON did not think they could obtain anyone who would do the work so well and take such interest in it as Mr. Jones for that amount.—Dr. STEELE : I don't think we could.—Dr. STEELE then moved that the resolution an- pointing Mr. Jones librarian at a salary of £25 per annum be rescinded, and that he be appointed secretary and libra- rian at an annual salary of £5O, this amount to include his remuneration for making the catalogue.—Mr. Siarysox : I have very great pleasure in seconding that motion. heartily approve of it,—Mr. Jones, who had been requested to withdraw, was called into the room and informed of the committee's decision by the Chairman. He said he was very much obliged to them for their kindness. He hoped his services would only show that they had not misplaced their confidence, and that he had the interests of the library at heart.—The meeting then concluled.
"CARD SHARPER" IN TROUBLE AT WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, John Cor. coran, alias Gulliver, who is well known to he police, was charged with being a convicted thief and attempting to steal from the person of Thomas Peacock, a gold breastpin, value 28., his property.—According to the statement of the affair by the Chief Constable, prisoner was a man who lived by his wits, playing at cards, and purloining from people when drunk. About half past ten on Saturday night the prosecutor, who was a pensioner residing at 48, Church' street, along with another man named William Woods, left the Swan public-house and proceeded along a passage that leads to the Crown and Sceptre entry. In this passage there were recesses and dark places, and all at Once out sprang the prisoner, who seizal prosemutor, got his left arm around the latter's shoulders, Woods at the time being in the rear. Prosecutor resisted his utmost in order to push prisoner away, and at the same time he felt a tug near his breastpin. Prisoner then hastened along the entry towards the Swan. Woods said to prosecutor, "Is the watch all right? Tnat'S Gulliver." Prosecutor replied that the watch was all right but that his breastpin was gone, as he believed it had at the time, although he subsequently found that the prisoner had not gained his purpose, the Pr, haying only been shifted from its proper position, tearing the tie. They returned to the Swan, thinking they might tind the prisoner there, but they found he had {lawn, all5lO formation was given to the police, which resulted in pr.iso- ner being arrested by Inspector James on Sunday morning. —The Inspector deposed that when brought to the police station, and on the charge being read over to him prisoner said, "So help me God, lam innocent of it. I was net there." When about to ba locked up prisoner appealed to Mr. Peacock not to prosecute, saying that he had six months before, and that the present case would go hard against !alp. He was thereupon told that he was only charged with attempting to steal, but prisoner replied knowingly that that meant felony in the eyes of the law.—The Chief Constable said that prisoner and three or four others got their limpg by card sharping and robbing people when they were In' capacitated through drink—Prisoner: Do not say that, Mr. Hunt. —The Chief Constable: It is true. You are a perfect dread to many in the town.—Prisoner : I never in town.—The Chief Constable: You are known all o'7o Warrington. Prisoner said if the magistrates dealt leniently with him he would leave the country.—He was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

THE KNUTSFORD POISONING CASE. A peculiar case of suspected attempt at poisoning has been partially investigated at linuteford Petty Sessions. A married woman named Margaret Wilkinson is accused of having attempted to poison her son and his wife. She effected an insurance upon the life of her son in December last, and the theory of the prosecution is that she was desirous of bene- fitting by his death. It is alleged that on the morning of ne 29th January, during the temporary absence of her daughter-in-law, she went into her son's house and placed a quantity of oxalic acid in the tea kettle. The milky colour which the water assumed aroused the suspicions of the son and his wife, and a por- tion of it was kept and afterwards analysed. The hearing of the case was adjourned from Friday in last week until Tuesday, when it had to be further adjourned till Monday next on account of the illness of the prisoner. Medical testimony was adduced that she was at present in the prison hospital suffering from fever, and that it was un- certain how long she would have to remain there. Mr. David Burr, one of the directors of the Wesleyan and General Assurance Society, produced the original proposals for insuring the lives of the prisoner and her own and her husband's children. It appeared that the agent, Mr. Fredk. Child, had allowed Mrs. Wilkinson to affix her mark to the proposal form in her son Wilitam's case, and he himself had witnessed the affixing of the mark, although it was well- known that the son was quite able to sign his own name. When asked how it was he signed his name as a witness to what purported to be Wdliam Burgess's mark, Child said the mother insured him, and the man's wife was present at the time. Mr. Fletcher, who appeared for the prisoner, said he should contend, apart fro n the demerits of the case for the prosecution, that practically the solution that was sub- mitted to Mr. Carter Bell for analysis was innocuous, and that where the poison, or the suggested poison, was of such a character as to be innocuous it could not be said to ha an attempt to administer a noxious thing or a poisonous sub- stance. Mr. Ashworth, one of the justices, said the bench were so far against the advocate's contention, and he invited his attention to a number of cases in Russell on Crimes.— It was given in evidence that the following policies were issued to prisoner on the 17th December, 1883:—Eunice Wilkinson. seven years of age, for £3 101. after three months, £5 after six months, and £lO after twelve months; John William Wilkinson, nine years of age, £4 10s. to £6 10s. ' • Margaret Wilkinson (herself), £2l 75.; William Wilkinson (her husband), £22 18s.; William Burgess (male prosecutor), 22 years of age, £7 17s. Prisoner also took out the following policies on the 31st December, 1883:—Frank Burgess, 18 years of age, £8 17e.; Annie Burgess, 15 years of age, £9 12e.; Annie Wilkinson, 13 years of age, £9 18s.; Maud Elizabeth Wilkinson, eleven years of age, £lO 3s.

div.head: ACCOUNTS.
div.p: THE ACCOUNTS.

The usual accounts were placed before the Board, the only bill of importance being one for £BO 8s 9d due to the London and North-Western Railway Company with regard to the laying down of sewers.—Mr. THOMASON said that be thought the account was a rather large one to be sent in as one item.—The CLERK explained that under the contract the Board were bound to ply the eccount as submitted; it was a case of " Hobson's choice."—The I•ccotints were then passed.

THE MAKAGEMENT OF BAKEHOUSES. Dr. Fox (medical officer) attended before the Board and reported that according to the re- quirements of the new Act he had inspected all the bakehouses in the township and district of the Local Board. The number of bakehouses was ten. The requirements of the Act were very simple and referred in the first place to ventilation and in the next to cleanliness, whitewashing twice a year, having nosonnection between the atmosphere of the bakehouses and the sewer, and also with regard to sleeping in a bakehouse, or keeping any animals in a bakehouse. The Act, he should imagine, would have more effect in large towns than in one the size of Lvmm. He was happy to inform the Boat d that there was not a bakehouse in the township in which they could not take their meals. (Hear, hear.) There was puled cleanli- ness in them;

OP TEM DISTRICr. Dr. Fox also reported on the state of the public health of the district. He must inform the Board how very fluctuat- ing death rates would he when they were calcule,eci upon a short period of time and upon a small poreeiation. In IN, month of January the death rate 'wag as low as 25 per 1,000, and in the month of February there were 12 deaths, which considerably increased the death rate; the average for the two months was 166 per 1,000. lie did not know that he should have mentioned this subject but for the fact that he had heard many complaints of sickness being pre- valent in the district. He thought that the remarks that had been made—in ordinary conversation, and also some- what officially—were exaggerated, because in the total re- turns general sickness was not apparent ; neither was it apparent in the returns received from the Guardians. He thought that it was often the case that when anyone was suffering from a particular complaint they afterwards discovered that many other people had had similar complaints, whereas rt they themselves had not suf- fered they would have known nothing about other people having done so. Perhaps some had had complaints, and had found that others had had the same, but he did not attach any significance to that. However, people should be very oarcful, and should keep their houses clean, especially at this particular time of the year. There would be nothing but benefit in that, but he thought that he should be doing wrong to alarm the public Jnind by saying that there was any particular amount of sickness, or liability to sickness, in the district at the present time. In the two months mentioned there had only been one death of any of the seven zymotie diseases, and that was one from diptheria. That was an isolated case, and he did not know of any more such within a radius of 20 miles. He ought, perhaps, to add that he had two deaths from diptheria at Northwich in Janaary, but at the present moment he did not think there was any case nearer than Crewe.—The CHAIRMAN supposed that the two death rates only showed an average when taken together.—Dr. Fox said that it was below the average; he should be sorry to give an average for one month. Seven- teen per thousand was a fair average in a large district.— In answer to questions from the Board, Dr. Fox proceeded to say that if diarrhcet were epidemic in the district it would soon appear in the sickness amongst the paupers or in the mortality returns. Therefore, he thought that if that disease existed it must be through Waal causes ; if he was called to investigate any such cases he should be glad to do so at the individual houses of the patients. As re- marks had beea made about the sickness in the district, he thought it better to attend before the Boat ito answer any questions they might require.— Mr. CHM:HIRST said that he had heard of a rather sharp attack of diarrhcea, but he did not know that there was any- thing dangerous about the case, and it was certainly not severe enough to make anyone go into father enquiries.— Dr. Fox said that he had made enquiries about the death from diptheria; he imagined that the house where it oc- curred drained into the trap of the sewer, and at any rate there was no manhole or ventilator there.—The Board ex- pressed the opinion that there should be some provision made for ventilation and the subject dropped.

LYMM AND STATHAM SEWAGE. Mr. JOHNSON, on behalf of Messrs. Wilson and Mulliner, reported that the works in connection with this contract having now been completed, they had very little further to say. They proposed to continue a periodical inspection during the contractor's liability for the maintenance. In accordance with the instructions of the Board they had obtained an estimate from Mr. Brazendale for the opening up of the Rush Green old-flushing chamber and handed it to the Board. The fence planted in Marsh's field, 198, not being satisfactory, had been grubbed up and re-planted with a better growth of quicks. Some of the distributing channels on the outfall land had also been strengthened. Mr. Brazendale had applied to them to ascer- tain their opinion on the subject of an application he in- tended making to the Board to pay to him at once one-half of the retention money, amounting to £9OO 2s 1041, due to him on the 7th of August next. So far as they could see, one-half of this amount, it conjunction with the collateral security held by the Board, would be sufficient to. meet any contin- gency likely to arise. The contract was drawn up to protect the interests of the Board in the fullest manner.—Mr. ROGERS: We are to understand as a matter of fact that we hays no power to do this ?—The CLERK: That is the important question. I should like to have the opinion of the Board. —Mr. TnomAstart instanced a case in which one-half of the retention money had been returned in a similar manner as now requested by Mr. Brazendale.—The Board generally expressed a willingness to oblige Mr. Braaendale, but several of the members feared,that if they did so they would be surcharged by the auditor.—Mr. AErywrON: The auditor is always surcharging something. If he did not surcharge when he went round they would think in London that he had done nothing. He must do that, and it will be a good job for him.—The CHAIRMAN said that he should not like to be surcharged.—Mr. TROXIASON then moved, and Mr. APPLEION secomied, that the applica- tion be granted, but after a conversational discussion, the motion was withdrawn, and the rhatter was adjourned, it being understoo4 that some members of the Board would have a personal interview with Mr. Bnizendale on the sub- jest.

AN OBNOXIOUS MEMORANDUM—TEACHERS AND SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The following memorandum had been issued to the head teachers in the school:—"sth February, 1884.—Memoran- dum relating to the attendance of children at school.—l am to call the attention of the teachers of the school district to the large number of irregulars reported, while the atten- dance are frequently equivalent to seven-tenths of the pos- sible whole, and I am to point out that it will be impossible in the future for the visitor to give his full attention to those childaan who have attended school to the extent of MX times out often. lam to remind the teachess that on the 10th November, 1883, the Education Depart- ment, in a letter which has appeared in all the principal public prints, expressed themselves as follows :—' With regard to irregular attendance, it should he borne In mind that this can be checked by nothing so effectually as by the co-operation of managers and teachers with the local authorities in the exercise of their compel- gory powers. That co-operation is often wanting. But better far than attendance legally enforced is that which reaulte from good teaching in the school and the active per- sonal influence of teachers on their scholars ent of school. Irregularity is one of the marks of an inefficient school. A good teacher is the best attendance officer in the district- but teachers too often seem to think that, since the introduction of compulsion, their duty to the children under their charge begins and ends with the hours of the time table. As regards the practice of returning the weekly reports, I am to state that in the opinion of the Board it is beyond the power of the visitor to make the full necessary enquiries into the numerous cases, and afterwards to report to the teachers.— F.ltiornaclerk.' "—A deputation from the head teachers con- slating of Messrs. T. H. Annett, A. Jordan, and H. Fitton, waited upon the Beard with reference to the memorandum. —Mr. JORDAN explained that at a meeting recently held by the head teachers of the district they had had under con- sideration the memorandum on school attendance. Their opinion was that if that memorandum was carried oat it would have an effect upon the attendance of children at school, which he was sure would be quite opposite to the desires of the Board and also of the teachers. It was decided at that meeting to present a memorial to the Board, and the teachers present were appointed a deputation for that pur- pose.—Mr. FITTON then read the memorial as follows: "1. The action adopted at your last two meetings has had a most prejudice' effect upon the attendance of children at school throughout the district over which you have con- trol. 2. Since the Government grant is now based upon the average attendance it must of necessity be the interest and the desire of both managers and teachers to assist the Board in every possible way in securing regularity of at- tendance. 3. From the last report of the department (page 369) it appears that the per centage of attendance in Run- corn is only 70. They regret that an implied charge of want of co-operation with the Board has been made, inas- much as they have furnished weekly large lists of irregu- lars, and in addition voluntarily spent much time in per- sonal visitation, thus showing their hearty willingness to second the efforts of the Board. They admit that good methods of discipline and personal influence of the teacher go far to secure regularity, bat they cannot accept the posi- tion assumed by the Board that it is part of their duty to do the work of an attendance officer. 4. The Education Act and your own bye-laws require attendance for the whole time the school is opened, namely, ten times per week ; and that local authorities are constituted and have the power of appoint- ing a sufficient staff of officers for the express purpose of seeing that these regulations are carried out. 5. They acknowledge the good effect of the past work of the Board upon the school attendance, but they regret that they are now in a worse position and have less power in enforcing regularity than before the introduction of compulsion. They are still prepared, as they have always been, to use their best efforts in securing good attendance, but they can- not pretend to be held responsible for matters beyond their control.—Signed on behalf of the teachers, ALBERT jOll. DAN, T. 11. Arninere, H. Farrow." Mr. Joneater said he could give the assertion that teachers seemed to think their duties began and ended in the hours of the time table a most unqualified denial. With regard to the want of co-operation between teachers and the local authorities, he might point out that in this district teachers regularly and weekly supplied large lists of irregulars, although the law did not compel teachers to do so, nor could the Board demand them. If the registers were open to the inspection of the officials of the Board, that was all the law required. Teachers had always made inquiries after absentees far more numefous than the lists of which the Board complained. It was the anxious desire of the teachers in the district to help the' Board as they had hitherto done in every way possible by ' inquiring after absentees, and sometimes visiting themselves, but they asked the Board to continue to exercise the power they had exercised for the last ten years, because if they did not it would have an ill effect upon the attendance of children at school.—Mr. Axwerrr said he did not think that the Board in giving sanction to this circular could possibly have looked at it in all its bearings. From the tone of the circular it appeared to him that the Board took it ter granted that the teachers were under their immediate control. It was well known that such was not the case. He had had , seven years' experience in Board schools, and he must say , that he had never seen a circular couched in such strong terms, and in such an offensive tone, as the circular the teachers of Runcorn had received. Speaking of the first paragraph, Mr. Annett said it would be in the recollection of the Board that a short time ago there was a strong discussion between the vice-chairman of the late Board (Mr. Simpson) and the clerk with reepect to the power of teachers to recover arrears of fees That the law as laid down by the Clerk was strictly accur- ate the teachers knew, but they regretted that the Clerk should have laid it down in the public manner he did— before that man Skeldon, for instance, for anybody that had any experience of him knew what a perfect adept he was at shirking the responsibilities thrown upon him by the Educa- tion Act. The law, since it had become public property, had had a most prejudicial effect upon the attendance of children at school. Be had had weekly to send home from 30 to 70 boys because they had not brought their fees, and that morning he had sent home six boys who had not paid their fees for the week. Of course this must bring down the average attendance very considerably, and seeing that at the present time the Government grants was based upon the average attendance the teachers were losers by sending home the children in the way they did. He begged to submit on behalf of the teachers and manners of the town that as the Board had laid down the law publicly, it behoved the Board to devise some ways and means whereby these children should be looked up almost immediately they were sent home. It was grievous to see the art that parents displayed in trying to evade the pay- ment of school fees and to keep their children at home.— The CHAIRMAN observed that if there was any apparent dis- courtesy about the circular be could only assure the de- putation that it was far from the wish of the Board, and the. Clerk too, that there should be any discourtesy in their com- munications with the teachers. The quotation in the cir- cular was merely to show the teachers that the Board were in a mess, and could not help themselves Their they laet- tendance officers had not time atm() visit s T ever would, therefore, have to decide t • every ca o ewer.—Mr. Axeurrr said the teachers' atileeT to Sir Francis Sandford bad appeared in the said whether the teachers' reply prints.—The CLERK was adequate or not did not touch the Board's case. Sir Francis Sandford was the secretary to the Education department, and with him the Board had to act. As re- garded the question of making a particular poi public, it Was made public in July 1881, when five judges gave their opinion that it wss competent for a teacher to refuse the ad- mission of any child into school intim the feee were paid.

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL. A special meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon for the purpose of considering the propriety of opposing in Parliament the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. Mr. Meadow- trot: presided and there were present Dr Steele, Messrs Pritchard, F A Lake, P Speakman, P Briscoe, E Timmins, W Whitaker, J Williams, R Shaw, T Norman, and W Brookes (secretary).—Mr SHAW moved that the Commissioners pre- sent a petition in Parliament agaiast the Ship Canal Bill through the law clerk; that the cast of and consequent upon such petition be charged upon the public funds, and that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee be empowered to confer with the Law Clerk during the progress of the peti- tion and take any measures they may deem needful to pro- tect the interests of the town.—Mr Shaw remarked teat the committee were in hopes of coming to a satisfactory ar- rangement with the ship Canal Company on Thursday. It was needful notwithstanding that they should pass that resolution so that they might be able to see that whatever c!tuses they agreed upon were placed in the Btll.—Mr Nola- MAN seconded the motion, which was carried.—This con- cluded the business. RATEPAYERS' MEETING. On Wednesday evening, a meeting of ratepayers convened by requisition, was held in Bethesda schoolroom for the purpose of considering the advisability of opposing the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill, and passing resolutions thereon. There was a good attendance. and Mr. George Moss was unanimously voted to the chair. Amongst those present were Dr McDougall, Messrs. R Shaw, F A Lake, P Speak- rein, H White, J W Lightburn. T Handley, W Littler, M Barker, J Curzon, W II Chadwick, W Stanway, T H Arnett, 1' Unsworth, J Le Gentler, T Watson, P Phillips, J Stubbs, Howard, J Jennion, F Sarnons, H Johnson, J Coolant, Jas J Beveridge, T Riley, and W Brookes (Secretary to the Commissioners.) Mr. R. SHAW described at length the negotiations that up to the present had taken place between the Committee of the Commissioners, and the promoters of the Ship Canal. He indicated the privileges the committee hoped to obtain, and said the promoters had stated they would agree to give the Runcorn people power to make a deep water dock at Run- corn, but they must not make it on land belonging to the Ship Canal Company. However, when the Company had acquired the Bridgewater Navigation Company's property they would be the owners of the whole of the foreshore, and it was quite clear the Runcorn people would not thus be able to make a dock that could be connected with the pres- ent canal. The Commissioners believed that they would obtain the clause they desired, and if they did, it would be of great service to the trade of Runcorn, because they would be able to compete with the Ship Canal, and he be- lieved would be able to hold a considerable portion of the traffic along the present canal, thus benefitting the people of Runcorn. It was necessary that the Commissioners in order to conduct the negotiations to a successful issue, should have powers to oppose the Bill, and these they asked for. The CHAIRMAN said it seemed to him to be a somewhat difficult matter for the ratep tyers of Runcorn to protect a private concern like the Bridgewater Navigation Company. H the chemical works were threatened by an attack, the proprietors of the works would ba the first to protect their own interests: it would not be left to the ratepayers of Run- corn to do. It seemed as if those who ought to be defend- ing the interests of the port had deserted their poets, and the people of Runcorn were in a similar position to what General Graham was when he went to relieve Tokhar. He found that the garrison had fled, and gone over to the enemy, and it seemed as though the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company had sold their interest and gone over to the enemy. (Applause.) It would not work well for Runcorn in the future if the port should be monopolised by another interest. The greatest safeguard for the future of Runcorn was that the Bridgewater canal should remain in the hands of the present Company, who would be compelled to defend the entrances to the port in their own interests. He should Like to ask those who had considered the matter whether it would not be wise to oppose the Ship Canal Company ob- taining powers to purchase the Bridgewater Canal. He thought if they did that they would receive considerable independent support as there was a strong feeling both in and out of Parliament against tne monopolisation of canals. It appeared to him that it would be a great misfortune if the Bridgewater Canal became the property of the Ship Canal Company. Mr. BROOKES read the petition forwarded by the Com- missioners to the House of Commons against the Bill, which stated that it would be in the interests not only of local trade, but the public generally that the Bridgewater Navigation Company's property should be in other hands than those of the promoters of the Bill—should be in the bands of a competing water carriage. The CHAIRMAN said that seemed to provide for what he had been contending for. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN stated that the Bridgewater Navigation Company had petitioned against the preamble of the Bill. There was no doubt the opposition in the Houle of Lords was as strong this year as last. Mr. STANWAY thought it would not be wise for the rate- payers of Runcorn to levy a rate to fight for advantages to the Bridgewater Navigation Company. (Applause.) Mr. Snew said as the Navigation Company were going to sell their property it was to the interest of every ratepayer to try to get as large a quantity of goods transhipped in Runcorn Docks as there was to-day, and more if they could —(hear, hear.)—when the Ship Canal was made. With this object the Commissioners were trying to obtain powers to make a deep watt r dock. (Applause.) Dr. McDonoeu. delivered a lengthy speech, and con- demned the Commissioners for not taking the ratepayers earlier into their confidence. They allowed the matter to go on until there was no possibility 0 receding from the position they had taken They were bound to oppose or they would get nothing at all. If a deep water dock was obtained they were indebted to Mr. Lightburn for ventilating the matter. Last year he got a great deal of cold water thrown upon him for the part he took, but if Runcorn obtained a deep water dock the credit must be given to Mr. Lightburn, for he obstinately stuck to it. Was there any possibility of the matter being arranged without opposing the bill in Parliament, and what would be the probable cost of the affair? Mr. Saaw replied that a deputation was to wait upon the promoters on the following day, and they hoped to be suc- cessful. After some further discussion, in which Messrs. Shaw, T. Handley, Le Coutier, Lightburn, and Lake took part, it was decided with only ose dissentiest to oppose the bill in Par- liament, the costs incurred to be defrayed nut of the general district rate.
------ ---- A vote ot thanks t,o the chairman concluded the meeting.

MAHRIAUB OF Ma. GEOROTGANIELE AT ST. HELENS. The marriage of Mr. G. Gamble, the fourth en of Lieut.-Col. Mary Gamble, St. Helens. with Miss Mar W o James Percival Watts, of Kirtltts, daughter of the Rev. in NnewSamtuarrelkaevt, took nlace in the Parish Church of St. Helen morning last. The ceremony was of a simplesaond possible, private nature. The bride was attended Yfa Per as Miss Gamble and Miss Hannah Gamble, and was given away by s her brother, Mr. Charles Watts. Mr. W. Gamble, brother of the bridngroom, acted as groomsman. There were also present Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble and Mrs. Gamble, Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Gamble, Mr. Win Gamble, and Mr. and Mrs. ,C. J. Bishop. The Rev. Canon Carr officiated. EARLEsTOWN BAPTIST BAND OF HOPE ANEVAL TEA. MEKTIN i G.—The annual tea meeting n connection with the i Baptist Junior Band of Hope was held n the Baptist School, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, when about 50 members sat down to an enjoyable tea. The ladies presi.d- in.; at the tea tables were Mrs. Adams, Mrs. Street, MISS Simond, and Miss Williams, while Mr. W. H. Adams, secre- tary, kad charge ef the arrangenlents, which were carried out in a most satisfactory manner. At the subsequent pro- ceedings there was an increased attendance. Mr. Cooper gave a magic lantern entertainment the subject being "John Ploughman's pictures." The connective readings were given by the Rev. W. C. Taylor. The proceedings were interest- ing, and at the close Mr. Cooper was accorded a hearty vote 421 Wanks.

Let them have high-born and Godly principles, and express them by their acts and speech, and they would wipe out their national disgrace. (Applause.) Mr. M. JoNics next addressed the meeting, and advocated total abstinence for the people and prohibition for the State. If he had his way he would that night shut up every existing public-house, and the country would be much the better for it on the morrow. They could not, however, do that at once, but he believed the day was fast coming. If they could not get all that they wanted, they would take what they could get. They must keep pegging away at that prohibition question, and if .tlaey could not get all that they required, they might accept what they could get. ("Hear, hear," and laughter.) In further observations the speaker referred to Sir Wilfrid Lawson's Local Option mea- sure, with which he expressed himself entirely in favour Total abstinence benefited the people domestically, phy- sically, and religiously, and lie hoped they would do their utmost in helping on those principles he had mentioned. Mr. SCOTT, in his address, said he took it that they were not met there that night to denounce the poor drunkard, neither were they, if he understood his positron aright, to declaim against the drunkard makers. Unless he had made a great mistake, they were there for the express purpose of attacking and doing what they could to destroy not only one of their recognised but legalised institutions of this country. Their object was to endeavour to do what they could to destroy the liquor traffic, and they proposed to do it first by taking the drink from the people as soon as they could, and inducing the people to leave it. The question suggested itself as to the right they had to attack an institution in each a way. Mr. Lowe had stated that the liqaor trade was as legitimate as any other. If Mr. Lowe was right they (the teetotalers) were wrong, and they had no right to attack that trade as they did and harass those engaged in the trade in the way they had done or were doing that night The good Old Book told them that they should know the tree by its fruits. If they looked at this tree they would find it was barren. Barren, did he say? Did it not bring forth the most horrible disease, crime, destitution, and death? But there was:a cry ringing out from John o' Groats to Land's End, and he hoped those present would swell the voice appealing to the country to cut it down. It was illegitimate and immoral and ought to tee destroyed. They demanded prohibition by the will ot the people. Drunken- ness was condemned universally, but he was there to say that drinking in itself was wrong, and the man who had drank even very moderately had taken the first step towards drunkenness. He could sympathise with the poor drunkard. Drink took a hold on the man with a large heart, the highest aspirations and capable of the best and grandest things, and it was upon such that drink hail the most de-' moralising effect. They should give such men the hand of friendship and it would do them more good than a sermon or lecture. If they took him by the hand and balled him "Brother " they would touch a tendei chord and good would accrue. (Hear, hear.) Alcohol was a poison and more than a simple poison—it was a brain poison. Alcohol had se- riously lowered the whole tone of society which was irre- parably worse owing to the drunken habits of the people. in conclusion, he appealed to his hearers to do all they could in supporting temperence principles and gettiag their friends to join the Independent Order of Good Tempters and other such societies. Bev W. MULES and other speakers followed and the meeting was a most succesful one.

WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS: SERMONS 'AND MEETING I AT EARLESTOWN.—The annual sermons in aid of the Home I Mission fund were preached in Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, I Cross-lane, Earlestown, on Sunday last, by the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, resident minister. The annual public meeting was held in the lecture ball beneath the chapel, on Wednes- day evening, when there was a fair attendance. Mr. George Burgess presided, and in opeaing the meeting he said that all who were in the habit of reading the daily and weekly newspapers must be convinced of the necessity for Home Missions.—The Rev. J. M. Fairbourn read the report, which stated that the total income last year was £34,921 Os 7d, and the expenditure £35,203 4s 10d. The St. Helens cir- cuit had contributed the sum of £l2l 88 id. He afterwards proceeded to speak of Home Mission,' in general, pointing Out that people seemed to have more sympathy for and seemed to support Foreign Missions more than Home Mis- sions. But he could not understand that, as the ignorance, degredatien, misery, and wickedness among the people of this country was every bit as bad as that elsewhere.—The ttev. G. Byrom, of Liverpool, gave an excellent and in- teresting account of his labours as a home missionary, and appealed to those present to support such a good and noble cause.—A collection was taken at the close. THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—An entertainment of a very interesting and amusing character was given in the Infant Schoolroom, Eariestown, on Satur- day last, by the members and friends of the above society, which was numerously attended. Taking into considera- tion that it is only about three months since this branch first opened, it has made wonderful strides in the parish. The secret, no doubt, of the success being the broad p'atform or double basis upon which the society is worked, admitting as its members not only those who abstain, but also those who use intoxicating drinks in moderation thereby justly entitling them to the term "Temperance moderation, " in its strict and broadest sense. The Rev. W. Chaplin, of St. Helens, was announced to preside, but having missed his train, the Rev. H. E. Smith, curate, opened the proceedings in his usual interesting way. The following programme was very ably rendered, but, owing to the numerous encores, the proceedings did not close until about 10 o'clock, although they commenced at a quarter-past seven. Song, "Mother- in-law," by Mr. J. Gorse, and for an encore, "The Picnic Party ;" song, " List, 'tis music stealing," by Miss Jones; song. " Mldshipmite' " Mr. W. Atkin; pianoforte duet, "The Opera Box," by the Misses Walton, encored. Mr. Chaplin having by this time made his appearance, gave a short, but practical address, in which he showed the advan- tages of the double platform, and made an earnest appeal to all those who are truly anxious to leave the world a little better than they found it to join the society in one section or the other, for although they might not be able to see their way clear to become total abstainers, they could snug help to check intemperance by being themselves strictly tem- perate in all things, thereby setting a good example to their weaker brethren. The first part closed with a humorous sketch, entitled "The Village Rivals," which was very ably given by Messrs. Simm, G. Makin, jun., E. Kenyon, G. E. Jackson, J. H. Boardman, and Miss Shaw. The second part opened with a sketch, entitled, "Wanted a, servant," by Messrs. Gorse and Atkin, causing screams of laughter. Then followed a song, "Down by the gate," by Miss Walton; encore, "The vacant chair.' Song, "The hungry army," by Mr. J. Gorse; encore, "Doctor Squill." Song," He wipes the tear from every eye," by Miss Both- well, was decidedly the best song of the evening, being very sweetly sung; and when recalled she gave "In the gloaming." Duet, "The upper ten and lower five," by Messrs. Gorse and Atkin, caused endless fun. The enter- tainnaent terminated with a nigger sketch, " The black doctor," by Messrs. W. Turner, J. H. Boardman, and J. Millington. The accompanists for the evening were the I Misses Walton and Birks, and Mr. T. Martindale. A vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. Boughton, and seconded by Mr. Makin, brought to a close a truly happy evening's entertainment.
Mr. Brighouse, coroner for the West Derby Division of the county, has appointed Mr. T. Husband, of Widnes, to be his deputy.

THE ALARMING STREET ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON. DEATH OF MRS. HALL: THE INQUEST. Last week we gave p uticulareof an accident which befel Mrs. Hall( a relation of Councillor Monks), 33, Liverpool-rd. who was driven over by a horse and cart in the charge of a young fellow named Kean, in the employ of Mr. Lawless, fishmonger, and sus abed serious injuries, which we regret to state culminated fatally on' Saturday afternoon last. Mrs. Hall was 73 years of age, and it was uot expected from the first that she would recover. The driver, Kean, was brought before the magistrates on Friday in last week, when the charge of furious driving preferred against him was dis- missed. The inquest on the body of Mrs. Hall was opened at the White Hart, Sankey-street, on Monday at noon, before the coroner (S. Brighouse, Esq.) Mr. Percy Davies watched the case on behalf of Kies, the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) and Mr. Thomas Hall, son of the deceased, being also present. At the outset the Coroner pointed out that the jury would have to consider whether the young fellow who drove the cart was guilty of the act accid.ntally or through culpable negligence. If they thought the occurrence was purely ac- cidental, then, of course, it would be their duty to'find a verdict of Accidental death."—Thom is Hall, the H‘llly, Liverpool-road, iron manufacturer, said the deceased was his mother, who was 73 years of age at the time of her death. He saw deceased the day after the accident, but she could not tell anything as to the cause which led to her injuries. He had asked her whether she knew what had hurt her, when she replied No."—ln reply to Mr. Davies, witness said his mother recovered coneeiduaneili On Wednesday. The inquiry before the magistrates was on Friday, when the woman was dying.—Mr. Davies: What , authority have you to say that the woman was dying ? Witness : My own. Mr. Davies : Not the authority of the doctor ? Witness : Most decidedly.—Dr. Richmond said that on the Sunday he re- ferred to that it was impossible that she could live.—This being the witness's evidence in chief, the Coroner intimated that the witness could make the remarks he wished in the first instance.—The witness said he wished to call attention to what he would term the on. usual and unprecedented Procedure of the magistrates at the Borough Court on the previous Friday. It was cus- tomary to give the relatives of the suffering person notice when the trial would come on, and to adjourn such trial until the injured person was pronounced out of danger. Not only himself but many people thought that by the action of the Warrington magistrates there had been undue haste in terminating the trial at the Borough Court.—Mr. Davies wished to point out to the jury that whatever the police had done as regarded calling the summons when they did the accused (his client) had nothing to do with.—The Cormaer said he was quite sure the jury understood their duty; they would not take notice of the magisterial pro- ceedings.—Mr. Hall observed that it was thought the Coroner's hands might be tied by the action of the magistrates.—The Coroner ; Nothing ties my hands or the hands of the jury. The jury are here to find a verdict en the facts. Whatever the magistrates have done, legally we are not supposed to knew their proceedings. I suppose, however, that the jury do know; but I feel cer- tain from what I have said the jury will take out of their minds that knowledge, and not nee it in this room.—The next witness was Elizabeth Harrison, wife of Amos Harri- son, labourer, 116, Liverpool-road, who deposed that on Saturday morning, the 23rd ult., she met the deceased at the Bon Marche in Sankey ztreet, and they walked to the corner of Parker-street. a there been no horse and cart coming they would have both crossed to the gas lamp. They left the pavement together, and got about if t. when they observed a Ish cart and horse coming down Sankey-street towards the station. Witness ran across to the gas lamp, and on turning roand saw deceased about 2fl. from tha pavement, and a little lower than the spot where they started to go across. The horse and cart, she thought, came rather too fast. She did not bear the driver call oat, but she was rather ded in the left ear. Deceased was knocked down, and subsequently conveyed to the In- firmary. They were about two yards down Parker-street when they attempted to cross. In reply to Mr. Davies, witness said she was eight yards from the deceased when the latter was knocked down.—At the conclusion of this evidence the Coroner intimated that he would ad- journ the inquiry. He then referred to a hard and fast line which he said he had laid down—viz., that whatever interest s were concerned should be represented by solicitors. Alluding to the presence of Mr. Thomas Hall there that day he had no objection to the latter watching the case in the interests of the family, but if he wished to examine the witnesses he must do so through the intervention of a solicitor or barrister. He would adhere strongly to that rule not to allow a non-professional man to represent in- terests. He was lately holding an inquest on the body of a man who was drowned in a canal belonging to the L. and N.-W. Railway Company. At that inquest a man named Shaw, the inspector of the canal, came into the room and said he was sent by the railway company to represent their interests and watch over the inquiry, but he (the Coroner) refused to hear him, and so he should any interests which were not represented in the coroner's, as in other courts, by a solicitor or barrister. He :would adjourn the inquest to Monday next partly for this purpose, and that additional evidence might be adduced. REFERENCES AT THE BOROUGH COURT. Upon the Magistrates taking their seats at the Warrington Boroagh Police Court, yesterday morning, Mr J White said that with respect to a case that had recently been before the Bench, in which a boy was charged with furious driving, he had seen remarks in the papers to the effect that the case was unduly hurried over, and that it should have been adjeurned until after the inquest upon the death of a lady who had been run over in the street had taken place. That statement, he thought, should not go forth to the public without some comment being passed upon it. The boy was not charged with having run over Mrs Hall, who unfortun- ately died afterwards, but he was simply charged with being guilty of furious driving. On that charge there was really no evidence upon which to commit, and what evi- dence there was was of a contradictory character. All the evidence that it was possible to procure was brought for- ward at the time and nothing else could be done in the matter. In regard to the charge of furious driving he thought that there was not sufficient evidence to commit upon. The remarks that had been made might convey a wrong impression to the public, and it should be understood that the charge was simply one of driving furiously, and that there was not sufficient evidence to warrant a commital or an adjournment of the case.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. R. B. White) said there was nothing to adjourn the I case for.—Captain Reynolds said that the case was a long one and that it was most deliberately gone through. He did not think that there was evidence sufficient to support the charge of furious driving.—The Chief Constable (Mr. S. Hunt) gave an explanation as to how the case came into court. It occurred, he said, in this way. The offence was committed—if there was an offence—last Saturday but one. In the usual course of things the defendant would have been summoned for last Monday, but on making en- quiries on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday Mrs. Hall was found to be better, and on the Wednesday morning she was decidedly better. It was thought that if it was a case of furious driving in the streets, and that if that offence had been committed, the sooner it was made known and the re- sult declared, the better, and the summons was taken a little out of the ordinary course so that the case might appear in the newspapers on Saturday. From the statement made by the persons who gave evidence last Friday, he thought with- out a doubt that there would be a conviction. He honestly brought forward persons to give their evidence, but he must say that they did not bear out before the emit the state- ments they made on the Sunday morn;ng, which were taken in writing. Their worships thought there was a doubt about the case, and gave him (the defendant) the benefit of it. He did not see why they should have to wait for a person to die before they could put him into court for an offence committed in that way in the street.—Captain Reynolds said that supposing that the woman had, died when the evidence was brought before the court, he should hnve given precisely the same verdict ts that which had been given. The charge was one of furious driving. There was a doubt about the case, and they gave the defen- dant the benefit of it, at the same time cautioning him. There wan too much furious driving in Warrington, but he was sure that the defendant in this case was not driving faster than many others did in Warrington.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hint) said that according to the evidence given at the inquest, the defendant was forty yards Away from Mrs. Hall when she turned again towards the footpath; otherwise she would have been safe.—The subject then idropped.

UNJUST SCALES.—At the Prescot Police Court, 012 Tuts. day, Charles Milner, vendor of American meat in Cyril. street, Prescot, was charged with having had unjust scales in his possession for use in trade.—Superintendent Barker said that on the 23rd ult he visited defendant's shop, and on examining the scales in question found them half an ounce out of balance against the purchaser. Mr. Milner sold beef and mutton in quantities so small as a quarter of a pound and purchasers of these quantities would all get half an ounce less than they should have, and the defen- dant would get the benefit of this. He (Superintendent Barker) cowl(' tit a very bad case. In answer to the Bench, Mr. nrker said the defendant belonged to Liver- pool and had only had a shop in Present for about two mentha.—A fine of 405 and I2s costs was imposed, or, in default, one month's imprisonment. THE SHOCKING DEATH OB A COLLIER AT ST. HELENS —An inquest was held last Friday morning by Mr. Brig., house, at the Sefton Arrns.3T. Helens, as to the death of the collier, William Burrows, who lives off College-street, St. Helens, and whose death under such shocking circum- stances we narrated last week. Evidence was given by three of the deceased workfellows—James Pickering, George Mawdsley, and James Ashton. Deceased had been working on the afternoon of the Monday previous at Sutton Heath Colliery cutting an air-road, when a small quantity of dirt fell upon him. He immediately attempted to get away from the place, but as he was doing so a heavy atone, weighing five or six tons, fell upon and crushed him. Strenuous efforts were at once made to lift the stone away, but this could not be done for about a couple of hours. Deceased was fearfully naangled,one of his arms being nearly mat off, and his feet also being badly maimed. He was not quite dead when reigned, but died on his removal up the shaft. The witnesses agreed in saying that to all appearance de- ceased's working placo was quite secure when ho went into it in the morning.—A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.—The Coroner then stated that Her Majesty's inspector of mines for the district had examined the spot, and was also of opinion that the accident neuld not have been prevented.
LATEST NEWS.
Last night's Gazette announces Sir Harry Parkes, British minister at Pekin, has also been appointed minister to Corea.
The Globe learns that the difficulties attending the ful- filling of the resolution of Parliament regarding cheap tele- grams ha—e rendered the prospect of a reduction more remote than ever.

COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR BRADFORD: 100 MEN ENTOMBED.—FIYe colliers were badly injured by an explo- sion of gas at the Bowling Iron Company's coal pit at Hians- worth, near Bradford, yesterday. One hundred were in the pit at the time, but all were got out safely. THE RisPILESENTATION OF SOUTH DERBYSHIRE. Sir Henry Wilmot, M.P. for South Deibyshire, yesterday in- formed a meeting of his constituents that he should retire at the general election. The Hon. George Carzon and Mr I Fitz Harbert Wright were adopted as Conservative candi- dates.

BOARD OD TRADE RETURNS.—The Board of Trade Returns issued yesterday show that the imports for Feb- ruary decreased £289,095,and the exports increased £627,567 as compared with the same month last year. Far the first two months of the year the imports decreased £380,720 and the exports decreased £628,551 compared with the similar period of 1883..

A BURGLAR'S BMOKINO PARTY.—B was discovered yes- terday morning that a tobacco manufactory in Easy-row, Birmingham, had been broken into. The burglars appear to have been in possession the whole of the night, and to have held a smoking party. Nearly all the different brands of cigars had been tasted, and the place was literally covered with cigar ends. Strange to say the burglars carried away the most worthless goods.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. Earl DELAWARE gave notice for the production of papers and correspondence relating to Malta.—Earl GRAIN VILLE, replying to Lord Leamington, said consular capitulations had not been abolished in Tunis. British subjects in Tunis were satisfied with living under French jurisdiction. Eng- land had, however, reserved all treaty rights, and all the great Powers had agreed to the principle of international tribunals in the regency.—The Speaker's Retirement Bill was read a first time. HOUSE OF COMMONS. METROPOLITAN BOARD OF WORKS BILL.—Sir J. HOGG moved the second reading of the Metropolitan Board of Works Various Powers Bill.—Sir S. WATERLOW objected to the Bill, as it interfered with the provisions of the Bill passed last session to provide dwellings for the labouring classes.—After a discussion, the Bill was read a second time.—Mr. LYULPII STANLEY moved it be an instruction to the committee not to permit any diminutions of accommoda- tion now required by the Artisans' Dwellings At for pro- viding dwellings for the labouring class, and this was agreed to. GRAND COMMITTEES.—The names of members appointed to serve on the Grand Committees was brought up.—Mr. SEXTON gave notice on an early date to call attention to the constitution of the Grand Committees, and to move a re- solution. HONE Lassos.—Mr. MUNDELLA, replying to Mr. Tal- bot, said no general instructions could be issued for pre- venting home lessons being given to children in Board schools. The subject was under consideration. THE SOUDAN.—Lord HARTINGTON said the highest au- thority had been consulted as to sending horse artillery to accompany General Graham's force. Great difficulty would have been encountered had such been sent owing to want of water for horses and the difficulty of camel transport. General Graham's small force had been adequately furnished with artillery. Replying to Sir O. Campbell, the noble Lord said he was not prepared to disapprove of the procla- mations issued by Admiral Hewitt and General Graham to Osman Digna's followers, although it was drawn up in Oriental style. GIBRALTAR AND SPAIN.—Mr GLADSTONE said no Com- munications had passed regarding seceding Gibraltar to Spain. THE EFFICIENCY OF THE SERVICE.—Dr. CAMERON called attention to the cruelty, waste of money, and danger to the British arms the recent campaign caused, by the defective organisation of the Indian and British transport and corn- missariat services, and moved that a select committee be appointed to inquire into the working of the transport and commissariat services of the British and Indian armies in the recent Egyptian and Afghan campaigns, and to con- sider what changes, if any, were required to secure increased efficiency in these services.—Mr. PULESTONE seconded the motion for a select committee, and expressed surprise that there should ba any opposition to the proposal in fans of the mistakes and blunders that had occurred in conveying necessary supplies to our forces on active service.—Mr. J. K. Cnoss admitted that during the first period of the Afghan war the transport and commissariat services were ' defective; but with regard to the second period of the war, matters had greatly improved. The Indian Government had taken efficient steps to bring about still further im- provements, and as those exertions were being continued, he thought the committee unnecessary.—Col. HORNE and Mr. Connurr supported the motion for a select committee.— Sir H. Vitamin/ said that notwithstanding 'large sums for army service were continually spent when war broke out, we were always unprepared. He supported the motion.— Mr. BRAND did not think the transport aervics was in the disorganised condition that had been represented. Much WAS to be attributed to the climate of Egypt as regarded the 3 sufferings of horses and ulea, and•with regard to the cora- -1 miseiart, considering the enormous amount of stores sent ' out very few mistakes occurred. As the committee was to confine its enquiry to the late Egyptian war and the trans- ' port and commissiarat services the Government would not ILEFT SITTING.]

div.head: EM PLOYE RS AND THEIR APPRENTICES. WARRINGTON APPRENTICES SUMMONED.
div.p: EM PLOYE RS AND THEIR APPRENTICES. WARRINGTON APPRENTICES SUMMONED.

At the Warrington Police Court yesterday morninz, be- fore Captain Reynolds (in the chair), an.l Mr. John White, two youths named Joseph Bennion and Joseph Maybury, apprentices employed at the White Cross Wire Works, ap- peared to answer summonses taken out by the company against them, claiming the sum of 55., as damages sustained by then by reason of the defendants having absented them- selves from work unlawfully and without sufficient excuse; the plaintiff company also asked that an order might be made upon the defendants to adhere to their contracts—Mr. W. H. Brook (town clerk), who appeared for the company, said that the contract between the defendants and the com- pany was entered into in the one case in 1880, and in the other case its 1812. The case was a very simple one. On Shrove-Tuesday last the two apprentices Bennion and Maybury, and eleven others, applied for permission to spend the afternoon off work. They could not be spared, however, but notwithstanding that they absented themselves. Next day the manager, Mr. Birchall, fined the defendants, according to custom, 1s each, but he told them that if they would come to their work he would remit the fine when he settled up their wages. The remainder of the apprentices who had absented themselves came back to work, but the defendants did not. There was plenty of work for them to do, and therefore there was no excuse for their absence.—Mr. Davies appeared for the de- fendants, and said he thought that he could prove that they did go back to work.—Mr. Birchall, the manager, was then called to support the statement of Mr. Brook.—Mr. Davies put in the objection that the indentures were not binding, and that there was merely an agreement betweea the parties.—The Magistrates' Clerk: It is a con- tract of appprenticeship, which is all that is required.—ln answer to Mr. Davies Mr. Birehall said that it was the cus- torn of the trade to deduct from the wages of the appren- tices who where on piece•work a certain amount for gas.— Mr. Brook said that they did not care about the claim for compensation ; what they wanted was an order for the de— fendants to return to work.—The Chairman said that if Mr. Davies would acknowledge the correctness of the indentures the defendants must go back to work, and if Mr. Brook waived the claim of 58 there was nothing before the Bench.—Mr. Davies: I submit that the indentures are not binding.—The Magistrates' Clerk thought that they were binding.—The Chairman thought that it would he wasting time to go on with the case, as, it the indentures were binding, the defendants 'must return to work.—Mr. Davies said that the boys had never had any complaints made against them by the company before, in whose employ they had been a considerable number of years, which showed that they were good workmen. On the Tuesday in question the apprentices in other works had a half-holiday, and he believed it was the custom for the apprentices to be allowed half-holidays four times in the year. He did not, however, think that the managers could say that the defendants had four in the year. He referred to the boys having been fined for their absence and charged for gas.—The Chairmen: Is that a custom of the trade ?—Mr Davies: A custom of the trade cannot affect the indentures. —Mr crook: It is a decided thing.—Tbe Chairman thought that perhaps the shilling should not have been deducted.— The defendant Maybury was put in the witness box, and said that Mr Birchen promised to give them, the shilling back, but when they went for it the next day he would net pay it them, but said he would do so the next Wednesday.—The Bench held that the contract was binding and granted orders for the return of the defendants to their work, making no order as to costs.—The case created con- siderable interest, and the Court was crowded.

THE ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A FRIENDLY SOCIETY'S SECRE- TARY AT PRESCOT.

div.head: COMMITTAL OF PRISONER.
div.p: COMMITTAL OF PRISONER.

At the Prescot Police Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Bo w- stead, till recently secretary of the Loyal Victoria (Prescot) Lodge of Oddfellows, was again charged on remand with having embezzled monies, the property of the lodge—Mr. Mackenzie prosecuted on behalf of the trustees of the lodge. From his statement it appeared that the prisoner was 0' pointed secretary to the lodge in 1889, and continued secre tary till 1883, at the annual salary of f.l3‘. One of his duties was to keep a correct account of the receipts and expel" diture of the lodge. He (Mr. Mackenzie) would prove that at the end of 1882' the prisoner, in accordance with his duties, rendered an account which was found to be substeh: tially correct, but that when a further investigation to" place at the end of 1883 it was discovered that during 18e the prisoner had received certain sums which he had neither entered in the books kept for the purpose, nor entered in the account rendered to the members of the society. BO the rules of the Manchester Unity members who removed te other districts were enabled to pay their contributions into the lodges in those districts, and it would be proved that several members of the Prescot lodge had lived at a dista.nee away and had paid certain amounts into lodges in various parts of the country, ond that the secretaries of those lodges had periodically remitted amounts to the prisoner which,how- ever, he had not accounted for. In consequence of the nem- ber of remittances and the distance of many of the towns.lis (Mr. Mackenzie) had not been able to get all the informattr that would be required to support certain cases, five or MT in number, and he would that day simply proceed with en! , of the cases in which a remittance had been made, mr ' another case in which a certain contribution bad been paid on a card. He would then ask that the prisoner be coin— mitted for trial.—Several witnesses were then called when evidence went to show that three sums of £1 6A., xr £1 9s. 3d. respectively, had been forwarded to the prisoner by the secretary of the " Birch " Lodge of Oddfellowe, 8!. Helens, and had not been accounted for by him.—The pfl Boner was then committed for trial without bail, it being al' timated that charges relating to money sent from Man; ohester, Runcorn, and COventry would then be preferreu against him.
